reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The current ablation study only verifies the number of branches in the dual-branch gating design. It does not isolate several other key design choices, including GGR itself, the concatenation of global context, the signal loss, the entropy loss, and the change from routing based on raw inputs to routing based on expert outputs. 2.Since the method introduces four experts, dual-branch gating, global-guided routing, and bidirectional alternating encoding, the paper should also compare its parameter count, training time, and inference cost against MoME (or relevant MoE-style baseline). 3.The novelty appears to be more of a structural modification to the routing mechanism of existing MoME models rather than a paradigm-level innovation. 4.The central claim of the paper is that expert outputs are less exposed to noise than raw inputs, and therefore produce more robust routing. The proposed two-stage design is intuitive, well-structured. 2.Evaluations on three standard TCGA datasets (i.e., BLCA, LUAD, UCEC) using 5-fold cross-validation show consistent and substantial C-index improvements over 11 SOTA methods. 3.The paper is overall well-written and easy to follow.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The proposed method primarily represents an engineering enhancement of the existing MoME framework, achieved by splitting routing stages and incorporating dual-branch and global guidance mechanisms, resulting in limited conceptual novelty. 2.The choice of exactly four fusion experts is not sufficiently justified. author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their time and thoughtful feedback. We deeply appreciate the constructive comments, which help us improve the quality of this work. Below, we clarify several aspects that the reviewers have raised concerns about. Novelty. We would like to clarify that the contribution of this work goes beyond a combination of existing approaches. We identify a systematic vulnerability in existing MoE-based methods that has not been explicitly addressed: routing weights computed directly from noisy inputs lead to expert weight misallocation and degraded prediction stability. We tackle it by decoupling routing into two stages — gating, which extracts routing signals from expert outputs to avoid direct noise exposure, and routing, which integrates these signals with global representations to compute stable expert weights — with DBG and GGR as their concrete instantiations. We have further elaborated on this distinction in the revised manuscript to make the conceptual contribution more explicit. Ablation Study Coverage. We would like to clarify that Table 2 does isolate the contribution of key components. The no-branch configuration retains GGR but removes DBG entirely, isolating GGR’s contribution alone (0.680/0.685/0.702 on BLCA/LUAD/UCEC). The single-branch variants isolate each branch’s individual contribution, and the full dual-branch model combines both. This progression jointly validates: (1) GGR alone improves over standard input-based routing; (2) DBG provides substantial additional gains on top of GGR; and (3) dual-branch generation consistently outperforms either branch in isolation. We have added a more explicit clarification of this in the paper to avoid potential misunderstanding. Computational Cost. DualGGR-MoME introduces modest overhead relative to MoME. On BLCA: parameters increase from 22.26M to 26.50M, training time from 13.6h to 14.1h, and inference time from 0.020s to 0.021s. All additional parameters are confined to the four routing modules, leaving the shared backbone unchanged. Given C-index improvements of 3.98%/5.08%/2.57% on BLCA/LUAD/UCEC and negligible inference overhead, we consider this a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. We have included these efficiency metrics in the revised manuscript for completeness. Theoretical Justification for Noise Robustness of Expert Outputs. Expert networks inherently attenuate input noise through three mechanisms: (1) RMSNorm normalizes feature magnitudes, reducing sensitivity to scale variations from additive noise; (2) GELU suppresses extreme responses to corrupted inputs; (3) global average pooling aggregates across the full sequence, averaging out localized perturbations. Acting in composition, these operations make expert outputs systematically less sensitive to input noise than raw encoded features. DBG extracts routing signals from these attenuated outputs, and GGR further stabilizes weight computation via global sample representations. Empirically, Fig. 3 provides direct evidence across three datasets, three noise types, and both modalities, consistently showing that DualGGR-MoME maintains stable risk predictions while MoME’s shift sharply as noise intensifies, constituting solid support for the central claim. We will incorporate this theoretical analysis into the final version of the paper. Number of Fusion Experts and Kaplan-Meier Curves. Both analyses were conducted but could not be included due to MICCAI’s strict page limit. The four-expert configuration was found to be optimal, and KM curve analysis confirms that DualGGR-MoME achieves better patient risk stratification than MoME across all three datasets. Presentation. We acknowledge that Figs. 1 and 2 are dense and will improve their layout in the final version. We once again thank all reviewers for their valuable time and feedback.

title: Enhancing Pathological VLMs with Cross-scale Reasoning
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The study introduces a novel cross scale reasoning paradigm that mirrors clinical pathology by requiring models to connect global tissue patterns with fine cellular details across different zoom levels. This approach is significant because it moves beyond simple image classification and forces the AI to learn the hierarchical logic pathologists use to verify architectural suspicions with high power visual evidence. By framing diagnosis as a coordinated process across scales the work addresses a major limitation in existing models that often struggle with tasks requiring multi view verification. 2.The researchers developed a leakage aware curation pipeline that uses adversarial screening to stop models from cheating through text only shortcuts. By employing multiple language models as adversaries to identify questions solvable without images the authors ensured that the SCALE-VQA benchmark reflects true visual reasoning. This rigorous data strategy is interesting because it addresses a widespread problem in vision language modeling where high accuracy often stems from linguistic biases rather than actual image understanding. 3.The model utilizes reinforcement learning through group relative policy optimization to achieve superior generalization and state of the art performance on both multi scale and single scale benchmarks. Unlike standard supervised fine tuning which can lead to catastrophic forgetting of original representations this reinforcement learning approach allows the model to discover optimal decision rules from outcome based rewards. This demonstrates a highly efficient way to build medical experts that remain robust across different diagnostic settings even when trained on a relatively small amount of high quality data.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The training dataset relies on a very small scale of 177 whole slide images. While the authors curated 4685 questions from this set the limited number of underlying source images restricts the diversity of pathological patterns the model encounters. This small scale limits the generalizability of the model to rare diseases or varying tissue preparations found in broader clinical practice compared to models trained on tens of thousands of slides. 2.The methodological approach lacks algorithmic novelty because the reinforcement learning optimization relies entirely on existing techniques. The authors use Group Relative Policy Optimization to train their model. This specific reinforcement learning method is an established algorithm previously introduced in other foundation model works. The primary technical contribution is applying this existing optimization method to a newly curated medical dataset rather than proposing a fundamentally new model architecture. 3.The evaluation is restricted to multiple choice visual question answering benchmarks which does not fully demonstrate true clinical feasibility. While the model is evaluated on the SCALE VQA and PathMMU datasets answering structured questions is far removed from real world diagnostic workflows. There is no evaluation showing how this model integrates into an actual clinical setting or whether it improves the diagnostic speed and accuracy of human pathologists working on open ended complex cases.

author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for the insightful feedback and will address main concerns below [1] Dataset scale (R1, R3): We acknowledge the limited scale and will avoid broad generalization claims. We’re actively scaling to include more WSIs, organs, and pathological patterns. Beyond the dataset, our contribution includes a reproducible, leakage-aware curation pipeline for visually grounded cross-scale patho VQA, which was appreciated as a “rigorous” strategy (R1) that “other benchmark papers should adopt” (R3). We’ll open-source Scale-VQA and the curation pipeline to benefit the community to build larger datasets. Also, our results suggest that a small but high-quality, outcome-verifiable cross-scale data can provide effective RL signals for patho VLM, consistent with recent evidence [a]. For WSI-level separation, multi-scale views and QA derived from the same WSI stay in the same split to avoid leakage [2] PathCLS regression (R3): PathCLS is converted from classification datasets into MCQs, whereas other PathMMU subsets are built from image-text sources with morphology-focused descriptions. Thus, PathCLS is closer to single-image category recognition, while the others more align w/ descriptive, evidence-grounded reasoning. Since our RL objective emphasizes cross-scale evidence integration, fine-tuning may shift the model away from some label-centric priors learned by Patho-R1, causing a trade-off on this subset, while improving other evidence-oriented subsets and overall PathMMU [3] GPT5.2 circularity (R3): We acknowledge the concern. To clarify, GPT-5.2 was used in text-based construction stage to draft candidate MCQs from cross-scale captions; its outputs weren’t directly accepted as final QA. The benchmark was finalized through leakage-aware screening and pathologist verification of visual support, answer correctness, and distractor plausibility. While GPT-5.2 may have advantages in text-based analysis, eval on our final pathologist-verified questions requires cross-scale visual evidence integration and image-text alignment ability. As shown in Tab.1, GPT has 58.51% ACC on Scale-VQA, far below ScaleReasoner-R1(82.89), suggesting that the commercial VLMs may rely on textual priors in med-VQA, and hence struggle with the cross-scale grounded visual reasoning required by our bench. This is also consistent with existing literature [b] [4] Reward weight (R3): We apologize for a notation error: answer correctness weight is 0.8, format is 0.2.As Patho-R1 already exhibits instruction-following ability, the format reward regularizes malformed outputs, while the dominant acc reward drives cross-scale reasoning improvement. We’ll correct the formula and add justification [5] Ablation&Comparisons&Stats(R2): Ablations on key pipeline components: (i)after leakage screening, text-only adversary ACC (%) drops to 32.8 (Qwen3Max) and 29.5 (Gemini3Pro), close to chance (25%), confirming shortcut suppression; (ii) Avg across 4 models and 5 dimensions, dropping 1 view reduces ACC (%) by 3.8, dropping 2 by 8.5, text-only by 17.8, confirming multi-scale dependency. Our experiments already include representative 7B medical VLMs for a fair same-param comparison in Tab.1-2.For stats significance, ScaleReasoner-R1 achieves 82.89 ACC, CI [80.43, 85.09], vs. Gemini (2nd best) at 60.90, CI [57.84, 63.87]. McNemar’s test confirms significance (χ² = 141.11, p < 0.001) across all dimensions [6] Clinical feasibility & novelty (R1): We agree that MCQ eval doesn’t fully demonstrate real-world feasibility. Our clinical involvement lies in expert annotation/validation, and Scale-VQA is positioned as a controlled benchmark for cross-scale visual integration. We also clarify that our novelty is not GRPO, but the clinically grounded cross-scale reasoning formulation&curation pipeline that makes outcome-based RL meaningful for patho VLMs. [a] Wang et al.RL for Reasoning in LLMs with One Training Example [b] Asadi et al. meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a clinically motivated cross-scale pathology VQA benchmark and training paradigm that addresses an important limitation of current pathology VLMs, which typically operate on isolated single-scale images despite pathologists routinely integrating evidence across magnifications. The Scale-VQA benchmark, pathologist-guided annotation process, and leakage-aware curation pipeline are meaningful contributions, and the reported performance of ScaleReasoner-R1 on the proposed benchmark is strong. The finding that cross-scale supervision transfers to overall PathMMU performance is also interesting. The main concerns are about interpretation and scope. The benchmark is built from a relatively small number of WSIs, so the generalization claims should be framed carefully. The authors should clarify in rebuttal how WSI-level separation was maintained, how GPT-5.2 was used during data/question construction relative to its role as an evaluated baseline, and how to interpret the observed regression on the PathCLS subset compared with Patho-R1.The rebuttal should also clarify the choice of the RL reward weighting and the extent to which leakage-aware screening was independent of the final evaluated models. | I recommend acceptance. The rebuttal addressed the main concerns by clarifying that multi-scale views and QA from the same WSI are kept in the same split to avoid leakage, that GPT-5.2 was used only to draft candidate MCQs from text captions before leakage screening and pathologist verification with its final Scale-VQA accuracy of 58.51% well below ScaleReasoner-R1 at 82.89%, that the PathCLS regression reflects a trade-off between cross-scale evidence integration and label-centric priors, and that the reward weighting is 0.8 for correctness and 0.2 for format with a notation error acknowledged. Additional clarifications on leakage-screening independence (text-only adversary accuracy near chance), multi-scale dependency, and McNemar significance testing (p<0.001) addressed R2 and R3’s points, leading R1 and R3 to maintain their positive recommendations. R2 lowered the score to Reject, citing evaluation and model-comparison concerns, and the small dataset size of 177 WSIs remains a limitation. Still, these are framing-level issues that cannot be expanded under the MICCAI rebuttal policy. The leakage-aware curation pipeline and cross-scale reasoning formulation are recognized as meaningful contributions to the community. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper introduces a cross-scale training and evaluation paradigm for pathology vision-language models. The main contributions are SCALE-VQA, a curated benchmark of multiple-choice questions grounded in pathology images across different magnifications, and SCALEREASONER-R1, a reinforcement-learning-trained model intended to improve cross-scale pathological reasoning by linking global tissue patterns with fine cellular details. The initial reviews were uniformly but weakly positive, with scores of 4 / 4 / 4.Reviewers appreciated the importance of cross-scale reasoning in pathology, the attempt to mimic pathologists’ diagnostic workflow, the leakage-aware curation strategy, and the potential value of SCALE-VQA as a community benchmark. The main concerns were the limited dataset size, possible data leakage or circularity in the data construction and evaluation pipeline, the small number of WSIs, insufficient validation of whether the benchmark truly requires visual cross-scale reasoning rather than exploiting textual or linguistic shortcuts, unclear PathCLS regression, limited statistical testing, and limited comparison to broader VLM baselines. The rebuttal addressed several key concerns. The authors acknowledged the limited dataset scale and agreed to avoid broad generalization claims. They clarified the leakage-aware curation pipeline, stating that QA pairs from the same WSI remain in the same split to avoid leakage. They also explained the PathCLS regression as a trade-off caused by shifting the model toward cross-scale evidence integration rather than single-image category recognition. In response to concerns about GPT-based circularity, they stated that GPT outputs were used as draft candidate MCQs but not directly accepted as final QA, and that the benchmark was finalized through leakage-aware screening and pathologist verification. The rebuttal also clarified the reward-weight notation and summarized ablation and comparison evidence supporting multi-scale dependency. Some concerns remain. The dataset is still relatively small, and the evaluation remains limited compared with the breadth of claims about pathology VLM reasoning. Some reviewers remained concerned about the benchmark construction process, possible residual leakage/circularity, and whether the task fully distinguishes visual reasoning from language priors. The final version should clearly describe the dataset construction pipeline, leakage-control steps, GPT-assisted generation and human verification process, statistical testing, and the limitations of the benchmark scale. After rebuttal, the reviewer opinions are A / R / A. Reviewer 1 recommended accept, stating that the major concerns regarding dataset leakage and evaluation bias were partially resolved. Reviewer 2 moved to reject, remaining dissatisfied with the evaluation methods and model comparisons. Reviewer 3 recommended accept and viewed the leakage-aware curation and cross-scale reasoning framing as valuable enough to create useful discussion. I recommend Accept. The paper is not without limitations, especially regarding dataset scale and the need for more rigorous evaluation of visual reasoning versus language priors. However, the problem is timely and important, the cross-scale pathology VLM framing is relevant to clinical diagnostic workflows, and the rebuttal addressed the most serious concerns about leakage and benchmark construction sufficiently for acceptance. The work should be accepted with clear limitations, and the camera-ready version should carefully document the curation pipeline, leakage prevention, model-comparison setting, and residual benchmark limitations, but the authors should avoid adding new experiments or new baseline comparisons beyond what is permitted by the MICCAI guidelines.

title: Evidential Fusion Network for Multimodal Survival Prediction Under Missing Modalities
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Addressing missing modalities in multimodal survival analysis is important for real-world deployment. 2.The paper evaluates different missing rates, which improves the practical relevance of the study. 3.Experiments are conducted on four TCGA cancer cohorts, which provides a relatively diverse validation setting.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) and GRFN-based survival modeling are not new (see [17, 18]). The main contribution of this work is applying these existing techniques to the missing modality setting, which is incremental and does not constitute a substantial methodological advance. 2.Some abbreviations such as ERFS are not defined at first use, naming is inconsistent (e. g. , Dispro vs. DisPro), and inconsistent bold formatting applied to both full sentences and individual words. 3.The symmetric KL divergence-based Alignment Loss (Eq. 11) for aligning pathology and genomics predictions is problematic, given that forcing distributional similarity between inherently heterogeneous modalities risks compromising complementary information, particularly in cases of modality conflict. The Prototype Learning component (Eq. 4) lacks specification of the prototype number K and initialization strategy, which severely hinders reproducibility and prevents a rigorous evaluation of the method’s robustness. 4.The experimental comparison is limited. The paper does not include several important missing-modality methods such as SMIL [20], M3Care [28], and Flex-MoE [27]. Using only DisPro and MUSE as baselines is insufficient to support claims of strong or state-of-the-art performance.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.It is a novel idea to use the Dempster–Shaferevidential theory and GRFNs to handle the modality missing problem, bypass the imputation hallucination and imputation-free’s information loss. 2.The paper is clearly written, well-structured and easy to follow.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.How many prototypes are used in each branch? It is also unclear whether these prototypes are semantically meaningful, for example, whether they correspond to distinct risk patterns. In addition, how are the prototypes initialized? Since there appears to be no explicit mechanism to encourage diversity or separation among them, what prevents the prototypes from becoming redundant or collapsing during training? 2.The interaction between modalities appears to be rather weak, as it is introduced only at the final Gaussian-distribution level. Since the WSI and genomic features are encoded independently and no explicit cross-modal feature interaction is modeled, could this lead to inconsistent or divergent modality-specific predictions before fusion? 3.Why are the epistemic strengths produced by the two unimodal branches directly comparable? Since the pathology and genomics branches are trained separately and may have different scaling behaviors, it is unclear what guarantees that their epistemic strengths are calibrated onto a common scale and can therefore be reliably used for cross-modal weighting in fusion.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: propose a method for missing data estimation based on uncertainty theory (Dempster-Shafer)
reviewer_3_weaknesses: see reviews. Present key results in the abstact.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive comments. We are encouraged that R2 (Accept) and R3 (Weak Accept) recognize the novelty and efficiency of our framework and primarily address R1’s concerns below. [R1] Novelty. We acknowledge that the unimodal survival modeling component of EMMS is related to prior GRFN-based methods. However, our main contribution is the treatment of missing modalities, which these works do not address. We introduce vacuous evidence as a DS-theoretic formulation for missing modalities within the GRFN framework, yielding a closed-form fusion rule (Eq. 9) that naturally falls back to the available modality when another is absent without imputation or heuristic masking. The formulation also provides an interpretable uncertainty term h_f reflecting epistemic uncertainty from missing information. As R2 explicitly notes, this bypasses both imputation hallucination and the information loss common in imputation-free approaches. To our knowledge, this is the first work combining DS theory and GRFNs for missing-modality survival prediction. [R1] Typos. “ERFS” = Epistemic Random Fuzzy Sets; “DisPro” capitalization and bold formatting inconsistencies have been corrected throughout. [R1] Alignment loss vs. complementarity. We respectfully note a misinterpretation. L_align operates at the decision level, not on feature representations z_p and z_g. Modality-specific information is therefore fully preserved upstream. A stop-gradient on variance ensures gradients from L_align affect only mu_p and mu_g, while sigma_p^2, sigma_g^2, h_p, and h_g remain unchanged, preserving each modality’s uncertainty profile and evidential strength. Since both modalities supervise the same event time t, aligning mu_p and mu_g regularizes central tendency only, not distributional shape. Residual disagreement is absorbed into sigma_f^2 by DS fusion as calibrated uncertainty. [R1, R2] Prototype details. K=50 prototypes per branch are deterministically initialized via k-means on training features, which partitions the feature space into well-separated regions and ensures initial diversity. During training, RBF affinity induces competitive activation among prototypes, and the product-intersection (Eq. 7) naturally down-weights prototypes with low affinity scores, preventing collapse without requiring an explicit diversity loss. [R1, R3] More baselines. SMIL [20], M3Care [28], and Flex-MoE [27] are designed for general classification tasks and were not considered survival prediction baselines. Nevertheless, we thank the reviewers for mentioning them and have 1) adapted Flex-MoE [27] for the survival task and 2) implemented a KNN imputer as suggested by R3 for comparison. EMMS consistently achieved the best performance across all four datasets. EMMS outperforms Flex-MoE by +0.037/−0.014 in mean C-index/IBS under 0% missing and by +0.069/−0.013 under 60% missing, and outperforms KNN by +0.103/−0.018 under 60% missing. Full results have been included in the final version. [R2] Divergent predictions. During training, L_align reduces inter-branch divergence by encouraging consistent predictions for the same target y=log(T). At inference, DS fusion (Eq. 9) handles remaining disagreement: the branch with higher epistemic strength h contributes more to mu_f, while disagreement is reflected in sigma_f^2, supported by strong calibration results (Fig. 2). [R2] Comparability of h. Prototype precisions h_k are initialized identically across both branches. The fused survival loss Lf_surv (Eq. 10) jointly backpropagates into h_p and h_g, providing a shared supervisory signal that continuously aligns their epistemic strengths during training. [R3] Readability. We have (i) included headline C-index and IBS in the abstract, (ii) reorganized Tables 1-2 with clearer G-only/P-only/Complete grouping, and (iii) revised captions accordingly.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a well-motivated, uncertainty-aware method for cancer survival prediction under missing-data situations. The reviewers raised critical concerns regarding technical details, experimental justifications, and methodological novelty. | The authors’ rebuttal and clarifications addressed most concerns. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes EMMS, an Evidential Missing Modality Survival Fusion framework for addressing missing modalities in multimodal cancer survival analysis. Its focus on missing modalities is both practical and clinically important. Overall, the work is solid and relevant, and I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Two out of three reviewers recommend acceptance after the rebuttal. The application of Dempster-Shafer theory and Gaussian Random Fuzzy Numbers to missing-modality survival prediction is a technically sound contribution. R2’s concerns were satisfactorily addressed.
