Largest gains (+42%/+10%/+15%/+27%) appear at ρ_200.To §3. B. UA-Flow (R3-W1) Eq. 5 follows Kendall-Gal [8]; novelty is (i) coupling it to flow-matching velocity regression and (ii) using learned per-gene σ_θ as the per-axis SDE coefficient (Eq. 6). UA-Flow (Han et al., 2026; concurrent) defines per-sample velocity uncertainty and propagates it through Jacobian dynamics for post-hoc reliability under deterministic ODE; we use per-gene σ_θ directly as SDE coefficient for intrinsically stochastic gene-modulated inference. §2.4 will clarify. C. Calibration (R3-W2) We agree the absence of direct calibration metrics is the most important gap. Indirect support: at NLL optimum σ_θ converges to true per-gene squared error; Table 3 B+P→Ours isolates the heteroscedastic-loss contribution with positive ρ_200 deltas (BC-II +0.036); σ_θ functions as SDE coefficient without degrading top-k metrics. Direct calibration (σ-vs-error scatter, PICP, MC-dropout) is the right verification and will be pursued in future work. D. Generalization (R1-W1, R2-W1) Cross-cohort (R1-W1): BC-I and BC-II are already independent cohorts (§3: BC-II “an independent cohort with different tumor subtypes”); consistent gains on both (ρ_200 .352/.545) demonstrate cross-subtype transfer. Leave-one-out CV across sections tests within-cohort generalization. σ_θ aggregates over the full training distribution, not a HER2+ prior. Strict train-A-test-B cross-cohort is new experimental work and an important next step we pursue in future work (Dawood et al., 2026). Pathway across tissues (R2-W1): Fig. 4 covers BC; pathway-enrichment on BC-II/SCC (shared cancer framework) and module-to-Allen-Brain-Atlas correspondence for Mouse Brain (hallmark databases being cancer-centric) are planned as future work. E. Sensitivity (R2-W1, R1-W2) K modules (R2-W1): Fig. 4 justifies K=6: modules learned without supervision recover gene groupings (secretory/adhesion, cytoskeletal/metabolic, ECM/signaling, stromal/immune, immunoglobulins) mapping to hallmark pathways (EMT, antigen processing, neutrophil degranulation). Exact K matters less than the decomposition: K=2,4,6,8 all improve substantially over the no-decomposition baseline (BC-I ρ_200 .169→.347 at K=2). K is empirically chosen; we welcome principled K-selection as an open direction for future work. M tokens (R1-W2): The ρ_200 variation across M ∈ {4,8,16,32} in Table 2 is small (BC-I 4%, BC-II 6%, Mouse 2%). Crucially, M=16 is optimal on all three datasets simultaneously (breast cancer and mouse brain, two distinct domains), indicating a structural property of inter-gene coordination rather than dataset-specific tuning. F. MSE/MAE trade-off (R2-W2) The trade-off is clearest in STFlow† (deterministic flow matching): on Mouse, STFlow† has the lowest MSE (.415)/MAE (.491) yet a low ρ_200 (.289 vs our .500); same on SCC. Minimizing pointwise error smooths expression and collapses the localized patterns ρ_k captures (Fig. 3). For downstream uses (niche identification, marker discovery), spatial fidelity and correlation are more biologically actionable. To §3.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): Paper Summary The paper proposes a generative framework for predicting spatial gene expression from histology images by modeling gene-specific relationships to morphology and inter-gene dependencies. It introduces gene binding modules for gene-selective morphological conditioning, regulator tokens for capturing gene–gene interactions, and heteroscedastic flow matching to model per-gene uncertainty and adaptive stochasticity during generation. Key Strengths The method is well-motivated and moves beyond standard regression by modeling the conditional distribution of gene expression. The design is coherent, with each component aligned to biological observations, and the empirical evaluation is strong with broad baselines and consistent improvements in correlation metrics. The interpretability analysis is particularly compelling, showing biologically meaningful gene groupings emerging from the model. Key Weaknesses The method raises concerns about generalization due to lack of cross-cohort validation and potential dataset-specific bias. Some modeling assumptions, such as fixed morphological programs and sensitivity to hyperparameters, are not fully justified. There are also missing evaluations for uncertainty calibration, incomplete details on sampling procedures, and fairness concerns in experimental setup. Performance on pointwise error metrics is less competitive. Review Summary All reviewers agree the paper presents a meaningful and well-structured contribution with strong empirical results and clear biological motivation. They also consistently note limitations in generalization, justification of design choices, and missing evaluations. While these concerns affect completeness, they do not outweigh the overall contribution and impact. Decision Provisional Accept. Please clarify and address the reviewers’ concerns, particularly regarding key design choices such as morphological programs and regulator tokens. Improve the positioning of the heteroscedastic formulation relative to prior work. Provide clearer implementation and sampling details, and ensure a transparent description of the experimental setup for fair comparison in the camera-ready version.

title: GeneRAG: A Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Spatially Resolved Gene Expression Prediction
reviewer_1_strengths: Interpretability: The retrieval-based formulation provides an intuitive and transparent mechanism for prediction. By explicitly selecting and weighting similar reference patches, the model allows one to trace predictions back to specific morphological patterns and corresponding gene expression profiles. This is a meaningful advantage over black-box deep learning approaches. The method is conceptually straightforward and avoids heavy architectural complexity. The use of a sparse optimization framework when imputing the expression. Generalization to unseen genes is a addressing the closed-set limitation Model-agnostic and can be integrated with different backbone models Despite its simplicity the method shows improved predictive performance across datasets
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: The core idea of retrieval-based reconstruction and bimodal dictionary-like modelling has been explored in prior multimodal and biomedical settings. The methodological contribution is minimal. The framework relies on sample-level similarity to approximate gene–gene dependencies. It would be interesting to compare against more direct approaches, such as conditional modelling or latent factor-based methods, which explicitly capture gene relationships. The multi-stage pipeline (initial prediction -> retrieval -> expression aggregation) may accumulate errors, particularly when the initial gene prediction is inaccurate. Dependence on reference bank: Performance is likely sensitive to the diversity and coverage of the training dataset, raising questions about generalization to out-of-distribution samples. The method assigns per-sample weights over a reference bank, which may limit its ability to generalize beyond the training distribution. This design makes the method inherently dependent on dataset coverage and raises concerns about robustness under domain shift as no cross-dataset validation results are reported.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The retrieval module introduces no additional trainable parameters. The sparse weight vector α is obtained by solving a convex ElasticNet optimization at test time, which guarantees a global optimum and eliminates the risk of overfitting in the retrieval step. This is a meaningful practical advantage over methods that require training additional neural network components for retrieval or alignment. 2.The decoupling between the optimization target (anchor genes and morphological features) and the reconstruction target (full gene panel) is a well-motivated design choice. By leveraging conserved gene-gene co-expression structure, the method enables prediction of genes that were entirely unseen during backbone training. The zero-shot extrapolation results on 5,000 genes, while requiring more rigorous baselines for proper evaluation, demonstrate a capability that most existing methods cannot offer by design. 3.The framework is genuinely model-agnostic. The authors demonstrate consistent improvements across three architecturally distinct backbones — a pure vision model (UNI), a multimodal foundation model (EXAONE Path 2.5), and a diffusion generative model (Stem). This plug-and-play flexibility lowers the barrier to adoption and allows practitioners to benefit from the retrieval module regardless of their choice of backbone.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The paper claims to be “the first universal retrieval-augmented framework for spatial transcriptomics,” but this is factually incorrect. BLEEP (Xie et al., NeurIPS 2023) already performs retrieval-augmented gene expression prediction from a reference bank of paired image-expression entries. 2.The zero-shot comparison against DeepSpot in Table 2 is fundamentally asymmetric. DeepSpot must predict 5,000 genes entirely from learned parameters, whereas GeneRAG retrieves ground-truth expression profiles from the training set. This is not a fair evaluation of the retrieval formulation. The appropriate baselines would be alternative retrieval strategies with access to the same reference bank — such as kNN in the image embedding space, kNN in the gene space, or kNN with a weighted dual-modality similarity — which would isolate the contribution of the ElasticNet sparse reconstruction over simpler retrieval mechanisms. 3.Computational cost is never discussed. The method solves an N-dimensional ElasticNet optimization for every test spot individually. A typical Visium slide contains ~5,000 spots, and the reference bank may contain tens of thousands of entries. The scalability of this approach to large cohorts or whole-slide-level prediction is unclear and could be a significant practical limitation that undermines the claimed ease of clinical deployment. 4.The foundation models used as backbones (UNI, CONCH, EXAONE Path 2.5) were pretrained on massive histopathology datasets that may overlap with the HEST-1k evaluation data. The paper does not discuss or rule out this potential contamination. Since the retrieval module relies on the frozen encoder’s feature space, pretraining data overlap would make the morphological retrieval artificially easy, inflating results in a way that is difficult to disentangle from the method’s actual contribution. 5.The “interpretability” claim is overstated. Showing top retrieved patches and their weights is a property shared by any retrieval-based method, including simple kNN. The sparse weights do not provide meaningfully richer explanations than similarity scores for the purpose of clinical reasoning.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The concept of performing retrieval using both image features and gene expression features appears to be a well-founded and reasonable design choice.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The paper does not provide details on how the dataset is split; could the authors clarify what experimental setting is assumed? In recent work, it has become common to evaluate under both intra-patient and inter-patient settings. However, when generalizing across patients, gene expression profiles can differ substantially due to batch effects. Does the proposed method still operate effectively under such conditions? It seems likely that certain assumptions are made, and therefore clearly specifying the scope of applicability and underlying assumptions of the method is very important. The definitions of each component in Equation (1) appear to be unclear and somewhat inconsistent. It seems that $D_{\text{img}}$ and $D_{\text{anchor}}$ are defined as a set, yet the output appears to have the same dimensionality as $f_{\text{img}}$. My understanding is that D is matrix $D_{\text{img}} = ( f_{\text{img}}^(1) … )$, and that a weighted aggregation over samples in the dataset is performed using $\alpha$, resulting in a single feature representation.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely appreciate the Area Chairs for managing the review process, and the reviewers for their constructive feedback recognizing our framework’s zero-shot scalability and ability to address closed-set limits. Following MICCAI policy prohibiting new experimental results, we address the major concerns grouped by topic below. 1.Phrasing, Notation & Claims [R1,R2,M] “First universal retrieval”: To prevent misinterpretation, as in our intro, we don’t claim priority over the retrieval paradigm. By “first universal,” we specifically meant the first model-agnostic framework—a plug-and-play module integrating with any backbone. We will refine positioning to a “model-agnostic retrieval-augmented framework.” [R2] Interpretability: We do not assert superior clinical reasoning, but simply emphasize our approach’s transparency compared to SOTA black-box models (e.g., Stem, TRIPLEX, Foundation-only). We will precisely articulate this as the “inherent transparency of reference-based models.” [R3] Eq.(1) Notation: For mathematical rigor, we will explicitly redefine D_img∈R^{dxN} and D_anchor∈R^{kxN} as matrices. 2.Scalability & Bank Dependency [R2,R3,M] Cost & Scalability: Test-spot optimization concerns are resolved by our joint structure. Eq.(1) is algebraically equivalent to a multi-output ElasticNet problem. Using FISTA solvers, it processes via batched matrix operations for fast convergence, completing inference within minutes per slide. Since large-scale ST profiling is typically run as offline batches clinically, we expect this to be highly practical. [R1,M] Bank Dependency & OOD: While OOD vulnerability is a universal challenge, we expect our bank dependency to turn it into a core strength. Just as traditional RAG dynamically adapts by updating reference documents, GeneRAG enables instant domain adaptation simply by replacing the bank with target data, without weight updates. This parallel inspired our naming. 3.Baselines & Experimental Setup [R2,M] Asymmetric baseline (DeepSpot) & ElasticNet Rationale: Comparing against DeepSpot was inevitable. No prior retrieval work attempted prediction on such a massive scale (5,000 genes). To our knowledge, DeepSpot is the most recent baseline attempting 5,000-gene prediction, making it the necessary benchmark to show how our zero-shot framework breaks their parametric “closed-set limits.” Furthermore, a direct comparison against the existing kNN-based SOTA model (BLEEP) is already provided in Table 1.Therefore, replacing ElasticNet with kNN here is an internal ablation, not a SOTA comparison. Simple kNN is inherently limited by heuristic constraints (e.g., fixed k) and redundancy. Adopting ElasticNet was a fundamental evolution; its L1 penalty actively penalizes redundancy, dynamically determining a sparse, complementary reference set that kNN cannot achieve. [R2,R3,M] Foundation models set up & Contamination: We strictly applied linear probing (frozen encoder) to assess pure representational power. While image-level overlap with HEST-1k is possible during pretraining, models were blind to ST labels (0% contamination). Low standalone backbone performance vs. the massive leap upon integrating GeneRAG confirms our pure contribution. [R3,M] Dataset Split & Batch Effects: We did not employ arbitrary splits, strictly adhering to the SOTA Stem (ICLR 2025) Leave-One-Slide-Out (LOSO) protocol (p.6, ‘~strictly following the experimental design [21]’). The datasets’ diverse compositions naturally subjected our framework to both scenarios: (Intra-patient): In Prostate and HER2ST, LOSO inherently tests intra-patient generalization. (Inter-patient & Batch Effects): In the Kidney dataset (23 slides, 22 patients), LOSO naturally forms a strict inter-patient test; test slides (e.g., ‘20-0038’) belong to completely unseen patients. To ensure the evaluation context is entirely transparent, we will explicitly clarify these setups in the text and release all codes via our GitHub upon publication.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Paper Summary The paper proposes GeneRAG, a retrieval-augmented framework for predicting spatial transcriptomics from histology images. It aims to address limitations of existing approaches, particularly lack of interpretability and inability to generalize to unseen genes. The method first generates initial gene expression predictions and morphological features using a pretrained backbone, then formulates a dual-constrained retrieval process that leverages both image similarity and partial gene predictions to retrieve relevant samples from a reference bank. A sparse ElasticNet optimization is used to weight retrieved samples, and the final full gene expression profile is reconstructed as a weighted combination of these references, enabling prediction of unseen genes and improving performance across multiple backbones . Key Strengths The paper presents a conceptually simple and interpretable framework that provides transparent predictions through explicit retrieval and weighting of reference samples. The approach is flexible and model-agnostic, allowing integration with different backbone architectures without additional training. It demonstrates consistent empirical improvements and introduces a principled optimization-based retrieval mechanism that avoids additional trainable parameters. The ability to generalize to unseen genes through leveraging gene correlations is viewed as a meaningful capability, and the combination of morphological and gene-based retrieval is considered a reasonable and well-motivated design. Key Weaknesses The novelty is considered limited due to similarities with prior retrieval-based approaches, and some claims about being the first of its kind are seen as overstated. Concerns are raised about fairness and clarity of experimental comparisons, particularly in zero-shot settings where the method benefits from access to a reference bank. The evaluation lacks sufficient detail regarding dataset splits, baseline implementation, and potential data overlap from pretrained models. There are also concerns about scalability due to per-sample optimization, as well as robustness and generalization under distribution shifts given reliance on a reference bank. Some methodological descriptions and formulations are unclear, and reproducibility details are insufficient. Review Summary All reviewers agree that the paper addresses an important problem and proposes an interpretable and flexible retrieval-based framework with promising empirical performance and zero-shot capabilities. There is consensus that the design is intuitive and that combining morphological and gene information for retrieval is reasonable. However, reviewers also consistently raise concerns about limited methodological novelty and insufficient clarity in positioning relative to prior work. There is further agreement that evaluation details and experimental fairness need improvement, particularly regarding baseline comparisons, dataset assumptions, and potential data leakage. Given these mixed perspectives, the paper would benefit from clarification and stronger justification before a final decision. Decision Invite to rebuttal. The paper shows promise but has unresolved concerns regarding novelty, evaluation fairness, and clarity. Rebuttal Focus The rebuttal should focus on addressing concerns, particularly by clarifying the novelty and positioning relative to prior retrieval-based methods, including correcting or moderating claims. The authors should justify the fairness of experimental comparisons, especially in zero-shot settings, and provide clearer descriptions of baseline implementations and dataset splits, including assumptions about intra- and inter-patient generalization. It is also important to address potential data leakage from pretrained models, discuss computational cost and scalability of the optimization process, and clarify unclear methodological formulations. | The rebuttal successfully addressed most of the key concerns raised in the initial reviews, particularly regarding novelty positioning, experimental protocol, baseline implementation, and scalability. These clarifications convinced two reviewers to raise their assessments to acceptance. While concerns about reference-bank dependence and OOD robustness remain, they are not sufficient to outweigh the method’s demonstrated effectiveness and practical value. Therefore, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses the limitations and black-box nature of deep-learning regression models in histopathology-based spatial transcriptomics prediction. The approach implements a dual-constrained sparse optimization method that explicitly selects and weights paired reference tissue patches to predict high-dimensional expression panels. Its key strengths include an interpretable inference trail, and a plug-and-play design. The rebuttal deflated original overstatements regarding priority, clarified the FISTA matrix operations and the dataset splits. The technical soundness supports acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes GeneRAG, a retrieval-augmented framework for spatial transcriptomics prediction with the ability to generalize to unseen genes. Reviewers appreciated the model-agnostic design, the retrieval-and-reconstruction formulation, and the strong performance across multiple datasets and backbone models. I agree with Reviewers #2 and #3 that the proposed framework addresses an important limitation of existing methods and provides a practical and interpretable solution. The main concerns were related to novelty positioning, scalability, and dependence on the reference bank. The rebuttal satisfactorily clarified the novelty claims, experimental protocol, and computational considerations. While the dependence on the reference bank remains a limitation, this is a common challenge for retrieval-based approaches and does not undermine the main contribution. Overall, I find the work technically sound, well evaluated, and worthy of acceptance.

title: Generative Anchor-Guided Federated Domain Generalization for Heterogeneous Pan Cancer Image Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a relevant and practically motivated FedDG setting with heterogeneous local semantics, which is more realistic than the standard shared-label assumption. 2.The benchmark is a useful contribution, spanning 4,796 WSIs across 8 cancer types under disjoint label spaces. 3.The method is reasonably organized, and the ablation suggests that both the anchor generation module and the regularization term contribute to performance.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The related-work positioning is incomplete. Although the proposed method is not identical to ETF-based methods, it is clearly related to the broader family of geometry-based classifier design in federated learning. In that sense, the paper would benefit from a more complete discussion of recent geometry-driven approaches and stronger comparison to this line of work. 2.Fig. 1 does not explain the method clearly enough. The overall pipeline is shown, but the interaction among orthogonal prompts, generated anchors, local supervision, and geometric regularization is still difficult to follow from the figure itself. 3.The empirical results are promising, but the current comparison set is not strong enough to fully support the claimed methodological advantage. Since more directly related geometry-based baselines are missing, the reported gains are not yet sufficient to demonstrate that the proposed formulation is clearly preferable to other structured classifier designs.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper targets a highly practical yet challenging scenario in federated learning where different medical institutions possess completely non-overlapping label sets. 2.The conceptual shift of redefining traditional classification as a geometric registration problem on a hypersphere is both innovative and mathematically sound. By utilizing a shared hypernetwork to map semantic-free latent prompts into generative anchors, the proposed framework effectively mitigates gradient conflicts typically caused by heterogeneous label spaces, ensuring stable knowledge aggregation across diverse clients. 3.The effectiveness of the proposed model is rigorously demonstrated through extensive experiments on a large-scale pan-cancer dataset. 4.The study provides profound insights into the model’s internal behavior using anchor similarity heatmaps and KDE-based feature distribution analyses. The empirical observation that adenocarcinoma subtypes from different organs converge in the latent space strongly suggests that the hypernetwork successfully captures organ-invariant histomorphological primitives. This finding provides compelling evidence for the model’s ability to learn biologically meaningful representations beyond mere label matching.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Alignment with Meta-Learning Paradigm and Missing Baselines While this paper claims to address Federated Domain Generalization, the proposed framework mandates fine-tuning with labeled support sets from unseen target domains. This “global pre-training followed by rapid local adaptation” pipeline is fundamentally aligned with the meta-learning paradigm established by Per-FedAvg [Fallah et al., NeurIPS 2020] and further explored by test-time adaptation approaches such as FedICON [Tan et al., NeurIPS 2023] or TTA-FedDG [Liang et al., AAAI 2025]. The absence of comparisons with these adaptation oriented baselines makes it difficult to assess whether the proposed approach offers tangible advantages over established adaptation strategies in federated settings. 2.Insufficient Coverage of Contemporary Baselines The selected baselines predominantly span 2021 to 2023 and do not adequately represent the current state of the art. Recent advances in federated domain generalization have introduced diverse strategies including domain adversarial generation (FedDAG [Che et al., TMI 2025]), test-time adaptation for federated settings (TTA-FedDG [Liang et al., AAAI 2025]), and non-IID histopathology-specific federated style transfer (HistoFS [Raswa et al., CVPR 2025]). Benchmarking the proposed geometric framework against such contemporary methods is necessary to substantiate its claimed superiority within the evolving research landscape. 3.Insufficient Justification for Architectural Design Reframing classification as geometric registration on a hypersphere is a compelling concept, yet several core design decisions lack empirical justification. First, the orthogonality constraint imposed on task prompts is presented as essential for maximal separability, but no comparison with random initialization is provided to validate this claim. Second, the choice to generate anchors via a shared hypernetwork, rather than learning them directly as trainable vectors per client, introduces additional architectural complexity. Since learnable anchors can realize an equivalent hypersphere classification structure without a generator, this design choice requires explicit experimental evidence demonstrating its necessity. 4.Incomplete Ablation and Sensitivity Analysis The reported ablation leaves critical hyperparameters such as memory bank size, temperature, and hypernetwork depth unexamined. Moreover, the support set ratio is fixed at 10% throughout all experiments, which constitutes a non-trivial amount of labeled data in the pathology domain. A sensitivity analysis across varying ratios (e.g., 1%, 5%) is essential to disentangle whether the performance gains originate from the quality of the pre-trained representation or from the GASD+GCR loss structure favoring the fine-tuning process.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This paper makes timely contributions to the fields of federated learning and computational pathology. Its strength lies in innovatively addressing the long-standing “heterogeneous label space” problem in pan-cancer image analysis within federated learning. By introducing the Generative Anchor-based Semantic Decoupling (GASD) mechanism, the authors cleverly disentangle feature learning from local, diverse diagnostic criteria, which is crucial for achieving truly generalizable pan-cancer diagnostic models. This approach not only solves a technical challenge but also aligns with pathological observations of shared invariant histomorphological features across cancer types. The inclusion of Geometric Consistency Regularization (GCR) further enhances the model’s robustness and the quality of feature representation, especially under limited batch sizes, by ensuring the compactness and separability of the learned latent space. Furthermore, the construction of a large-scale multi-cancer benchmark dataset is a valuable contribution in itself, providing a standardized evaluation platform for future research in this domain. The significant performance improvements and the in-depth interpretation of the model’s internal mechanisms (e.g., through anchor similarity heatmaps) strengthen the paper’s persuasiveness and credibility.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: While FedGMA demonstrates excellent performance, several aspects of the paper could be further refined. Firstly, as the paper states that a strictly orthogonal static latent prompt matrix is used in Generative Anchor-based Semantic Decoupling (GASD) to ensure maximal separability of the initial latent space, a more detailed mathematical derivation or theoretical analysis regarding the profound theoretical basis for choosing “orthogonality” as a specific constraint, and its unique advantages in fostering the learning of a “consistent geometric lexicon,” could be provided. Furthermore, the paper could elaborate on the intrinsic mechanisms and design choices of the Hypernetwork in transforming semantic-agnostic latent prompts into task-specific geometric anchors. Secondly, the Geometric Consistency Regularization (GCR) module plays a crucial role in ensuring the compactness and separability of the latent space. However, the paper lacks sufficient sensitivity analysis for key parameters within the GCR module, such as memory bank size and negative sampling strategies. The absence of systematic ablation studies demonstrating how these parameters impact model performance, stability, and generalization ability (e.g., comparison across different memory bank sizes) limits a comprehensive understanding of the module’s robustness. Additionally, although the paper indicates that fine-tuning and evaluation were performed on unseen target domains, it does not elaborate on the “costs” associated with this fine-tuning process, including the required amount of fine-tuning data, the number of iterations, and the actual contribution of fine-tuning to the final performance. If FedGMA can perform well without fine-tuning or with minimal fine-tuning data, it would further highlight its domain generalization capabilities; thus, a more transparent presentation of fine-tuning inputs and outputs would be highly beneficial. Finally, despite significant performance gains, the absolute AUC values for certain cancer types like BLCA and UCEC remain relatively low (e.g., BLCA 59.74%, UCEC 64.61%). This might suggest higher heterogeneity or diagnostic difficulty for these specific cancer types, warranting further discussion on the model’s limitations or future improvement directions in addressing such particular challenges. What’s more, as the paper has demonstrated statistically significant differences between FedGMA and other methods using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, the AUC result table does not report 95% confidence intervals. Including 95% CIs would more intuitively display the credible range and stability of AUC estimates, providing readers with more comprehensive performance evaluation information, especially when comparing different methods.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank AC and reviewers for the constructive feedback. Q1: Comparisons with meta-learning and geometry-based methods (R1Q1, R1Q3, R2Q1) A1: Our FedGMA achieves an average AUC of 76.42%, outperforming Per-FedAvg (49.07%, meta-learning, 2020), FedCCFA (56.69%, geometry-based, 2024), and TTA-FedDG (72.40%, test-time adaptation, 2025). Regarding meta-learning-based methods, Per-FedAvg struggles with extreme label heterogeneity because gradients from conflicting local semantics lead to severe interference in the shared encoder. Standard geometry-based methods inherently assume a predefined and shared global label space, making them mathematically inapplicable to our completely disjoint label space setting. We will discuss these contemporary methods in the revised related work section. Q2: Contemporary baselines selection (R2Q2) A2: Most FedDG methods assume a shared global label space, making them inapplicable to our disjoint setting. Our benchmark prioritized compatibility with extreme label heterogeneity, focusing on strategies like the prototype-based family. Specifically, we included FedAdapterProto[17] (2025) to represent the state of the art. We acknowledge that recent works such as FedDAG provide valuable insights and will incorporate these comparisons in our journal extension. Q3: Missing hyperparameter ablations (R2Q4, R3Q2) A3: We conducted extensive ablations in our preliminary experiment. They were omitted due to space limitation. For the support set ratio, zero-shot evaluation yields 67.42% AUC. Fine-tuning with 1%, 5%, and 10% data yields 72.85%, 75.10%, and 76.42%. For memory bank size, the performance is robust (76.31% for M=16 vs 76.42% for M=32). Other parameters such as temperature and hypernetwork depth were selected based on standard empirical practices to balance representative capacity and training stability. Full sensitivity analyses will be provided in our anonymized repository upon acceptance. Q4: Fine-tuning cost and implementation details (R3Q3) A4: The training and fine-tuning frameworks maintain consistency. We utilize SGD optimization with a learning rate of 1e-3.The fine-tuning process is performed on a 10% support set and lasts for 10 epochs. Q5: Justification for orthogonality over random initialization (R2Q3, R3Q1) A5: Mathematically, orthogonal initialization ensures maximum and uniform inter-class margins, a principle consistent with Neural Collapse (Papyan et al., 2020). Empirically, random initialization fails to maintain this margin, causing severe feature collapse. Our preliminary experiments showed that random initialization drops the average AUC by approximately 9%. Q6: Rationale for shared hypernetwork (R1Q3, R2Q3, R3Q1) A6: Our hypernetwork acts as a universal geometric dictionary designed to transform semantic-agnostic latent prompts into task specific anchors. If clients learned these anchors directly as local trainable vectors, the vectors would severely overfit to their highly heterogeneous and disjoint local label spaces. This would re-introduce exact semantic conflicts during server aggregation. Q7: Clarity of Figure 1 (R1Q2) A7: We will revise Figure 1 based on the reviewer’s suggestions to enhance clarity. Q8: Low performance on certain classes and absence of confidence intervals (R3Q4) A8: The lower performance on BLCA and UCEC is caused by their inherent and notoriously high intra class morphological heterogeneity. However, FedGMA still outperforms baselines on these difficult classes by a significant gap of 2-8%. Addressing extreme intrinsic heterogeneity remains a future direction. Regarding the confidence intervals, we completely agree that they improve rigorousness. Due to strict space limits, they were initially omitted, but we will add them for all metrics in the revised version.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): Based on the three reviews (two “Weak Reject” and one “Weak Accept”), the paper is clearly borderline. The reviewers raise substantial concerns that can potentially be addressed. In the rebuttal, the authors must: (1) add missing geometry‑based and meta‑learning baselines (e.g., Per‑FedAvg, TTA‑FedDG, FedDAG); (2) provide ablation on key hyperparameters (memory bank size, support set ratio); (3) clarify the orthogonality choice and the hypernetwork design; and (4) improve Fig. 1 to clearly explain anchor generation and interactions. | Two of the three reviewers raised their scores to accept after the rebuttal, acknowledging the paper’s conceptual strength (geometric registration for federated domain generalization with disjoint label spaces) and its valuable benchmark. Hence, I recommend Accept. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses a federated domain generalization under completely disjoint label spaces. Reviewers appreciated the practical motivation, the large-scale pan-cancer benchmark, and the consistent performance improvements across unseen target domains. The proposed FedGMA framework introduces an interesting geometric formulation that decouples feature learning from local label semantics using generative anchors and geometric consistency regularization. The experimental results and visualization analyses support the effectiveness of the approach. Although the reviewers raised concerns regarding the theoretical justification, baseline coverage, and positioning relative to prior geometry-based methods, the rebuttal addressed these issues reasonably well. Therefore, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper has initially received mixed reviews and it was invited for rebuttal. The authors submitted a rebuttal to address the comments of the reviewers. After the rebuttal, two reviewers updated their scores indicating that their comments had been properly addressed in the rebuttal and even if they highlight that the paper is borderline, they propose its acceptance. The AC read the paper, reviews, rebuttal and justification of rating and they agree that the paper is borderline, but it could be interesting for the community.

title: Genetically Aligned Patient Representations Improve Hematological Diagnosis
reviewer_1_strengths: —The paper addresses a clinically relevant and underexplored problem in computational hematology by aligning blood smear morphology with cytogenetic and molecular information. The proposed multimodal setting is well motivated. —- overall good quality of work —- The manuscript is well prepared with good writing except a few places in the Methods
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The main weakness is the lack of clarity and organization in the Methods section. —In Section 2.4, EMA is introduced without explanation. Some symbols are introduced only partially or without explicit description at first use. —. The notation is also confusing because the symbol lambda is reused for different loss weights in Sections 2.4 and 2.5.. While not mathematically wrong, this reuse reduces clarity and should be avoided. —The manuscript does not clearly define how the BCE loss is formulated, whether it is applied separately for mutation and karyotype reconstruction, or how it is averaged across samples and dimensions.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.This study leverages a relatively large cohort in the field with rich multimodal data, including single-cell images and matched cytogenetic and molecular profiles, and includes an independent test set. The evaluation across multiple publicly available tasks further supports the robustness of the framework. 2.The proposed method demonstrates improved and more balanced performance across datasets compared to baseline foundation model approaches. The experimental design is reasonably comprehensive, including multiple setups and ablations, and highlights the advantage of the method even with comparatively less data used in the self-supervised pretraining stage. 3.The paper presents clear figures and well-structured experimental settings, which help improve the readability of the methodology and make the overall workflow and evaluation easier to follow.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The performance on out-of-domain tasks appears limited, and the lack of strong or well-matched baselines in this setting makes it difficult to fully assess the generalizability of the proposed framework. 2.The formulation of the patient-level embedding is not fully justified. Although the task is inherently multimodal, the representation appears to be primarily derived from single-cell image features, raising questions about how effectively multimodal information is integrated. 3.The comparison with existing methods may not be entirely fair. In particular, benchmarking against cell-level foundation models would provide a more appropriate and convincing evaluation than comparisons with models trained on lower-magnification (e.g., 20×) histopathology data.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: S1.Novel and clinically well-motivated problem. Hematology is underserved in computational pathology, and the tight coupling between blood smear morphology and genetic alterations in leukemia is a natural fit for multimodal alignment. S2.Strong methodology. The two-stage design (self-supervised pretraining then supervised contrastive alignment) is principled. The reconstruction loss (L_BCE) to prevent representational collapse is a thoughtful design choice, validated in the ablation (Table 3: removing it drops S->K MRR by 36%). S3.Outperforms much larger models with less data. GenBloom’s small ViT (~6 layers) outperforms GigaPath (86.3M params, 171K WSIs), PRISM (99M, 587K WSIs), and TITAN (42.1M, 335K WSIs) on hematology tasks despite training on orders of magnitude less data. This highlights the value of domain-specific pretraining. S4.Proper statistical analysis. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni correction, 1,000 bootstrap iterations for retrieval, Friedman test for overall ranking. S5.Cross-modal retrieval is a genuinely useful capability. Retrieving genetic profiles from morphology (and vice versa) has direct clinical utility for triage and prioritization of confirmatory genetic testing. S6.Good reproducibility commitment. Code and model weights promised on GitHub. Carbon footprint reported (~7.26 kg CO2eq). Three evaluation datasets are publicly available.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: W1.Very small sample sizes throughout. Genetic alignment uses only 146 training patients. Test sets are tiny: AML-Hehr subtypes have 6-9 test patients per class, APL-AML has 12 test patients, AMH has 20.With such small n, even the reported statistical tests have limited power, and results may be unstable. W2.Cross-modal retrieval performance is modest in absolute terms. Top-1 accuracy for slide-to-karyotype is 0.09-0.14 (Table 1). While significantly above random, these numbers are far from clinically actionable. The authors should discuss what level of retrieval performance would be needed for practical utility. W3.Genetic alignment is limited to AML only. It is unclear whether the alignment approach generalizes to other hematological malignancies (MDS, MPN, lymphoma) that are present in the pretraining set. The out-of-domain evaluation (APL-AML, AMH) tests generalization of the visual encoder, not of the genetic alignment.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and recognition of our contributions, including the clinical relevance of genetic alignment in hematology (R1, R3), use of large scale single cell dataset (R2) and baseline comparisons with proper statistical analysis (R2, R3). Below we discuss additions to the camera ready to address the reviewer comments. R1: Notations – We now expand the explanations of some of the terms that were previously not explained sufficiently, including EMA and L_BCE, and use separate lambdas in the formulas to increase clarity. EMA refers to the Exponential Moving Average of weights. L_BCE is the binary cross-entropy loss between each real and predicted genetic mutation, including both karyotype and molecular genetics, and is used to preserve the biological information of embeddings while aligning them with the patient representations. R2, R3: Out-of-domain evaluation is missing, test datasets are small – Hematopathology suffers from a lack of large and extensive benchmarks, especially at the patient level. We tried to include all publicly available test datasets in our evaluations. Across all datasets, we ensured that the test sets were held out and never seen by the model. In the APL-AML dataset, the staining also differs significantly from that of the other datasets. R2: Baseline evaluations may not be fair – We acknowledge that slide-level models (e.g., TITAN) were mainly trained on histopathology images. However, to the best of our knowledge, no hematology slide-level encoder is currently available to include in the evaluations. We trained our slide-level model using DinoBloom (Koch et. al., 2024), which is the only available single-cell foundation model. As a fair comparison, we added simple mean pooling of DinoBloom embeddings (see Figure 2a). R3: Discussing retrieval capabilities – Although retrieval between image and genomic embeddings is promising, its clinical utility requires extensive evaluation and validation across different diseases. In this work, we present, to the best of our knowledge, the first proof-of-concept cross-retrieval framework in hematopathology, paving the way for future genetics-aware smear analysis. R3: Cross-retrieval generalization to other diseases – Our genetic alignment cohort consisted of AML patients. To test whether genetic-to-image retrieval can be used in other diseases, we included myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN) patients in the gene retrieval task for JAK2 (186 were diagnosed with MPN and 10 with MDS/MPN out of 213 patients, Table 2). We will highlight this point in the text more clearly.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The reviews are consistently positive, with two weak-accept and one accept recommendation. The paper addresses a clinically relevant and underexplored problem in computational hematology by aligning blood smear morphology with cytogenetic and molecular genetic information. The reviewers recognize several strengths, including the hematology-specific patient representation framework, two-stage pretraining and genetic alignment strategy, use of a large single-cell image cohort, comparisons with pathology foundation models, statistical analysis, and the clinically meaningful cross-modal retrieval setting. The main concerns are the relatively small sample size for genetic alignment and test sets, limited absolute cross-modal retrieval performance, incomplete demonstration of generalization beyond AML, and the need for clearer methodological details and more directly comparable cell-level baselines. These issues should be addressed or discussed in revision.

title: GFR-MIL: Glance–Focus–Reflect Based Multiple Instance Learning for Multi-Scale Whole Slide Image Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1) The authors have modeled the image-reviewing process of pathologists, with a meticulously designed framework that provides a counterintuitive discussion of the necessity of each component. 2) The authors conducted a comprehensive evaluation of their method against nine other approaches across six datasets, covering cancer prognosis prediction and cancer subtyping tasks; overall, their method is competitive.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1) Although the authors conducted extensive comparisons of model performance, the improvement in subtype prediction performance on TCGA-NSCLC relative to the baseline appears to be minimal, and the authors did not report on statistical significance. 2) Unlike other datasets, confidence intervals were not reported when comparing with BRCAS. 3) During the sampling phase of the Glance Module, the authors claim to select the top-k% instances, but they do not report the value of k nor analyze the impact of varying k on model sensitivity. 4)While the paper repeatedly emphasizes computational efficiency through coarse-to-fine selection and claims that GFR-MIL achieves strong performance while attending to only 30% of slide regions, the actual end-to-end efficiency remains insufficiently substantiated. In particular, the framework still requires dual-resolution preprocessing and feature extraction, iterative stacked GFRBlocks, cross-scale feedback through the Reflect module, recycling of unselected regions, and multi-round feature aggregation, all of which may introduce non-trivial computational and memory overhead.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The proposed GFR-MIL framework is well motivated by the diagnostic workflow of pathologists and provides a clear and intuitive coarse-to-fine reasoning paradigm. 2.The proposed gated sampling, entropy regularization, and recycling mechanism together form a relatively complete sparse selection pipeline that is both practical and technically sound. 3.The iterative Reflect module with memory constraint introduces a meaningful multi-round refinement strategy, which is conceptually appealing for WSI analysis and has the potential to improve representation completeness.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.In Fig. 1, the number of stacked GFRBlocks is denoted as N, but the manuscript does not clearly specify its value. It is also unclear whether the parameter D introduced later refers to the number of GFRBlocks. This point should be clarified, as it appears to be a key architectural hyperparameter. 2.The paper does not provide any analysis of the computational cost, such as FLOPs, inference time, or GPU memory consumption. Since the proposed GFRBlocks appear to introduce nontrivial overhead, and the dual-resolution design may further increase both computational complexity and inference latency in practical deployment, it would be important to analyze the trade-off between performance and efficiency. 3.The visualization in Fig. 2 is currently not sufficiently clear. In particular, the semantic meaning of different colors (e.g., red vs. blue) is not well explained, making it difficult to understand what exactly the figure is intended to demonstrate. More interpretable visualizations and clearer figure captions would strengthen the paper. 4.Since the method is based on multi-round Glance–Focus–Reflect reasoning, it would be helpful to analyze whether different blocks attend to different types of regions. For example, do earlier blocks focus on the most salient lesions, while later blocks identify complementary or previously overlooked regions? Such analysis is currently missing.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper studies an important problem in WSI analysis, namely the limitation of irreversible region selection in existing coarse-to-fine MIL methods. The overall motivation is reasonable, and the proposed framework is intuitive and easy to follow. Another positive aspect is that the method is evaluated on both subtyping and survival prediction tasks across several public datasets, and the reported performance is generally strong.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The main concerns are mostly on the experimental side. First, the baseline comparison is not fully convincing, since the paper does not clearly compare with the most relevant coarse-to-fine or hierarchical multi-scale methods. Second, the BRACS results are reported without standard deviation, which makes it hard to judge the stability of the method. Third, although the paper emphasizes efficiency, this aspect is not quantitatively evaluated with metrics such as runtime, memory, FLOPs, or processed patch ratio. Fourth, for the survival task, the evaluation is limited to C-index only, and additional survival-related analysis would make the results more convincing. Finally, the visualization section only presents the proposed method, without qualitative comparisons to other baselines, so the interpretability advantage is not fully demonstrated.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for the constructive feedback, and code will be released upon acceptance. Q1 for R2&Meta: NSCLC Improvement. Subtyping on TCGA-NSCLC is a near-saturated task as it depends on a few discriminative patches[26]. GFR-MIL matches top performance while reducing preprocessing cost by 44% (27.5s vs 48.9s for ABMIL-Gated, median 15,135 patches @20x). On prognosis tasks requiring global WSI context [27], GFR-MIL consistently outperforms all competitors across five datasets with notable C-index gains (Table 1). GFR-MIL thus offers efficiency on saturated tasks and accuracy on challenging ones. [26] IEEE TMI, vol. 44, no. 9, pp. 3756-3769.[27] CVPR, 2025, pp. 5144-5153.Q2 for R2, 8&Meta: BRACS Confidence Intervals. BRACS provides official fixed train/val/test splits (Sec 3.1), we follow this standard protocol for direct comparison with prior work. Q3 for R2: Top-k% Sampling Ratio. The two GFRBlocks use k = 20% and 10% (Sec 3.2), selecting ~30% of patches in total, consistent with [28]. Notably, the closed-loop Reflect module recovers regions missed in round 1 during round 2, making GFR-MIL architecturally robust to k. This is supported by SOTA performance across 7 datasets with widely varying patch counts (Tables 1, 2). [28] arXiv:2603.00667 Q4 for R2, 3, 8&Meta : Computational Efficiency and Trade-Off Recycling Mechanism is training-only to ensure gradient flow (Sec 2.2). At inference, GFR-MIL processes only the 2.5× WSI and ~30% of 20× patches. On TCGA-KIRC (median 19,187 patches @ 20×), preprocessing (dual-resolution feature extraction) drops from 51.3s (full 20×) to 30.4s per slide, and the full pipeline (stacked GFRBlocks, Reflect feedback, and multi-round aggregation) costs 85.7G FLOPs, 0.55GB memory, and 11.3ms inference, versus 189.5G/0.93GB/14.5ms (TransMIL) and 571.7G/2.0GB/29.8ms (RRT). Similar trends hold across all 7 datasets. These omitted details will be added. Q5 for R3: Parameters N and D. N in Fig. 1 denotes the number of stacked GFRBlocks, equivalent to D in Sec 3.2, with a value of 2.We will unify this notation in the final version. Q6 for R3: Fig. 2 Visualization Clarity. The red highlighted areas denote the high-attention regions identified by GFR-MIL, while the blue areas indicate the low-attention regions. We will clarify this in the caption. Q7 for R3: Multi-Round Attention Behavior. The two GFRBlocks are functionally complementary by design. The first selects salient top-ranked regions, and the memory mask (Sec 2.4) then suppresses them, forcing the second to find overlooked yet discriminative ones (0% spatial overlap). Ablation confirms each contributes (Table 3). We will color-code Fig.2 by round, with the first round in black boxes and the second in green. Per-round histological profiling is left for future interpretability work. Q8 for R8&Meta: Coarse-to-Fine Baselines. We addresse coarse-to-fine baselines from two angles. (1) RLogist [13], a representative coarse-to-fine method, reports in its own paper that it underperforms high-resolution MIL baselines. We therefore prioritized comparisons with the latest and strongest high-resolution methods [19, 20], where GFR-MIL achieves SOTA across all 7 cohorts. (2) In Table 3, replacing our bidirectional Reflect with a unidirectional Gumbel-Softmax reduces GFR-MIL to a standard coarse-to-fine pipeline, and the resulting drop confirms our design’s advantage. Q9 for R8: Survival Evaluation Metrics. C-index is a standard metric in computational pathology survival analysis, widely adopted in recent works [20, 27]. GFR-MIL ranks first across all 5 distinct cancer cohorts, validating its superiority. Further KM analyses will be conducted in future. Q10 for R8: Qualitative Baseline Comparison. GFR-MIL achieves unique interpretability. Unlike conventional MIL with diffuse whole-slide attention heatmaps [2], it outputs discrete localized boxes for per-round selected regions (Fig. 2). Qualitative baseline heatmap comparison is left for future work.

title: Group Equivariant Diffusion for Anomaly Detection in Computational Cytology
reviewer_1_strengths: Strong logical grounding: The author provides theoretical guarantees in Section 2.3 to address potential concerns regarding the proposed framework. Specifically, they show that symmetrizing the denoiser does not increase the DDPM training risk, and that symmetry-respecting averaging preserves the false positive rate without degrading the detection trade-off. Clarity and coherence: The paper clearly presents its core objective and maintains a focused narrative throughout. Most components of the proposed framework appear well-motivated (e. g. , the introduction of equivariant noise coupling to enforce symmetry in the diffusion process). The experimental results provide convincing empirical support for the claims. In addition, the inclusion of pseudo code (Algorithm 1) improves the reproducibility of the method.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The overall methodological novelty appears somewhat limited, as most components are adaptations of existing techniques. The main contribution lies primarily in their integration rather than the introduction of fundamentally new methodological ideas. The theoretical guarantees rely on strong symmetry assumptions that may not strictly hold for real cytology data, where cell morphology and acquisition conditions are not perfectly D4-invariant.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The observation that diagnostic class should not change under rotations and flips for single-cell patches is reasonable, while standard generative detectors treat rotated views as distinct inputs, inducing orientation-dependent score variation. The paper is well motivated from a computational cytology perspective. 2.The method is clearly presented and the algorithmic is easy to follow. 3.The ablation study includes the comparison between FA-only, FA+EN, together with the reported reduction in anomaly-score variance across rotations and flips, which provides evidence that the proposed method improve transformation consistency.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The novelty is limited. Based on Section 2, the main components are U-Net denoiser with a D4-equivariant architecture [9,16], diffusion anomaly detection via partial reconstruction [22,35], and inference-time symmetry enforcement through equivariant noise coupling (EN) and frame averaging (FA) [22,35], all of them are individually known. Consequently, the proposed approach seems more like a combination of known components than a substantially new diffusion framework. 2.The experiment results are inconsistent across two datasets and often small against the strongest baselines, which weakens the central claim and raises concerns about the generalization of the proposed method. The paper on Page 8 shows that the D4 model is statistically inconclusive on AML LMU. So the positive result is mainly on MLL. Does this suggest that the effectiveness of the method may depend on the specific dataset rather than reflecting a robust improvement? As a result, it remains unclear whether the proposed method generalizes reliably across different cytology dataset, or whether its effectiveness is sensitive to the underlying data distribution. 3.There are some inconsistent ablation study results across two datasets. Section 3.4 states FA-only slightly degrades AUC on MLL, while FA+EN improves it, why FA+EN performs worse than FA-only in terms of AUC on AML LMU? Besides, the D4 convolutional U-Net slightly outperforms the attention-augmented variant in MLL but not on AML LMU. This suggests that the performance gains may be sensitive to implementation details and dataset properties . 4.The theoretical section is supportive, but some claims are insufficiently justified and therefore not fully convincing. Section 2.3 gives intuitive statements about D_4 averaging can not increase DDPM risk and invariant detection under class-conditional symmetry, but no proof is provided in the paper. Besides, the analysis relies on strong symmetry assumptions that may not hold in real cytology patches. 5.The qualitative results in Figure 2 raise concerns about the practical localization ability of the method. The displayed MSE values are very small and the anomaly maps appear weak and poorly localized. This suggests that the method may be capturing patch-level differences without producing sufficiently clear or clinically meaningful pixel-level abnormality maps. 6.In section 2.1, the notation is somewhat inconsistent: x_0 is introduced as coming from the normal training distribution , but is also used to denote a test sample. 7.Some typos: in section 2.3, “Invariant detection under class-conditional symmetry:Let Y…”
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The application of dihedral group equivariance (D4) to diffusion models specifically to address the biological invariance of single-cell cytology is well-motivated. The authors evaluate the method using a highly realistic metric for budgeted clinical review workflows: the number of true positives in the top-K retrieved anomalous predictions (e.g., TP100/200/400). Section 2.3 provides risk bound via Jensen’s inequality and justification of invariant scoring under group symmetry. This significantly strengthens the contribution beyond empirical work. The study benchmarks against a wide array of relevant methods, including multiple instance learning (ItS2CLR), deep one-class models (Deep SVDD), and several generative detectors like f-AnoGAN, THOR, and BerDiff. AUC improves from 0.63 → 0.68, TP400 improves from 57 → 78 (large practical gain).
reviewer_3_weaknesses: While the performance gains on the MLL dataset are clinically and statistically significant, the improvements on the AML LMU dataset are statistically inconclusive. This limits the strength of the generalizability claims across different cytology modalities. The ablation studies reveal that the $D_{4}$ convolutional U-Net without attention performs best on the MLL dataset, whereas the attention-augmented variant achieves the strongest performance on the AML LMU dataset. The paper lacks a deeper investigation or hypothesis regarding why this architectural discrepancy exists between the two datasets. Only two cytology datasets, where both are similar modalities (single-cell patches). Missing whole-slide validation and cross-domain generalization Assumes perfect D4 invariance, which may not fully hold for staining artifacts or slide preparation biases, Need analysis of symmetry violations.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for recognizing the motivation of our work, its clear formulation, theoretical grounding, strong evaluation, top-K gains, and practical relevance. A. Novelty (R2,R3,R4): Our contribution is the first systematic study of dihedral equivariance for diffusion-based unsupervised anomaly detection in cytology, with a unified algorithm treating architectural and inference-time equivariance as complementary routes to the same invariance property. This is a non-trivial adaptation to partial-diffusion anomaly scoring, where the goal is not generation/translation but stable top-K ranking under budgeted cytologist review. Prior cytology or diffusion-based medical anomaly-detection work has not enforced D4 structure or measured score variance under symmetry. We agree that equivariant convolutions, partial diffusion, and test-time averaging have precedents; our novelty lies in their task-specific integration and validation for cytology anomaly detection. B. Statistical significance (R3,R4): Our primary clinical endpoint is budgeted top-K retrieval: reducing thousands of candidate cells to a few hundred suspicious patches for cytologist review. AUC summarizes global ranking, while TP@K measures this operational goal. On MLL, the gains are clear: FA+EN improves AnoDDPM from TP400/200/100 = 57/30/18 to 78/53/34, with significant AUC and TP400 gains (p<0.001 and p=0.006). On AML-LMU, the margin is statistically inconclusive (AUC p≈0.125, TP400 p≈0.275), but D4 variants still give the best or tied-best top-K results: TP400=325, TP200=162, TP100=86.Thus, AML-LMU shows favorable but not statistically conclusive gains, not a contradiction of the method. C. Architectural ablation differences (R3,R4): Our claim is not that one D4 backbone is universally optimal, but that D4 structure improves transformation-consistent scoring. The attention variant mainly adds capacity/context modeling. Thus, D4-conv may suffice for MLL’s smaller 250x250 bone-marrow patches, while attention can help on AML-LMU’s larger 400x400 peripheral-blood patches with greater visual diversity. Both support the trend: D4-conv improves MLL over AnoDDPM (AUC/TP400 0.675/74 vs 0.633/57), and D4-conv+attn improves AML-LMU (0.720/325 vs 0.694/311). We clarify that attention is dataset-dependent, not the core contribution. D. D4 assumptions and proof clarification (R2,R3,R4): We agree real cytology data are not perfectly D4-invariant due to staining/acquisition effects. Our assumption is instead class invariance: rotating/flipping a centered square single-cell patch should not change its normal/abnormal label. Sec. 2.3 is an idealized justification for symmetry-respecting scoring; the empirical question is whether this reduces orientation-induced score variation, which our D4 variants do while improving top-K retrieval. For R3, the DDPM-risk result follows from Jensen’s inequality applied to the group-averaged denoiser, and the detection result from class-conditional label symmetry. We will clarify the assumption in the proof sketch. E. Qualitative anomaly maps (R3): Fig. 2 is only a qualitative visualization; the method and metrics use scalar patch-level anomaly scores. Unlike MRI, OCT or X-ray lesions, cytology abnormalities are often not sharply localized, but expressed through nuclear size/shape, chromatin texture, nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, cytoplasm, staining, and overall atypia. Thus, maps show reconstruction-deviation patterns within suspicious cells, not pixel-level segmentation. Since our goal is to reduce thousands of patches to a few hundred for cytologist review, patch-level top-K retrieval is the endpoint. We have revised the caption accordingly. We will address other comments (x0 notation, Sec. 2.3 typos, Fig. 1/2 captions). For R4’s whole-slide/cross-domain point, we agree this is important future work; this study focuses on controlled single-cell patch evaluation for rare-cell retrieval before slide-level deployment.

title: H2M-Net: Hierarchical Hyperbolic Memory Network for Pathological Report Generation
reviewer_1_strengths: (1) The motivation for using hyperbolic geometry is clear and well justified. Modeling the local-to-global hierarchy of whole slide images in a non-Euclidean space is a sensible idea, and the paper explains this rationale effectively. (2) The proposed geometric losses are well designed and appear complementary. The ablation results suggest that both contribute to performance, and the visualization provides useful qualitative support for the intended hierarchical structure. (3) The experimental evaluation is thorough and appears fair. The use of consistent data splits and feature extraction across methods is appreciated, and the results show consistent improvements across both datasets and multiple metrics.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: (1) The overall idea is interesting, but the methodological novelty appears somewhat incremental. Many of the main ingredients, hyperbolic embeddings, entailment-style losses, hierarchical WSI modeling, and hyperbolic attention, have been explored previously. The paper would benefit from a clearer explanation of what is technically new in this work and why the particular integration is non-trivial. (2) The experimental evaluation is somewhat limited. The results are reported on two subsets with standard text generation metrics, but there is no clinical or semantic evaluation to support the claim of diagnostically accurate report generation. (3) The hierarchical text decomposition appears central to the method, but it is not described in sufficient detail. Since the approach depends on reliable segmentation of reports into local, regional, and global components, more explanation and some validation of this preprocessing step would be important. (4) The baseline comparison could be expanded. In particular, comparisons with more recent pathology vision-language models and with prior hyperbolic approaches for WSI analysis would help clarify whether the observed gains come specifically from the proposed geometric design. (5) Several implementation details are missing or unclear, including the curvature setting, important loss weights, and the embedding dimensionality. Reporting these details would improve reproducibility. (6) The paper would also benefit from qualitative examples showing generated reports at different hierarchy levels alongside the reference reports. (7) Minor issue: References [4] and [5] appear to cite the same paper.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: (1) The methodology is interesting and reasonably well motivated. The paper introduces a hyperbolic-space formulation for pathology report generation, which is a distinctive and methodologically meaningful idea. Instead of treating multi-scale pathology semantics in a flat Euclidean space, the method is built around the assumption that both WSIs and reports have an inherent local–region–global hierarchy. The use of hyperbolic geometry gives the work a clearer modeling motivation than a simple architectural modification, and the hierarchical memory mechanism together with the geometric constraints makes the framework more coherent. (2) The experimental design is reasonably thorough and generally supports the proposed method. The paper evaluates the model on two benchmark subsets, BRCA and LUAD, and compares against several prior pathology report generation methods under a unified setting. The results are reported across multiple metrics, and the paper also includes ablation studies, hyperparameter analysis, and embedding visualization. These additional analyses are useful because they provide evidence for the role of the main design choices rather than relying only on final benchmark numbers. (3) The paper is clearly written and well organized. The overall structure is easy to follow, and the motivation, method, and experiments are presented in a logical order. The figures are also helpful for understanding both the conceptual idea and the architecture, especially the overview of the bottom-up hierarchical framework. Overall, the manuscript communicates a technically interesting method in a relatively clear and readable way.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: (1) The current evaluation metrics do not sufficiently demonstrate the clinical efficacy. The paper mainly relies on general NLG metrics such as BLEU, METEOR, and ROUGE. These scores are useful as a basic reference, but they are not sufficient to show whether the generated pathology reports are medically accurate or clinically meaningful. This issue is especially important here because the paper’s main claim is hierarchical diagnostic consistency, yet the evaluation does not separately assess performance at the local, region, and global levels. Overall, the current evaluation does not fully demonstrate the claimed medical or practical value of the method. (2) Some key methodological details are still under-specified. In particular, the report hierarchy is constructed using keyword prompts and regex-based matching, but the paper does not provide enough detail about the actual rules, prompt design, or how different text segments are assigned to the local, region, and global levels. Since this hierarchical decomposition is a core part of the method, the lack of implementation detail weakens reproducibility and also makes it harder to judge how robust the reported hierarchy really is.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper identifies an important limitation of prior WSI report generation methods: pathology data and pathology reports are inherently hierarchical, but many existing methods treat representations as relatively flat Euclidean features. This is a reasonable and interesting observation for this task. 2.The use of hyperbolic geometry, specifically the Lorentz model, is an interesting contribution to pathology report generation. The paper goes beyond simply replacing the embedding space by also introducing hierarchy-aware constraints, including radial position loss and entailment loss, which are conceptually aligned with parent-child semantics. 3.The bottom-up, cascaded framework with a visual encoder, a memory encoder, and a text decoder is a sensible architecture for local-to-global diagnostic reasoning. The memory mechanism is a meaningful design choice because it tries to preserve information as the model moves across levels of abstraction.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Clinical validity of the generated reports remains insufficiently assessed. The evaluation relies entirely on BLEU, METEOR, and ROUGE-L. These are standard text-generation metrics, but for pathology report generation, they are not enough to establish factual correctness, diagnostic safety, or clinical usefulness. A pathology-specific factuality evaluation, section-level correctness assessment, or expert review would substantially strengthen the paper. 2.The “hierarchical report decomposition” seems heuristic and under-specified. The paper states that keyword prompts and regular-expression-based matching are used to split reports into local, regional, and global parts. This step is important because it defines the supervision hierarchy, yet it is only briefly described. It is unclear how robust this segmentation is across reports, how much manual engineering is involved, and whether errors in this decomposition propagate into training. 3.The breadth of validation is limited, and some claims are slightly stronger than the evidence supports. The experiments use two PathText subsets and a unified feature extractor/preprocessing pipeline. It would be helpful to know whether the gains are robust across other pathology datasets, encoders, or report styles, and whether performance holds under domain shift. Then, the conclusion mentions “diagnostically accurate reports,” but no direct clinical accuracy studies or pathologist assessments are presented. That wording should be toned down unless stronger evidence is added.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their insightful comments, and especially the positive recognition of our motivation (noted as ‘clear and well justified’). [Report Decomposition (R1,R2,R3)] Reports are decomposed using a “low-level priority” regex matching principle designed by our pathologists: individual sentences are categorized via lexicons (Global: diagnosis/carcinoma/stage/grade/subtype/conclusion/overall/status/malignant/benign; Region: size/diameter/infiltration/invasion/margin/boundary/multifocal/location/gross finding/lymphovascular invasion; Local: atypia/differentiation/mitosis/necrosis/calcification/stroma/pleomorphism/papilloma/proliferative/in situ), with unmatched sentences defaulting to Global. Empty levels are backfilled with the full report. During training, the supervision of the Global level is nested, encompassing both the global report and all sub-level reports.This design ensures semantic consistency, preventing error propagation even if minor matching deviations occur. The following comparison (TCGA-B6-A0IP) validates our approach: unlike Bi-Gen, which misidentifies cancer type and size, our method ensures an accurate Global diagnosis while precisely capturing Region (size) and Local (morphology) details. GT (Decomposed): [Global] The pathological diagnosis is infiltrating carcinoma, lobular type… [Region] The gross examination revealed a 1.7 cm tumor with no lymphatic/vascular invasion. [Local] The non-neoplastic breast tissue showed proliferative fibrocystic changes. Ours: [Global] The findings are consistent with invasive lobular carcinoma of the breast… [Region] Gross examination identifies a 1.7 cm solitary lesion; no macroscopic evidence of multifocality. [Local] The presence of intraductal papilloma and fibrocystic changes. Bi-Gen: The pathological slide indicates that the patient underwent a modified radical mastectomy on the right breast. The mass was found to be a poorly differentiated invasive ductal carcinoma with a tumor size of 2.0 cm. [Evaluation Metrics (R1,R2,R3)] We report BLEU and METEOR to maintain consistency with prior MICCAI works like HistGen. To address medical validation requirements, we provide the following supplementary evaluations: Diagnostic Accuracy: Subtype identification accuracy on the BRCA dataset reached 0.613, significantly outperforming Bi-Gen (0.525). Clinical Semantics: Our model achieved a $Fact_{ent}$ score [1] of 0.483, surpassing Bi-Gen (0.479) and MI-Gen (0.467). Furthermore, balanced scores across the Local (0.535), Region (0.510), and Global (0.483) levels confirm the model’s diagnostic reliability across all granularities. [About Novelty (R1)] 1.We emphasize that this work is the first to introduce hyperbolic geometry to pathology report generation. WSIs and reports naturally possess hierarchical structures; leveraging this hierarchy effectively mitigates logical inconsistencies during report generation.
