Accordingly, we utilize Hyperbolic Space to unify both modalities. 2.The radial position constraint explicitly regulates the hierarchical mapping by embedding global features near the hyperbolic origin while pushing local details toward the boundary. 3.Unlike traditional single-modality hierarchical WSI modeling, we propose a cross-modal hierarchical framework. By using a Memory Bank to fuse historical semantic priors with current visual features, our model simulates a pathologist’s global-to-local reasoning, ensuring strict logical consistency across diagnostic granularities. [Other questions (R1)] Implementation Details: Image embedding dimension is 1024, text is 512, and initial curvature $\kappa = 1.5$. Weights for $L_{ent}$ and $L_{pos}$ are set to 0.1.Code will be open-sourced. References: The duplicate citations resulted from different BibTeX sources(GitHub vs. Google Scholar) and will be corrected in the revised version. [1] Improving factual completeness and consistency of image-to-text radiology report generation.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All three reviewers acknowledged that this paper does have merits. It proposes an interested and well justified idea. The experimental designs are also reasonable and, in principle, support the proposed idea. The paper is well written. However, the reviewers also raised some major concerns. All three reviewers consider the current evaluation is not sufficient to demonstrate the clinical effectiveness and usefulness of the proposed model. Some reviewers argued that while the idea is interesting, the methodological novelty is somehow limited. The reviewers also suggested comparisons with some recently proposed/released models. Many implementation and experiment details should be further clarified. In the rebuttal, please carefully study the comments raised by the reviewers, and provide responses to them particularly to the major concerns mentioned above. | After rebuttal, all reviewers suggest accepting this paper. Please further revise the manuscript bases on the comments in the final version. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a well-motivated and novel approach for pathology report generation by modeling the inherent local-to-global hierarchy of whole slide images within a hyperbolic Lorentz space. In their rebuttal, the authors successfully resolved the reviewers’ primary concerns by detailing the text decomposition pipeline and providing clinically meaningful evaluation metrics, such as diagnostic accuracy and factual completeness. Because all three reviewers found these additions compelling and upgraded their final opinions to “Accept,” the paper is recommended for the conference. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers appreciate the novelty of incorporating hyperbolic geometry for hierarchical modeling in pathology report generation and acknowledge the coherent framework. However, key concerns include the incremental nature of the technical contribution, limited evaluation scope, insufficient demonstration of clinical reliability, and missing methodological details. Based on the authors’ rebuttal addressing these issues satisfactorily, the general consensus is to recommend acceptance, with suggestions for further strengthening the clinical significance in the final version.

title: Harnessing Adversarial Distillation to Customise Debiased, Disease-Specific Pathology Foundation Models for Breast Cancer
reviewer_1_strengths: Well-motivated problem: Deploying billion-parameter PFMs and robust models in clinical pathology workflows is a real bottleneck. Jointly addressing model compression and bias mitigation in a single framework is a meaningful contribution, these two problems are usually tackled independently. Principled debiasing mechanism: The adversarial distillation idea is good, train a dedicated model to capture exactly what you want to remove, then use gradient reversal to penalise the student for encoding those features. This is more targeted than generic stain normalisation, which can destroy diagnostically relevant variation. Thorough experimental design: The paper evaluates across 3 external cohorts, 8 student architectures spanning CNNs and ViTs, single- and multi-teacher settings, and ablates each component (distillation → adversarial → full objective). The consistent stepwise improvement across these axes is convincing.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: BRACS performance gap remains large: On the 7-class BRACS task, even the best SmartStu variants reach ~0.51 bAcc vs. teacher baselines at ~0.51 as well, but this is still low. More critically, the gap between student and teacher is relatively small on easy binary tasks but the absolute numbers on the harder multiclass task suggest the representations may struggle with fine-grained subtyping, which is arguably the most clinically important scenario. Statistical reporting is weak: Five-run means are reported but no standard deviations or confidence intervals. Provide statistical test would make it better.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The bias-removal mechanism designed in this paper is quite innovative. By explicitly modeling and suppressing site-specific features, adversarial distillation breaks away from the passive approach of traditional distillation. Compared to the domain classifiers commonly used in domain generalization, the noise model actively captures edge-dominated interference cues (such as scanner grating and staining batch effects) rather than generic domain labels. This work achieves over 30-fold parameter compression and supports a wide range of deployment scenarios, from MobileNet to ResNet. By simulating real-world clinical variations, it enhances the model’s stability on heterogeneous data, making it highly practical for engineering applications.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Adversarial models require pre-training on multi-center data and rely on site labels. This may result in prohibitively high training costs for new diseases or rare cancers where metadata annotations are lacking. Although the attention heatmap shows that SmartStu focuses more on tumor regions, there is a lack of fine-grained visualization or ablation analysis to determine which feature channels the adversarial distillation specifically suppresses and which disease-related patterns it preserves. The entire model remains a black-box process. There are too many training hyperparameters, and since the paper doesn’t list them all, it’s very difficult to reproduce the results. Finally, is this supplementary material submission compliant with the guidelines? It seems that supplementary materials of a non-pathology demonstration type are not permitted.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Unlike standard knowledge distillation that propagates useful features from teacher including site-related bias, here in SmartStu, the use of a dedicated noise model as a counter-example (via gradient reversal) during distillation seems like a novel way to address the distribution mismatch & non-biological site-specific bias inherent in tissue agnostic pre-training Interpretability analysis is also a standout feature of the work. Authors demonstrate that adversarial debiasing leads to more biologically relevant features. Visualizations using attention heatmaps & Eigen-CAM show that SmartStu suppresses spurious background activations & concentrates its focus on actual tumor ROI, outperforming even its larger teacher models in localization Author also address the deployment bottleneck of massive PFMs in resource-constrained clinical workflows, achieving over 30x model compression while preserving or even improving downstream performance.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The current validation of the framework’s disease-specific claims is limited to breast cancer. To demonstrate broad applicability, it would be important to validate the framework on another more prevalent cancer types, such as lung or prostate cancer. Another concern is that the adversarial debiasing process may over-clean the learned representations, for eg the adversarial teacher, trained to detect site-specific signs, risks eliminating important biological variations, such as site-specific patient morphology, potentially mistaking them for nuisance noise. The paper seems to miss out a discussion or maybe a sensitivity analysis to demonstrate that this debiasing does not also remove clinically important features merely correlated with collection sites.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their thoughtful comments and for recognising the novelty, practical relevance, and strong evaluation of SmartStu. We just would like to clarify a procedural issue: the supplementary PDF was not uploaded in error. It was an anonymised version of a related concurrent MICCAI submission, provided in accordance with the MICCAI 2026 guidance for authors submitting closely related papers. We also appreciate the constructive suggestions on statistical reporting, broader disease validation, more quantitative assessment of debiasing, and further positioning against emerging compact pathology foundation models and robustness benchmarks. These comments are valuable and will inform the camera-ready version and our future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a framework for compressing large pathology foundation models into debiased, disease-specific pathology foundation models. The bias removal algorithm is novel and the parameter compression makes it very promising for real-world deployment. Most reviewers agree that the evluation is strong.

title: Hepato-LLaVA: An Expert MLLM with Sparse Topo-Pack Attention for Hepatocellular Pathology Analysis on Whole Slide Images
reviewer_1_strengths: The clinical motivation is well-grounded. The paper identifies a real limitation in existing WSI-MLLMs — the mismatch between 1D sequence modeling and the inherently 2D spatial structure of pathological tissue — and proposes a concrete architectural response. The hierarchical diagnostic reasoning embedded in the dataset pipeline (coarse-to-fine, macroscopic to microscopic) aligns with actual pathologist workflows. The Sparse Topo-Pack Attention is a reasonable design. The local-pack / summary-token structure is intuitive, and the paper makes a plausible case that it reduces redundancy compared with dense slide modeling. HepatoPathoVQA is a meaningful dataset contribution. Covering three spatial scales with both VQA pairs and caption data for pre-training, and validated by three pathologists under blind evaluation (Pearson r=0.96, <2% rejection rate), it addresses a genuine data gap in HCC-specific computational pathology. The quantitative results are strong and the ablation studies are reasonably comprehensive. The comparison across connector types, token counts, and training strategies in Tables 2 and 3 provides clear support for the main design choices. The gap between Hepato-LLaVA (Avg 0.83) and the next best method (0.66) is substantial. Code is made available via an anonymized link, which supports reproducibility.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The main weakness is that the evaluation is largely self-contained. The training data and benchmark are both derived from the same Gemini-assisted pipeline on the same pool of 200 WSIs, so it is hard to judge how much of the gain would transfer to an external cohort with independently curated labels. I also think the paper could do a better job isolating where the gains actually come from. The method combines a new sparse encoder, a new multi-scale dataset, and a multi-stage training recipe, but the ablations do not fully separate these factors. In particular, the contribution of the MoCo stage is not shown directly. Another missing piece is efficiency evidence. The paper motivates the method partly in terms of redundancy and computational cost, but does not report runtime, memory, or inference cost. Finally, the open-ended evaluation relies partly on LLM-based scoring, and I would have liked to see either stronger human evaluation or at least more detail on how reliable that metric is in this setting.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper proposes a WSI topology-aware attention mechanism. Most recent WSI models treat patch tokens as a flattened 1D sequence during processing, which overlooks the inherent 2D structure of WSIs and breaks the underlying tissue topology. In addition, tissues or lesions often span multiple neighboring patches while exhibiting weaker correlations with distant patches; thus, tokens from neighboring patches should be more important than distant tokens in the local view at the lowest scale. The proposed Sparse Topo-Pack Attention organizes patch tokens into several 2D hierarchical views and processes them hierarchically, effectively preserving the 2D tissue topology while efficiently aggregating global WSI information across patches. 2.The paper constructs a multi-scale WSI VQA dataset with three different scales of HCC samples. The authors claim that this is the first multi-scale WSI dataset for HCC, which helps bridge the gap between research datasets and real-world clinical practice, and provides a valuable resource for future studies.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The ablation study is incomplete. The paper conducts experiments on different design choices of the connector; however, the connector is only a part of the proposed MLLM. A more comprehensive ablation, with different proposed modules enabled or disabled, is suggested to better evaluate the effectiveness and individual contributions of the proposed components. 2.The proposed method is compared with six state-of-the-art methods on the constructed HCC dataset. However, although the models are trained on an HCC dataset, the proposed method may have the potential to generalize to other diseases. It would strengthen the paper, especially for a journal extension, to include comparisons on additional HCC datasets or datasets from other diseases. 3.A minor issue: the full name of VQA should be defined before introducing the abbreviation.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The motivation is well grounded, and the proposed Hepato-LLaVA surpasses previous pathology-specific multimodal large models on hepatocellular carcinoma analysis. 2.The authors also construct HepatoPathoVQA, a large-scale multi-scale dataset that provides a strong foundation for subsequent hepatocellular pathology analysis on whole-slide images. 3.In addition, they introduce HepatoPathoBench, which facilitates a more systematic evaluation of existing multimodal large models in hepatocellular pathology analysis.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The proposed Sparse Topo-Pack Attention (STPA) appears to be applied in the slide encoder, whereas the ablation results in Table 3 focus on the connector. This discrepancy makes it hard to determine whether STPA itself improves token efficiency. 2.The paper also introduces additional MAE pretraining and MoCo pretraining stages, both of which may bring independent performance gains. Since existing models such as SlideChat and WSI-LLaVA do not adopt these training stages, it remains unclear whether the performance improvement truly comes from STPA.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all the reviewers and the Area Chair for their insightful comments and recognition of our work. Below, we address the main concerns regarding Ablation, Data, and Inference. Q1.Ablation (Component Disentanglement & STPA Effectiveness) Dear reviewer #2, #3, #4, Our proposed modules act as an integrated whole to solve redundancy and information deficiency issues in existing slide encoders when processing WSIs. Both the MoCo training and the Q-Former connector depend on the summary tokens produced by the STPA slide encoder. Due to this tight coupling and strict page limits, our paper only included the connector ablation. We now provide additional results on HepatoPathoBench. First, Hepto-LLaVA w/o MoCo scored 0.75, validating the effectiveness of our two-stage pre-training strategy. Although lower than our full Hepto-LLaVA (0.83), it still higher than SlideChat (0.66) and WSI-LLaVA (0.65), which is also consistent with the findings of Prov-GigaPath[1]. Second, fine-tuned WSI-LLaVA scored 0.70, which uses LongNet as the slide encoder and trains on the same dataset. This is higher than WSI-LLaVA (0.65) but lower than Hepto-LLaVA (0.83), directly validating the effectiveness of our designed STPA architecture. Together with the additional ablation results, these findings further demonstrate that the performance gains mainly originate from our designed STPA architecture, and that each proposed component consistently contributes to the overall improvement. Q2.Data (Quality, Evaluation Fairness, and Generalization) Dear reviewer #2, #3, We strictly separate the training and validation sets at the patient level with no WSI overlap. All samples are generated through the same unified pipeline rather than curated as dataset-specific groups. To guarantee high quality and avoid homogenization, the pipeline integrates 3 different resolutions and 8 sub-categories, and all annotations were subjected to strict quality control. Three professional pathologists conducted blind evaluations of the generated data, achieving high consistency (Pearson r=0.96) and a rejection rate of <2\%. Furthermore, the LLM-based open-ended evaluation results strongly align with our human expert judgments. We also note that the currently available HCC subset in WSI-Bench contains only 27 WSIs and 103 QA pairs, while our HepatoPathoBench further introduces multi-resolution evaluation, making the benchmark more comprehensive and challenging. To further validate cross-dataset generalization, we directly evaluated our model on the HCC subset of WSI-Bench without additional adaptation. Our Hepto-LLaVA scored 0.502, remaining competitive with the current SOTA result of 0.566. Q3.Efficiency and Computational Complexity Dear reviewer #2, #4 By restricting patch-level interactions within local packs and utilizing summary tokens for inter-pack global context, STPA reduces the theoretical attention overhead to roughly 1%. Coupled with a lightweight backbone and blank-patch filtering, our end-to-end feature extraction (from SVS to PT tensors) averages 4.3 mins/slide, a significant acceleration compared to the 19.3 mins/slide required by Prov-GigaPath [1]. Furthermore, our slide encoder and connector condense the final visual input for the LLM to just 32 tokens, whereas Prov-GigaPath requires 576 tokens, yielding substantial efficiency advantages during downstream LLM processing. Q4.The Minor Issue Dear reviewer #3 We will add the full definition of Visual Question Answering (VQA) before its first occurrence in the revised manuscript. [1] Xu et al., “A whole-slide foundation model for digital pathology from real-world data”, Nature 2024.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper introduces a multi-modal large language model for fine-grained analysis of hepatocellular pathology which utilizes a “sparse Topo-pack” attention mechanism to integrate local and global information. Additionally, they introduce a multi-scale visual-question-answering dataset, HepatoPathoVQA. Reviewers agree that the dataset with its multi-scale setup addresses an important task and gap in digital pathology. They further appreciate the overall design of the attention mechanism and the model from coarse to fine. They criticize, however, that the evaluation is largely self-contained (see comments below) and that the ablation studies do not sufficiently disentangle all components. Additionally, no information about runtime or computational complexity is provided. In the rebuttal, the authors should address how reliable/independent a benchmark is on a dataset that shares substantial parts of the pipeline with the pipeline for generating training data, and why performance improvements can be expected to translate to independent tasks or datasets. Furthermore, please address the comment on how well the ablation studies demonstrate the utility of the proposed method and to what extent changing (pre-)training steps may bias the results. Please note there should be no new results added in the rebuttal phase. | Reviewers agree that the authors adequately addressed concerns in their rebuttal and univocally vote for acceptance. The overall assessment however may be seen as borderline as the authors added new ablation studies in their rebuttal. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a meaningful methodological contribution, supported by a valuable dataset resource and strong experimental results. Overall, the paper is considered to make a solid contribution and meets the acceptance threshold for MICCAI. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The main concerns raised by reviewers are the lack of external validation, reliance on a self-constructed benchmark, and insufficient evidence supporting the effectiveness of the Sparse Topo-Pack Attention strategy for HCC pathology. The authors have addressed most of the concerns in the rebuttal.

title: HERO: Hypothesis-Driven Evidence Retrieval from Omics for Multi-task Breast Cancer Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: This paper presents an interesting and well-motivated framework for multi-task breast cancer analysis from whole-slide images and matched multi-omics. The main strength of the work is its clear methodological position. Instead of treating omics as a standard parallel feature stream, the proposed method uses omics to guide two key parts of the pipeline: where to look in the slide and whether the retrieved visual evidence is sufficient to support the molecular hypothesis. This is an important distinction from prior approaches, which mainly rely on post-hoc MIL localization, VLM-based reading without specific priors, or conventional multimodal fusion. In this sense, the paper offers a clear and recognizable contribution. Another strong point is the coherence of the overall design. The pipeline forms a closed loop from the omics-derived intent vector m, to the keyword set Q, to Top-64 patch retrieval, to the visual evidence vector v, the consistency score c, the deficit term d=m−v, and finally the repair step. This information flow is logically connected and easy to follow. I also appreciate that the method uses checklist matching and TF-IDF retrieval instead of relying only on embedding-based retrieval. This makes the retrieval and verification process more transparent and easier to inspect.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Insufficient methodological detail limits reproducibility. The paper presents a clear four-stage framework, but many details that are important for reproduction are still missing. For example, the prompts, output formats, decoding settings, and keyword extraction rules are not fully described. These are not minor implementation choices, because they directly affect retrieval quality and evidence verification. 2.Eq. (1) and several Stage 1 definitions remain unclear. The formulation of Eq. (1) is not fully precise, especially the normalization term, whose exact meaning is difficult to interpret from the current text. In addition, the paper does not provide the full definitions of the 16 morphology axes, the checklist terms, or the detailed pathway-to-axis assignments in W. As a result, the proposed prior is conceptually appealing, but still difficult to reproduce in practice. 3.The implementation of Stage 3 repair is still under-specified. Stage 3 is one of the most important parts of the method, but some key steps are not explained clearly enough. In particular, it is not clear how the final “best 64” patches are selected after the repair patches are added back to the pool. It is also unclear whether the model captions the full 8×8 mosaic, each 20× patch separately, or both. 4.The text-based bridge is interesting, but it may introduce a same-model bias. The method uses text as an intermediate bridge between omics and image evidence, which is an interesting design choice. However, the same model family is used both to generate intermediate captions and to make the final prediction. The paper shows that Qwen2.5-VL can generate captions, but it does not yet show strongly enough that these captions are pathologically accurate and stable enough to support the downstream reasoning process. Why not chose medical domian VLMs ? 5.The risk of shortcut learning from omics is not fully excluded. The omics input is highly related to several prediction targets, especially HER2, subtype, and possibly risk. This raises the concern that the model may rely heavily on molecular priors instead of truly learning to organize image evidence. Although the paper compares different retrieval strategies under the same diagnosis head, stronger control experiments, such as removing or shuffling omics, would be needed to rule out this alternative explanation more convincingly. 6.The data and label sources are not described clearly enough. The experimental section clearly reports the TCGA-BRCA cohort, including 930 WSIs, 878 patients, 14,115 CpGs, and 315 miRNAs, as well as the prediction targets ER, PR, HER2, subtype, and risk. However, the manuscript does not explain in enough detail how these target labels were obtained or defined. For example, it is unclear whether ER/PR/HER2 labels come from IHC/ISH results or from clinical phenotype tables, how subtype is defined, and how the risk labels are constructed. This weakens the interpretation of the results, especially because omics is used as an input while the targets are also strongly related to molecular status. 7.The fairness of the baseline comparison needs to be discussed more carefully. The paper states that, for fairness, all multimodal baselines were implemented using the same concatenated DNA methylation and miRNA vectors as the proposed method. While this makes the input setting more uniform, it may also move some baselines away from their original or best-performing configurations. As a result, the comparison may reflect performance under a unified input protocol rather than the true strength of each baseline in its intended setting. This point is particularly important for methods such as MCAT, MOTCat, and SurvPath, which are based on different modeling assumptions. 8.External validation is missing. All experiments are conducted on TCGA-BRCA using patient-level 5-fold cross-validation, which is a reasonable internal evaluation setup. However, this is still a single-dataset, single-cohort, and single-cancer study. For a method that depends heavily on caption quality, predefined vocabularies, and omics-to-morphology correspondence, the lack of external validation makes it difficult to assess robustness across scanners, staining conditions, institutions, and population shifts. The proposed consistency gate may improve internal reliability, but it does not by itself demonstrate cross-center generalization. 9.Table 3 provides only limited support for the importance of W. The paper uses W-noise, W-drop, and W-shuffle to argue that the prior W captures meaningful biological structure. However, noise and drop lead to only small performance changes, while shuffle causes a more visible drop. This suggests that the coarse structure of W may be useful, but it does not strongly demonstrate that the precise expert-designed mapping is essential. In addition, the paper does not clearly define how noise and drop are implemented or how strong these perturbations are, which makes the robustness claim harder to evaluate. 10.The ablation study is still incomplete. The paper focuses the main ablation study on HER2 and Risk, which is reasonable because these tasks are likely to depend strongly on retrieval quality. However, since the method is presented as a unified multi-task framework, it would also be useful to show whether similar trends hold for ER, PR, and subtype. In addition, while the paper shows that text-based retrieval outperforms visual-only retrieval and that gate+repair is helpful, it does not provide more direct ablations of the final diagnosis stage, such as using only the final 20× mosaic, only the molecular narrative, only the consistency summary, or removing the narrative input altogether. Without these analyses, the contribution of each Stage 4 input remains unclear.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: One notable aspect is the concept itself. Most papers merely regard biological data as an additional feature or something similar. However, in this case, it is utilized as a hypothesis that directs the entire retrieval process. I appreciate this methodology. The consistency gate mechanism, where the author(s) assess whether the observed image corresponds with the molecular signal, is quite ingenious. If the score falls below a certain threshold, it automatically seeks different patches. This approach is logical. The results are also exceptionally robust. The author(s) conducted tests on the TCGA dataset, which comprises 930 slide images, and they outperformed all other methods. The enhancement in HER2 is 0.050 AUC, which is a significant figure. Additionally, the improvement in risk prediction is 0.030 C-index. These enhancements are particularly noteworthy for challenging prediction tasks. Another commendable aspect is the transparency of the system’s operations. One can observe which regions it focuses on, the features it identifies, and how these contribute to the final outcome. This transparency is crucial for doctors or clinics, as they need to understand the rationale behind the machine’s decisions. The author(s) employ word matching instead of complex embedding techniques, which ensures that interpretations do not deviate into nonsensical territory. Everything can be traced back to the actual text. The ablation study presented in table 2 is informative. When the author(s) compare text-based retrieval with visual-only embedding, the text-based approach significantly outperforms by a margin of 0.077 on HER2 AUC. This finding is intriguing as it indicates that the significance of pathology terminology outweighs the aesthetic appeal or prominence of the images. Furthermore, the robustness aspect concerning the W matrix is commendable. The author(s) manually constructed W based on medical guidelines, and when they shuffled it, the performance decreased by 0.033.In contrast, when they merely added noise, the performance drop was only 0.009.This demonstrates that the author(s) are not merely fitting random elements but are genuinely encoding authentic biological knowledge.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Initially, the author(s) conduct tests using only a single dataset. While TCGA is well-known, it is essential to evaluate other datasets to demonstrate the general applicability of the findings. Furthermore, the 930 slides are relatively small compared to contemporary standards. Regarding the axes defined, specifically the 16 morphological features, are this exclusive to breast cancer? Can this methodology be applied to other types of cancer? This remains uncertain. Additionally, the speed of the process raises concerns. They report a duration of 57 seconds per slide using two powerful GPUs, which is quite substantial. In a real hospital setting, such a wait time per case is impractical. Moreover, the VLM model is invoked multiple times at various stages, and the repair process occurs in 37% of the slides, indicating a significant amount of additional computation. The authors should provide more insight into which components consume the most time. Why was K=16 selected in the first place? As shown in Table 3, K=32 yields nearly identical results (0.867 vs. 0.865). Why not opt for 32 or even 8? Although they perform a sensitivity analysis, this suggests that the author(s) may not have thoroughly optimized this parameter. Which specific 16 axes did the author(s) choose, and what was the rationale behind selecting these particular axes? There is also a lack of discussion regarding potential failures (the sad path). They present one successful case in Figure 3, but what happens when the system identifies incorrect regions? What if the genetic data does not align with the morphological data? Such discrepancies can occur in real cancer cases. While the consistency gate provides some assistance, what about these adverse scenarios? The entire system relies on the Qwen2.5-VL model for generating image captions. If this model inaccurately describes the morphological features, it could lead to failures downstream. They claim that a structured prompt enhances reliability, yet the author(s) do not provide any analysis to support this. For instance, how often does the VLM misdescribe features? What percentage of the captions is genuinely accurate? The construction of the W matrix is also ambiguous. The author(s) mention adherence to WHO guidelines, but the specifics are unclear. What happens when different pathways suggest the same axis? To what extent is human judgment involved in this process? Would different individuals arrive at different W constructions? Finally, for actual deployment in a hospital setting, validation on entirely different datasets is necessary. This includes variations in hospitals, scanners, and staining techniques. Five- Five-Fold CV on single dataset is not enough.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Novelty: HERO’s main strength is the introduction of a RAG-like pipeline for whole slide images (WSIs), where retrieval is not treated as a one-shot step but is coupled with a verification and repair loop. This verify-retry mechanism ensures that retrieved omics evidence is actively checked against expectations and refined when necessary, leading to more reliable outputs. The approach also represents a shift from standard practices.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Abstract’s opening claim: The first sentence of the abstract appears somewhat strong, as there is existing literature supporting the claim that predicting biomarkers and prognosis from WSIs benefits from matched multi-omics data. For example: Hu, Jia, et al. “Prediction of clinicopathological features, multi-omics events and prognosis based on digital pathology and deep learning in HR+/HER2− breast cancer.” Journal of thoracic disease 15.5 (2023): 2528.- Terminology and claims in the introduction: The term “evidence drift” could be reconsidered in favor of more established terminology such as “retrieval bias”, which may better convey the underlying issue. Additionally, the statement that VLM-based WSI readers and multi-agent systems explore without endpoint-specific priors appears somewhat strong. In practice, such priors can often be incorporated through prompting, and acknowledging this could provide a more balanced perspective. Limited clarity in methodology: While the architectural components are presented, the overall description remains quite concise, which may hinder full comprehension. In particular, some variables and acronyms are not explicitly defined. A more structured and detailed exposition of the pipeline, including clearer definitions and intermediate steps, would improve readability and make the method easier to follow. Training and fine-tuning details: It is not entirely clear why only Stage 4 is fine-tuned with LoRA. Clarification on whether tuning other stages was considered, and how this might affect performance, would be valuable. Moreover, additional details on the training process across all models, especially regarding convergence criteria and fine-tuning protocols for the baselines, would help ensure a fair and transparent comparison.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their careful reading and constructive feedback. It is encouraging that the main point of HERO was clear: we use omics not as another feature vector, but as a hypothesis that tells the model where to look and then checks whether the retrieved tissue evidence agrees with it. Several parts of the paper were too compressed, and a few claims should be worded more carefully. We do not add new experiments here; instead, we will use the camera-ready revision to add concise clarifications where space permits. We will add a compact algorithm/table with the 16 morphology axes, example checklist terms, the Stage-1 output schema, the 10x/20x prompts, decoding settings, and the construction and perturbation of W. Eq. (1) will be rewritten to state that the denominator is pathway-wise averaging over selected features, and that the negative sign converts promoter hypermethylation and miRNA-mediated repression into pathway down-regulation scores. We will also state that W is binary/nonnegative before row normalization, fixed across folds, and not learned from endpoint labels.We will also clarify the repair step. The 10x captions are generated for the 300 representative patches. The selected 20x crops are arranged into a coordinate-labeled 8x8 mosaic and processed by the VLM in one call, which returns structured tile descriptions. If c < tau_c, we compute the deficit from m-v, score unselected representatives by score_10 + w’^T a_i, add the top 32 candidates, and rebuild the final 64-patch mosaic from this repaired pool before one more 20x captioning pass. This final selection step will be described more clearly. We do not claim that omics alone is uninformative; several targets are molecularly related by definition. Our point is that HERO uses omics to organize visual evidence, not to replace it. We will clarify that endpoint labels come from TCGA clinical/molecular annotations and survival endpoints, not from the input omics vectors used by HERO, and we will spell out the definitions for ER/PR/HER2, subtype, and risk. We will also soften wording such as “prevents shortcut learning”: W, lexical retrieval, and the controlled VLM baselines are safeguards and diagnostic checks, not proof that shortcuts are impossible.For baselines and parameters, we will add the missing caveats. Multimodal baselines were run with the same DNA methylation+miRNA input for a controlled comparison, but this may not be each method’s best original setting. K=16 was chosen as a practical middle point: K=8 is less specific, while K=32 gives little extra gain but requires more vocabulary design. tau_c=0.5 was not tuned per endpoint; the sensitivity results show similar behavior from 0.3 to 0.7.We will also define W-noise, W-drop, W-shuffle, and state that TF-IDF is fit locally on the 300 representative captions of each slide. Only Stage 4 is tuned because Stages 1-3 are kept deterministic and frozen, so the effect of the retrieval and verification mechanism can be isolated. We used Qwen2.5-VL because it gives an open and reproducible captioning/diagnosis pipeline under one setup. However, structured prompting does not guarantee pathologic correctness. We will revise the text to say that checklist matching and the consistency gate make the evidence chain inspectable, while caption errors and possible same-model bias remain limitations.Finally, we will state the other limitations more directly. TCGA-BRCA 5-fold CV is internal validation. We also acknowledge the computational overhead (57s/WSI) raised by Reviewer #3; optimizing the multi-stage VLM calls and inference speed is a critical next step before real-world clinical deployment. We will replace or qualify “evidence drift” as “retrieval bias”, soften the abstract opening, improve Fig. 3 readability, fix the long equation formatting, and add the missing LoRA/training details.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The authors propose HERO, a novel retrievel framework to integrate omics data in computational pathology analysis. While the paper could benefit from providing more methodological details and experimental reporting, all reviewers agree that the method is novel and promising. The paper can create opportunity for discussion and potentially inspire similar work. Therefore I recommend acceptance.

title: HomoSeg: A Weak-Label-Guided Semi-supervised Framework for Tumor Microenvironment Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper proposes a data reconstruction strategy that formalizes the pathological prior that WSI-cropped patches tend to contain a single tissue category, enabling supervised training subset construction without any pixel-level annotation. The paper introduces a superpixel-based synthesis strategy that improves boundary quality over standard CutMix, where irregular boundaries better align with real tissue morphology and directly address the most challenging boundary regions in TME segmentation. The paper incorporates an offline distillation strategy that substantially reduces training cost without compromising segmentation accuracy, offering practical reference value for clinical deployment scenarios.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The paper lacks quantitative evidence to support the homogeneity hypothesis. The authors do not report the actual proportion of single-label patches within the training set, making it impossible to assess the validity of this prior across the utilized datasets or the sensitivity of the proposed method to this assumption. The paper exhibits high architectural similarity to HisynSeg, as both leverage image synthesis and consistency regularization for weakly supervised pathology segmentation. However, the manuscript fails to provide a targeted comparative analysis to clarify the fundamental methodological distinctions between the two frameworks. The paper adopts a pseudo-label generation strategy for CAM calibration that simply computes an unweighted average of CAM activations and segmentation predictions. This approach fails to model the confidence disparity between the two branches, potentially introducing noise during early training stages when both components are unstable. Notably, the paper provides neither analytical discussion nor ablation studies to justify this design. The paper lacks a discussion on the application boundaries of the proposed method. Its performance remains unverified in scenarios involving rare tissue categories or extreme class imbalances, leaving the limits of its generalization capability unclear.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The authors propose a novel data reformulation strategy based on the observation that all pixels in a patch can share the same label when the patch contains only a single tissue type. This strategy is useful for converting weak labels into dense labels and further supports synthetic data generation. 2.The HomoSeg framework achieves satisfying experimental performance.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The proposed method has a fairly heavy design with many components, while each individual component brings only marginal gains, as shown in Table 2.In particular, synthetic data generation appears to be a substantial part of the claimed contribution, but removing it leads to only limited performance differences, especially on LUAD-HistoSeg. 2.Regarding the semi-supervised part: the labeled/unlabeled split with a Siamese network, strong/weak augmentations, multi-task co-training, using CAM for pseudo-label generation, and the loss designs all seem to be fairly common practices in semi-supervised learning from recent years. Rather than simply stacking these components together, could the authors clarify what the main distinguishing idea of this part is? 3.Regarding the distillation part: the paper does not specify how the student model is initialized, and I assume it is trained from scratch. The supervision signal is derived from the averaged CAM and teacher predictions, so its performance should in principle be bounded by that signal unless there is some additional design that enables further improvement. Why not directly use the combined teacher and CAM predictions instead of retraining a student model? I am also confused by the comparison in Table 3.My understanding is that the teacher model corresponds to the full pipeline in Stage II, while the student model is the distilled encoder-decoder segmentation model. However, the student model cannot exist unless the teacher model has already been trained. In that case, distillation does not reduce the end-to-end training time or memory cost, and the reported inference time also shows no difference. 4.Some presentation details also need clarification. In Figure 1, please specify what “SSN” stands for, either in the figure or in the main text. In Equations (2) and (3), does the symbol denotes multiplication? In Table 1, please also define the abbreviations such as TE and NEC.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1) Elegant exploitation of a domain-specific prior. The observation that WSI patches tend to be spatially homogeneous and thus single-label patches yield reliable global pixel masks, is both biologically motivated and practically effective. This insight elegantly bridges the gap between weak and semi-supervised learning without any additional annotation cost. 2) Well-integrated three-stage pipeline. The three components (data reformulation, semi-supervised training, distillation) are logically coherent and each addresses a distinct limitation of the prior stages. The CAM-calibrated pseudo-label fusion (Eq. 7) is a sensible design to handle early-training instability in the segmentation branch. 3) Computational efficiency gains from distillation. Table 3 shows a dramatic reduction in training cost (852 > 217 s/epoch, 17.89 > 5.74 GB GPU memory) with simultaneous accuracy improvement, which is practically very relevant for clinical deployment.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1) Single-label proportion not reported. The central assumption of the method, that a meaningful proportion of training patches are single-label, is never quantified for either dataset. If only a small fraction of samples satisfy ||y||₁ = 1, the homogeneity-driven reformulation may be of limited benefit, and the method may not generalize to datasets with different WSI cropping strategies or tumor types. 2) No comparison with pixel-supervised upper bounds. The paper does not include any fully supervised baseline to provide an upper bound on performance. Without this, it is unclear how much of the performance gap remains relative to the “ideal” scenario, which would better contextualize the practical clinical utility. 3) Limited discussion of failure cases. The qualitative results in Fig. 2 show only relatively favorable examples. There is no analysis of where HomoSeg fails (e.g., rare tissue categories, highly ambiguous boundaries, samples that violate the homogeneity assumption), which would help readers understand the method’s limitations. 4) Synthetic data realism is not validated. The superpixel-based CutMix synthesis creates composite images with artificial tissue boundary arrangements that do not occur in real histology. There is no qualitative or quantitative analysis of how realistic or harmful these synthetic boundaries are. The claim that they are “morphologically realistic” is not substantiated beyond the method description.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the Meta-Reviewers and reviewers for your constructive feedback. We address core concerns below, with all evidence strictly from the submitted manuscript. We systematically clarify the key issues: 1.Homogeneity Hypothesis Validation & Application (R1Q1/Q4, R3Q1, Meta) Exact dataset statistics: 27.55% of LUAD-HistoSeg and 40.04% of BCSS-WSSS training patches are single-label, confirming spatial homogeneity is prevalent in WSI cropping. Our method does not require majority single-label samples. The mined subset only serves as initialization anchors, with weak-to-strong consistency propagating supervision to all multi-label samples. The submitted results demonstrate robustness to extreme class imbalance: HomoSeg achieves 77.32% mIoU on the 4.18% rare LYM category and outperforms all SOTA methods on the minority NEC category. 2.Methodological novelty of HomoSeg (R1Q2, R2Q2, Meta) The core contribution of HomoSeg is not simply stacking semi-supervised modules, but reformulating strict weakly supervised tissue segmentation into a semi-supervised paradigm without manual pixel-level annotations. Existing WSSS methods suffer from localization bias, while conventional SSSS frameworks require expensive pixel-level labels. HomoSeg bridges these paradigms by automatically constructing a reliable labeled subset through spatial homogeneity mining. Furthermore, compared to HisynSeg, HomoSeg differs fundamentally: (1)Framework: HisynSeg combines disjoint fully/weakly supervised learning; HomoSeg reformulates the task as a unified semi-supervised framework. (2)Strategy: HisynSeg uses mathematical generation (Bézier curves) introducing artificial structures; HomoSeg uses superpixel-based CutMix preserving real biological boundaries. (3)Consistency: HisynSeg only enforces CAM-segmentation consistency; HomoSeg implements weak-to-strong consistency leveraging unlabeled data directly. Results validate these advantages: HomoSeg outperforms HisynSeg by 3.06% mIoU and 1.69%. 3.Pseudo-label Strategy & Component Synergy(R1Q3, R2Q1Q3, R3Q2, Meta) Clearer experimental analysis and interpretation. The moderate performance gain from synthesis on LUAD-HistoSeg mainly arises from its lower proportion of single-label samples, limiting synthesis diversity compared with BCSS-WSSS. Regarding the unweighted CAM-segmentation averaging, we intentionally adopt a simple calibration mechanism to avoid introducing noisy confidence estimation under weak supervision. The averaging acts as a lightweight mutual regularization between localization priors and dense predictions. Furthermore, the student surpasses the teacher because the teacher is optimized under multi-task objectives with dynamic pseudo-label noise, whereas the student learns from static, refined ensemble targets under a single segmentation objective. This offline distillation mainly aims to suppress optimization noise, simplify the optimization pipeline, and reduce computational overhead compared with iterative refinement strategies. Finally, a recent TMI 2025 study showed that advanced weakly supervised pathology segmentation can approach fully supervised performance with only marginal gaps on BCSS-WSSS, justifying current upper bounds. 4.Regarding synthetic realism (R3 Q4) Unlike rectangular CutMix, our superpixel strategy inherently preserves tissue continuity. These synthesized boundaries serve as auxiliary perturbations for consistency regularization rather than direct pixel-level targets, making our morphology-driven approach significantly more histologically plausible than mathematical geometric synthesis. 5.Clarity & Reproducibility (All Reviewers) We sincerely apologize for unclear presentations, and will revise the final manuscript to complete missing abbreviations, clarify symbol definitions, correct grammatical errors, and publicly release the full code and pre-trained models.. Thank you again for your valuable time and feedback, which has greatly improved our manuscript.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Authors should meticulously address reviewers’ concerns. Especially, the concerns about the homogeneity hypothesis, method novelty, more clear experimental result analysis, and critical settings (i.e., proportion of single label), etc. | The reviewers recognize the value and effectiveness of the proposed framework, and the rebuttal addressed several clarification concerns, leading to two positive recommendations. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes HomoSeg, a weak-label-guided semi-supervised framework for tumor microenvironment segmentation. The key idea is to exploit the spatial homogeneity prior in histopathology, where a WSI-cropped local patch often contains a single tissue category, to transform image-level weak labels into pixel-level supervision. The framework uses a data reconstruction strategy, superpixel-based synthesis, and consistency/distillation components to reduce the cost of pixel-level annotations for TME segmentation. The initial reviews were mixed but overall positive, with scores of 2 / 4 / 4.Reviewers 2 and 3 appreciated the practical motivation, the weak-to-semi-supervised reformulation, the attempt to reduce dense annotation burden, and the reported empirical gains over existing methods. Reviewer 1 was substantially more critical and raised concerns about the validity of the spatial homogeneity hypothesis, the lack of quantitative evidence supporting that assumption, the unclear distinction between weakly supervised and semi-supervised formulations, limited comparative analysis against relevant WSSS and semi-supervised methods, insufficient ablation of the core modules, and unclear application boundaries. The rebuttal addressed several of these concerns. The authors provided dataset statistics supporting the prevalence of single-label patches, clarified that the mined single-label subset is used only as initialization anchors rather than requiring most samples to be single-label, and argued that weak-to-strong consistency propagates supervision to multi-label samples. They also clarified the methodological distinction between HomoSeg, HistoSeg, and HiSynSeg, explaining that HomoSeg reformulates strict WSSS into a semi-supervised framework without manual pixel-level annotation. The rebuttal further explained the role of superpixel-based synthesis, pseudo-label calibration, offline distillation, and consistency regularization, and committed to improving clarity and reproducibility. Some limitations remain. The spatial homogeneity assumption is better supported after rebuttal, but it remains a dataset- and patch-size-dependent prior that should be discussed carefully. The paper should also more clearly define its application boundaries, especially for highly heterogeneous TME regions. Some of the comparison and ablation concerns remain only partially addressed, and the final version should strengthen the explanation of why each component is needed and where the method may fail. After rebuttal, the reviewer opinions are R / A / A. Reviewer 1 maintained reject, stating that the rebuttal improved clarity but did not fully resolve concerns about the homogeneity assumption, methodological distinction, and lack of targeted validation. Reviewers 2 and 3 recommended accept, with Reviewer 3 noting that the authors clarified the requested experimental details and addressed other concerns. Reviewer 2 also found the weak-to-semi reformulation acceptable despite noting that the pipeline remains somewhat complex. I recommend Accept. Although one reviewer remained unconvinced, the majority of post-rebuttal opinions are positive, and the rebuttal substantially improved the framing of the key assumption and methodological contribution. The paper addresses an important annotation-cost problem in tumor microenvironment segmentation and presents a practically useful framework. The remaining concerns should be explicitly discussed in the camera-ready version, especially the limits of the spatial homogeneity prior, application boundaries, and the need for clearer ablation and comparison details. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After carefully reviewing the rebuttal and the post-rebuttal reviewer comments, my recommendation is to accept the paper. The paper proposes HomoSeg, a weak-label-guided semi-supervised framework for tumor microenvironment segmentation in histopathology images. Its main contribution is the use of a spatial homogeneity prior to reformulate image-level weak labels into dense supervisory signals, followed by semi-supervised learning and offline distillation. The reviewers generally recognized this as a useful and domain-relevant idea, with consistent empirical improvements on public pathology benchmarks and practical efficiency gains from distillation. Although concerns remain regarding the quantitative validation of the homogeneity assumption, the distinction from closely related methods such as HisynSeg, and the complexity of the overall pipeline, the majority of reviewers found the rebuttal acceptable and supported acceptance. Therefore, I recommend acceptance, with the expectation that the authors will more clearly quantify the homogeneity assumption, clarify methodological differences from prior work, and discuss failure cases and application boundaries in the final version.

title: Hyperbolic Contrastive Learning with Entailment for Spatial Transcriptomics
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper proposes a hyperbolic contrastive learning framework that maps histopathology patches and gene expression embeddings into a shared hyperbolic space, aiming to capture the intrinsic hierarchical relationships in spatial transcriptomics data. 2.The proposed gene-to-image entailment loss captures the asymmetric relationship between gene expression and tissue morphology, going beyond conventional symmetric contrastive alignment. 3.The experimental evaluation is conducted on 26 datasets under the SpaRED benchmark, with consistent improvements in both MSE and PCC, and is supported by ablation studies validating the roles of hyperbolic geometry and entailment objectives.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The claim that hyperbolic space better captures hierarchical structure is not fully substantiated, as the hierarchical relationships in gene expression or tissue organization are not explicitly analyzed or validated. 2.The method ultimately relies on a retrieval-based prediction scheme (top-k nearest gene embeddings), which limits its ability to model the underlying gene expression generation process. 3.The experimental comparison includes several methods that are relatively dated, which may limit how well the results reflect performance against more recent approaches. 4.The framework builds on pretrained foundation models (UNI2-h and Geneformer), but the contribution of the proposed hyperbolic contrastive learning is not clearly isolated from that of the underlying pretrained representations. 5.While the method improves MSE and PCC, the performance gains are relatively limited, and the biological relevance of the learned representations is not further validated through additional analysis or interpretation.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1）Introduce a novel gene-to-image entailment loss that addresses the conceptual shortcomings of previous contrastive learning methods, which treat the image-gene relationship as purely symmetric. 2) The transition to hyperbolic space is fundamentally motivated by the hierarchical structures inherent in gene regulation. This provides a significantly stronger inductive bias for modeling biological data compared to standard Euclidean distance metrics.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1).The directional ablation is not fully convincing. Although “gene entails image” performs better than “image entails gene” (0.899 vs. 0.919 MSE), the gap is small, and the paper does not report per-dataset results or statistical testing for this comparison. It is therefore unclear whether this reflects a robust effect across all 26 datasets or only a marginal average gain. 2) The retrieval-based inference is insufficiently analyzed. Prediction relies on k-nearest-neighbor retrieval in the learned hyperbolic space, but the paper does not discuss how this strategy generalizes when test samples are underrepresented in the training set, such as rare morphologies or distribution-shifted cases.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: (1)The motivation for using hyperbolic space is sensible in this setting, since the authors argue that gene regulation and tissue morphology are organized in a hierarchical way. This makes the method feel more principled than many purely architectural refinements. (2)The proposed gene-to-image entailment loss is a nice addition. The paper does not simply assume that image and gene embeddings should be matched symmetrically; instead, it encodes the idea that gene expression constrains morphology. I think this is one of the more interesting parts of the paper, and the directionality experiment in the ablation section helps support that this choice is meaningful rather than arbitrary. (3)The results are reported on 26 SpaRED datasets, which gives a broader picture than papers evaluated on only a few datasets. The comparison set is also reasonably strong and includes several recent methods. HyCLoST achieves the best average MSE and PCC, and the statistical testing further strengthens the empirical claim. (4)The visual comparisons suggest that the method is better at preserving spatial variation and dynamic range, while some competing methods tend to produce flatter predictions. Since over-smoothing is one of the issues raised early in the paper, it is good to see qualitative evidence that the proposed method addresses that point.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: (1)At inference time, predictions are obtained by averaging the gene expression vectors of the top-k nearest training gene embeddings. This is simple and effective, but it may raise questions about sensitivity to k, memory/computation at scale, and whether a more direct decoding strategy could further improve generalization. The paper specifies k=80, but deeper analysis of robustness to this choice would strengthen the work. (2)The model relies on foundation encoders (UNI2-h and Geneformer) and hyperbolic operations. Although embeddings are precomputed to reduce computation, the paper provides limited discussion of training/inference efficiency, resource requirements, and whether the method is practical in lower-resource settings.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for recognizing HyCLoST’s contributions: hyperbolic contrastive learning for spatial transcriptomics (ST) alignment, directional gene-to-image entailment, and broad SpaRED evaluation with statistical testing, ablations, and qualitative evidence. We respond by issue. Hyperbolic motivation and isolation from foundation encoders (R1, Meta). HyCLoST treats hyperbolic geometry as an inductive bias for the multi-scale organization, linking tissue morphology to underlying regulatory programs [8]. We do not claim to discover a new biological hierarchy; rather, we test this inductive bias through controlled comparisons. Tab 2 provides this test under matched conditions: replacing hyperbolic with Euclidean while keeping identical UNI2-h/Geneformer increases MSE from 0.899 to 1.043, isolating the geometric contribution from the foundation encoders. Leveraging strong pretrained representations is complementary to our approach, as improvements in foundation models can directly benefit our framework. We will clarify this motivation and biological scope. Directional entailment (R2). Gene-to-image entailment encodes a biological asymmetry: gene expression is the underlying causal state and image morphology its observable manifestation, so morphology should be “entailed by” expression rather than the reverse. Tab. 2 (Row 5 vs Row 7) compares gene-to-image vs image-to-gene under identical settings on all datasets; gene-to-image yields lower average MSE (0.899 vs 0.919), consistent with the biological asymmetry argued in Sec. 2.3.The mean gap is moderate, but the effect is consistent across datasets. Inspecting the per-dataset results underlying Tab. 2, gene-to-image obtains lower MSE in 21/26 datasets and higher PCC in 23/26.We will discuss these results in the final version. Retrieval robustness, k-sensitivity and scalability (all reviewers). Sec. 2 specifies non-parametric inference: each test patch is projected and predicted by averaging its top-k nearest training gene embeddings under the Lorentzian inner product (k=80, Sec. 3.1). The design is motivated by SpaRED’s heterogeneity across tissues and species: a single parametric decoder must compress these heterogeneous output distributions, whereas retrieval adapts locally to the nearest learned morphologies. At scale, embeddings are precomputed once per dataset, so KNN cost grows linearly with dataset size and remains negligible relative to encoding. We acknowledge finer k-sensitivity and alternative decoder studies as valuable future work, but per the rebuttal guidelines, we do not introduce new experiments here. Efficiency and practicality (R4). UNI2-h/Geneformer embeddings are precomputed once; training and inference then run on a lightweight projection head. HyCLoST trains on a single GPU in ~2h on small datasets and ~1 day on the largest; inference takes 1–2 min per dataset, making the method practical for lower-resource settings. Magnitude of gains (R1). Tab. 1 reports robustness measures beyond the mean. HyCLoST attains the best average rank (2.792) under the Friedman test. Across 9 baseline methods, HyCLoST is best on 10/26 datasets and significantly outperforms 10/11 configurations under paired Wilcoxon tests with Holm–Bonferroni correction. Given SpaRED’s heterogeneity across 9 tissue types and 2 species, these complementary statistics indicate consistent, not marginal, gains. Comparison with dated methods (R1). 7 of our 9 baselines are from 2023 or later, including MERGE [7] and M2TGLGO [20] (both 2025). We attempted to include NH2ST (Qu et al., 2025) and HAGE (Dang et al., 2025), but key implementation details were unavailable, preventing a fair, reproducible comparison. However, we will include these methods in the related work section. In the camera-ready, we will (i) clarify the geometric motivation and biological scope, (ii) discuss per-dataset directional results, and (iii) note the additional 2025 methods.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): On the positive side, the reviewers found it generally sound in terms of the technical details and the quality of the evaluation. They particularly liked how the work introduces the usage of hyperbolic contrastive learning and a directional gene-to-image entailment loss. The biggest issue that the reviewers found with this paper is that the justification behind the hyperbolic/hierarchical assumption is not well supported by both biological and empirical evidence. There is also a concern about the proposed retrieval-based inference strategy with respect to robustness, sensitivity to k, scalability and generalization, particularly in rare/shifting test scenarios. They also raised concerns about the claimed contribution versus what could be attributed to strong foundation pretrained encoders in use here. Overall, while the performance is consistent, the improvements are not significant. They would also like to see better support in the form of more biological interpretation/statistics and stronger comparison with prior/recent works. The author is recommended to provide responses to all of the raised points with particular attention to: the modeling assumptions, the justification of components of the proposed method, robustness beyond just averaging over the benchmarks. | After rebuttal, the available post-rebuttal opinions are clearly positive: R2 accepts after the authors clarified the hyperbolic motivation, directionality, efficiency, and performance, R4 also maintains Accept and states that the authors have addressed the concerns sufficiently. R1 did not submit their final rating, but after review, I think that most of the concerns could be fine. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The proposed combination of hyperbolic contrastive learning and directional gene-to-image entailment is novel, technically sound, and well motivated. The paper is supported by a comprehensive evaluation across 26 SpaRED datasets, demonstrating consistent improvements over strong baselines. The rebuttal satisfactorily addressed the main concerns regarding the motivation for hyperbolic geometry, the contribution beyond foundation encoders, and the role of the entailment objective. While some limitations of the retrieval-based inference strategy remain, they do not outweigh the paper’s methodological contributions and strong empirical validation. However, the paper provides only a brief mention of this in the implementation details without elaborating on the data scale, annotation protocol, or generalizability of this segmentation model. 2.The identification of non-specific staining (NSS) artifacts via color deconvolution and segmentation priors is a reasonable and well-motivated strategy. However, the paper does not provide any qualitative or quantitative evaluation of the NSS detection pipeline itself. For example, visual examples of detected NSS masks, or comparison against manually annotated artifact regions. 3.All experiments are conducted on a single in-house dataset of orbital mass biopsies scanned at 40x magnification. reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper is well motivated, clearly identifying that IgG4 assessment requires instance-level quantitative consistency, which is not adequately addressed by prior virtual staining methods. 2.The problem of NSS as noisy supervision is practically relevant, and the paper explains this issue clearly with convincing motivation. 3.The overall framework is conceptually clean, with SGIA and noise-aware adversarial learning well aligned with the problem formulation. 4.Experimental results show consistent improvements over prior methods across both image quality and pathology-oriented metrics, and ablation studies support the contribution of each component.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The method heavily relies on a pre-trained segmentation model to identify NSS and guide learning, but the reliability of this model is not sufficiently justified, raising concerns about error propagation. 2.The NSS handling strategy (e.g., thresholding, mask generation, and interpolation) lacks detailed analysis, and it is unclear how sensitive the method is to these design choices. 3.The evaluation depends on another frozen segmentation model (e.g., HoVerNet) for key pathology metrics, without sufficient validation of its suitability for this task. 4.Experiments are limited to a single dataset, making it difficult to assess generalization across different data distributions or clinical settings. 5.The framework requires additional components (e.g., segmentation prior), which may limit applicability to other datasets without extra annotation effort. 6.Some minor clarity and presentation issues remain (e.g., notation inconsistencies, insufficient explanation of intermediate variables).
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This paper exhibits several notable strengths, particularly in its strong clinical motivation and highly targeted methodological design. First, the clinical problem is well-identified: the authors insightfully recognize that diagnosing IgG4-related diseases requires preserving discrete, sparse plasma cell instances rather than merely matching global tissue textures, addressing a significant limitation in standard image-to-image translation approaches. Second, the proposed IgG4-QPC framework introduces logically sound components to tackle this specific challenge, notably the Segmentation-Guided Instance-Level Alignment (SGIA) module that cleverly leverages semantic priors to enforce instance-level consistency, and a highly practical Noise-Aware Adversarial Learning strategy designed to mitigate the real-world issue of non-specific staining (NSS) artifacts. Finally, the evaluation methodology is comprehensive and well-aligned with the paper’s core claims; by incorporating pathology-specific quantitative metrics—such as cell density error (MAE) and spatial distribution correlation (Pearson-R)—alongside standard image quality assessments, the authors effectively demonstrate that their approach yields more reliable instance-level pathological consistency and cleaner backgrounds compared to conventional generative baselines.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: This paper addresses the clinically important problem of virtual staining from H&E to IgG4 for quantitative assessment of IgG4‑related disease, with a specific focus on generating sparse, discrete plasma cell instances and handling non‑specific staining (NSS) artifacts. The authors propose a Segmentation‑Guided Instance‑Level Alignment (SGIA) module that uses a pretrained segmentation network to align cell‑level features and enforce density consistency, and a Noise‑Aware Adversarial Learning strategy that identifies NSS artifacts and applies spatially adaptive weighting to suppress background noise. Experiments on a paired H&E‑IgG4 dataset of orbital mass WSIs show improved image quality and pathology‑relevant metrics over several GAN‑based baselines. However, several methodological and reporting concerns need to be addressed to strengthen the validity and reproducibility of the claims. 1.The noise‑aware cleaning pipeline relies on a frozen segmentation network to produce the cell probability map, which is then used to construct the NSS mask. If the segmentation network was trained on real IgG4 IHC images that already contain NSS artifacts, it may have learned to misinterpret some NSS patterns as positive cells, causing the cleaning algorithm to underestimate artifact regions and compromising the quality of the cleaned target image. The authors should clarify whether the segmentation training data included NSS examples, and ideally provide precision and recall of the segmentation network for distinguishing true plasma cells from NSS, either briefly in the main text or as supplementary material. 2.Key quantitative metrics in Tables 1 and 2 (PSNR, SSIM, MAE, PCC, KL) are reported only as point estimates without any indication of variability or uncertainty, making it difficult to judge whether the observed improvements are statistically reliable or could arise from random variation across test patches or slides. The only exception is KID which includes a standard deviation. The authors should compute and report standard deviations for these metrics (e.g., via bootstrap resampling or per‑slide statistics) and consider reporting p‑values from paired tests against baselines. 3.The paper does not provide a detailed description of how the segmentation network for positive plasma cells was trained and validated. It is mentioned that the network was pretrained using coarse annotations from Cellpose and fine‑tuned on a small set of pathologist‑annotated positive cells, but the size of the fine‑tuning set, the performance of the segmentation model (e.g., Dice, precision, recall on a held‑out test set), and whether it generalizes across different staining variations are not reported. Since the SGIA module heavily depends on the quality of this segmentation prior, the authors should report key segmentation metrics and discuss the potential impact of segmentation errors on the virtual staining results. 4.The comparison with existing virtual staining methods includes several GAN‑based approaches but does not include more recent diffusion‑based or transformer‑based virtual staining methods that have been published in the last two years. While the selected baselines are reasonable, the authors should justify the choice of baselines or at least discuss how the proposed method would compare to emerging architectures. Additionally, the paper does not include any evaluation by a pathologist (e.g., Turing test or diagnostic agreement study), which would be valuable to assess clinical utility beyond quantitative metrics. 5.The ablation study in Table 2 shows that removing the noise‑aware learning component (w/o NA) yields a model with MAE=3.2318 and PCC=0.3524, while the full model achieves MAE=3.4201 and PCC=0.3658.The trade‑off is that w/o NA has lower MAE but also lower PCC, and the differences are small. The paper does not discuss why the noise‑aware component slightly increases MAE while improving spatial correlation, nor does it provide statistical significance for these differences. The authors should provide a more nuanced interpretation of these results, including confidence intervals, to help readers understand the practical benefit of the noise‑aware learning strategy.

title: Imbalance-Aware Distributional Alignment of Heterogeneous Modalities for HER2 Status Prediction
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem by exploring multimodal fusion of WSI and MRI for HER2 status prediction. reviewer_1_weaknesses: The experimental validation is not sufficiently comprehensive. In particular, the dynamic gradient modulation module lacks stability analysis and sensitivity evaluation, making its robustness unclear. In addition, although the paper introduces “distributional alignment,” the approach essentially reduces to KL-based alignment, which is a commonly used technique, and the necessity and advantage of modeling features as distributions are not well justified. Overall, the methodological novelty is limited and the design choices are not thoroughly validated.

To effectively mitigate modality imbalance, the authors incorporate a dynamic gradient modulation module that adaptively adjusts the contributions of WSI and MRI during optimization, enabling more effective use of fused information.
