author_feedback: We thank the Meta-Reviewer (MR) and Reviewers 1, 2, and 3 (R1, R2, R3) for their insightful feedback. We organize our responses as (1)–(11), with “<>” indicating the corresponding reviewer(s). (1) <R1, R2, R3, MR> If accepted, we will release our code and dataset. (2) ACC-G for clinical utility: After additional analysis on the performance of the model on gleason score classification (CLS) following HistGen’s CLS protocol, Gleason CLS AUC improves from 0.71 (baseline) to 0.77 (Ours). It is higher than ACC-G since ACC-G is extracted from generated reports, where the model is optimized for free-text generation rather than score prediction. But the gains over baselines and the pathologist-involved analysis in Response (9) support its clinical utility. (3) Generalization: Our observation on PathoGaze [1], a breast-cancer attention dataset with classification (CLS) labels, suggests that human-attention alignment can also improve CLS on another domain from 0.833 to 0.989. (4) Error Analysis: For small tumor regions where the baseline VLM is strongly mislocalized, alignment provides only partial correction as it remains constrained by the VLM backbone. (5) Methodological novelty: While we acknowledge GazeVLM in Sec. 3.2, our primary contribution is the novel end-to-end pipeline for pathology report generation. We define a new research task and provide a proof-of-concept for grounding clinical narratives in pathologist attention. (6) Component coverage: We excluded rare components such as seminal vesicle invasion (positive in only 2 slides), that are insufficient for reliable attention supervision and evaluation. (7) Influence of personalization: While our six pathologists (2 specialists, 2 generalists, 2 residents) show diverse gaze behaviors, our "positive-component-filtering" distills shared diagnostic evidence from individual attention. For multi-reader slides, this approach increases heatmap similarity from 0.55 to 0.71. (8) Regularization effect and uncertainty: Gains in Tab. 2 suggest that improvements stem from visual grounding rather than mere text-side regularization. Manual verification showed 100% agreement with the LLM results due to the structured reports. (9) <R2, R3> Evaluation of Interpretability: Our goal is not to add a new visual-support output, but to make existing attention maps more clinically useful, as shown in Tab 2.Pathologists’ evaluation confirms that our method provides strong tumor-focused and clinically meaningful visual support, preferred in 80% of cases over baselines on overall quality and component-specific diagnosis. (10) “Plug-and-Play”: Our method requires no architectural changes and adds no parameters. The finetuned layers and original loss coefficients follow each backbone’s default design, while the KL-loss coefficient is shared across models. The only model-specific difference is dataset preprocessing, i.e., grid alignment between gaze heatmaps and visual tokens. Using last-layer attention follows standard grounding practices [2,3] and consistently achieves the best. (11) Lack of translation: We focus on prostate cancer report generation, which adapts pre-trained pathology VLMs to a clinical domain. While human attention provides efficient, diagnosis-aware supervision (3 min/slide), segmentation masks are 10-times more costly and frequently unavailable for report-level components like surgical margins. Also, synthetic masks add noise due to current Gleason classification limitations, discussed in Response (2). We expect strong transfer properties to novel cancers once attention data is scaled (discussed in Response (3)), with future work focused on broader cross-domain generalization. References: [1] Eye-Tracking, Mouse Tracking, Stimulus Tracking,and Decision-Making Datasets in Digital Pathology. [2] Grounded Language-Image Pre-training. [3] Pointing and Asking: A Context-and-Task-Aware Framework for Visual Question Answering.

title: PCRP: Progressive Coarse-to-Fine Refinement for Pathology Grounding
reviewer_1_strengths: Important task setting. Pathology visual grounding is a meaningful and relatively underexplored problem in computational pathology, especially because precise region localization from clinical language has practical value. Strong empirical performance. The reported results on RefPath are impressive, with clear gains over prior methods, particularly on low-magnification images where grounding is more difficult. Reasonable overall framework. The coarse-to-fine design is intuitive, and the use of visual cue enhancement plus mask-based refinement is well aligned with the challenges of small targets and blurry boundaries in pathology images. Clear presentation. The paper is generally easy to follow, and the ablation study helps explain the contribution of each module.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. In my view, the main weakness is that the proposed method is largely a combination of existing ideas rather than a clearly new technical contribution. Cross-attention-based vision-language fusion, gated residual updates, coarse-to-fine refinement, curriculum-style training, and the use of SAM-generated priors are all familiar design patterns. While the integration is reasonable, the paper does not sufficiently demonstrate what is fundamentally new beyond adapting these components to pathology grounding. Heavy reliance on external priors weakens the novelty claim. A substantial part of the performance gain seems to come from using SAM3 as a teacher to provide mask priors for refinement. This is practically useful, but it makes the improvement feel more like a strong engineering pipeline built on top of an external foundation model, rather than a novel grounding method in itself. The paper should better clarify how much of the gain comes from the proposed architecture versus the external segmentation prior. Experimental validation is still somewhat limited. Although the gains on RefPath are large, evaluation is restricted to a single benchmark. This makes it difficult to judge generalizability. In addition, the paper does not report variance across runs, statistical significance, or deeper analysis of failure cases. Given the surprisingly large improvement over previous work, stronger validation would be important. Some claims are stronger than the evidence provided. The paper repeatedly emphasizes robustness on difficult cases such as tiny targets, blurred boundaries, and low magnification, but the supporting analysis is still relatively limited. More targeted breakdowns or controlled experiments would make these claims more convincing. Overall, I think this is a well-motivated and practically useful paper, and the empirical results are strong. However, for me the technical novelty is not sufficient, and the current experimental evidence is not yet strong enough to fully support the scale of the claimed advance. Therefore, my current recommendation is weak reject.

reviewer_3_strengths: (i) The paper studies a meaningful and relatively underexplored problem in computational pathology, namely visual grounding from pathology-specific referring expressions. (ii) The quantitative results are strong. The qualitative examples are also helpful.

author_feedback: We thank all reviewers and the AC for their constructive comments. We address the major concerns below. Q1: Gains attributed to SAM3 priors. [AC,R1,R2,R3] SAM3-derived priors provide useful boundary information, but PCRP’s improvement cannot be simply attributed to SAM3.The first row of Table 2 is already a SAM3-assisted PKNet-style baseline. On 20×, SAM3 prior substantially improves PKNet, increasing Acc by +13.64; however, on 40×, its standalone gain is limited, increasing Acc by only +1.92.In contrast, on top of this SAM3-assisted baseline, full PCRP further improves Acc by +2.92 and +2.64 on 20× and 40×. This shows that SAM3 alone cannot explain the final performance; VWF, CBP, and PPT provide additional gains under different magnifications, especially on the 40× baseline. Q2: Potential GT leakage through SAM3.[R2] Sorry for the confusion. We would like to clarify that GT is NOT leaked, because the GT will be used ONLY in the training process. During inference, GT is NOT used for prediction. We will clarify this in revision. Q3: Problem-driven formulation beyond known components. [R1,R2] We understand the reviewer’s concern. While some components are inspired by existing techniques, our novelty lies in the coarse-to-fine pathology-grounding framework. Our method combines coarse localization for tiny/subtle abnormal regions with SAM3-guided refinement, enabling a coarse-to-fine solution specifically designed for pathology grounding rather than a simple module combination. The strong empirical results further show that this design is effective, achieving clear improvements over prior methods. We will better clarify the framework-level novelty and its performance advantages in the revision. Q4: RefPath-only evaluation. [AC,R1,R2,R3] We understand the importance of external dataset validation. However, pathology visual grounding is a new task, and to our best knowledge, RefPath is currently the only public pathology visual grounding dataset. For this reason, we conduct evaluation of our method on RefPath. It is worth noting, RefPath contains two test subsets with different magnifications, including 40× and 20×, and uses various metrics for evaluation. Our PCRP achieves state-of-the-art results on both subsets, showing its efficacy and robustness in handling images of different resolution in real scenarios. We will clarify this in revision. Thanks! Q5: Reliability, failure cases, and overhead. [AC,R1,R3] PCRP doesn’t directly use SAM3 masks as final prediction, but converts them into boundary cues and injects them into stage-2 for grounding. CBP suppresses noisy priors caused by inaccurate prompts, so the model does not unconditionally rely on SAM3 prior. Severe stage-1 deviation, noisy SAM3 prior, or ambiguous expression are possible failure cases. Fig. 2 in the submitted paper has qualitatively shown that stage-2 can alleviate part of the grounding drift. Regarding computational overhead, two-stage refinement and external mask generation will bring additional cost. We will provide discussion about the accuracy-efficiency trade-off and failure modes in the revised version. Q6: Candidate refinement vs. missed-target discovery. [R2] Thanks for this insightful comment. We agree that discovering tiny or overlooked pathological regions is important in clinical practice. Our framework is designed for tiny objects and subtle abnormal regions. Stage-1 performs coarse localization to capture a potential abnormal region, and stage-2 further refines localization and boundary. Thus, PCRP is not merely candidate refinement, but progressively handles subtle pathology targets through coarse-to-fine localization. We will clarify this motivation. Q7: Reproducibility. [R2] We will release our full source code and model, and provide more implementation details in the revised paper. Q8: Presentation errors. [R3] Thanks for pointing this out. We will double-check and carefully polish the paper in revision. Again, thanks!
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper presents a clear and empirically strong pathology visual grounding method, but its overall standing remains borderline because the strongest gains are closely tied to the SAM3-assisted refinement stage and the validation is limited to a single benchmark. The strengths of the submission are the relevance of the task, the clear coarse-to-fine formulation, and the large performance improvements reported on RefPath, including especially strong gains on the more difficult 20x subset. The paper also provides a basic ablation showing that VWF, CBP, and PPT each contribute to the final result, and the method is generally presented in a coherent and understandable way. The decisive concerns are threefold. First, the method relies materially on SAM3-derived mask priors, and the manuscript itself indicates that much of the gain comes from this refinement stage; this raises a legitimate question about how much of the contribution is due to the proposed framework design versus the external prior. Second, the empirical validation is restricted to RefPath, so the current evidence for generalization remains limited. Third, the analysis of sensitivity to prior quality, failure modes, and computational overhead is limited. At the same time, after checking the manuscript, some reviewer criticisms are only partially supported. In particular, the concern that the method directly uses ground-truth masks is incorrect: the paper uses SAM3-derived masks and states that ground-truth boxes are used only in an early training warm-up before transitioning to predicted boxes, with inference aligned to the latter. Accordingly, I assign limited weight to the stronger leakage claim. Similarly, the criticism that the method is clinically misaligned because it performs refinement is not persuasive for a visual grounding paper, where a coarse-to-fine localization design is consistent with the task being studied. | The main concerns remain the moderate methodological novelty and the dependence on an external segmentation prior. Several components, including cross-modal fusion, gated residual updates, coarse-to-fine refinement, curriculum-style prompt transition, and SAM-based priors, are individually familiar. The contribution is therefore best viewed as a task-specific integration and refinement framework rather than a fundamentally new grounding paradigm. In addition, the strongest gains appear closely related to the SAM3-assisted refinement stage, and the submitted paper does not fully isolate the effect of the proposed architecture from the benefit of using a strong external prior. The evaluation is also limited to RefPath, without external validation, variance estimates, statistical significance analysis, detailed sensitivity to prior quality, or runtime/overhead analysis. The rebuttal clarified an important point: the method does not use ground-truth masks at inference time, and the use of ground-truth boxes is restricted to an early training warm-up before transitioning to predicted boxes. This reduces the weight of the strongest leakage concern raised by R2.The rebuttal also argued that the improvements cannot be attributed solely to SAM3, since the ablation baseline is described as already SAM3-assisted and the full framework adds further gains through VWF, CBP, and PPT. This clarification is useful, although it does not completely remove the concern that a large part of the total improvement over prior work is enabled by the external SAM3 prior. The response to the single-dataset concern is also reasonable to some extent, given the limited availability of public pathology visual grounding benchmarks, but the generalization evidence remains limited. In reconciling the reviews, I gave substantial weight to the consistent agreement that the task is relevant, the method is clearly presented, and the quantitative results are strong. I also considered R1’s continued concern about incremental novelty and limited validation, R2’s initial concern about privileged priors but subsequent post-rebuttal acceptance, and R3’s weak accept position based on the strong benchmark performance despite practical and generalization limitations. Overall, the paper is above the acceptance threshold, but only marginally. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a two-stage, coarse-to-fine, progressive framework for pathology visual grounding on the RefPath benchmark. The reviewers acknowledged the clarity of the formulation, the strong gains on the harder magnification subset, and the per-module ablation. The decisive concerns were reliance on SAM3 mask priors and the attribution of gains; potential ground-truth leakage through SAM3 prompted by training-time boxes; evaluation restricted to a single benchmark; and limited analysis of sensitivity to prior quality and failure modes. The rebuttal addresses the leakage concern by clarifying that ground-truth prompts are used only during training and never at inference, and by disentangling the SAM3-prior contribution from that of the proposed modules, as reported in the ablation. The single-benchmark concern is partly mitigated by the fact that RefPath is currently the only public pathology visual grounding dataset. The most consequential reviewer concerns are substantively addressed, and the practical contribution is meaningful. The camera-ready must include the failure-case analysis and the computational-overhead reporting promised in the rebuttal. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The scores after rebuttal are mixed. The contribution remains heavily tied to SAM3-derived refinement priors, making it difficult to isolate the proposed framework’s novelty from the external segmentation prior. Evaluation is limited to a single benchmark, with insufficient analysis of prior quality sensitivity, failure modes, computational overhead, and generalization. The method appears more like an engineering pipeline than a sufficiently novel grounding approach.

title: PhaseAT: Fourier Phase Adversarial Training for Medical Image Domain Generalization
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Novel adversarial perturb on the fourier phase domain: This is one relatively novel method considering most current works are mainly focused on the intensity distribution or style diversification. Adversarial attack on the phase domain can provide one novel insight for enhancing the model’s robustness. 2.Strong single-source DG results with large margins: Table 1 show substantial and consistent improvements across all source domains on both datasets. 3.Comprehensive ablation study: Table 3(b) systematically isolates each design choice — phase-only vs. amplitude-only vs. both, with/without saliency mask, RGB vs. YCbCr vs. luminance-only, adversarial vs. random perturbation.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Incomplete baseline comparison: Notable missing baselines include: (a) standard Fourier-based augmentation methods like FedDG (b) Traditional augmentation based methods like DeepAug 2.Evaluation limited to classification only — no dense prediction tasks: The paper claims PhaseAT is a general medical DG framework, yet only evaluates on patch-level classification while the absence of any segmentation benchmark significantly limits the demonstrated generality. Minors: Figure 1: it seems the raw image and image after pertubation remain the same. Table 1: the author need to report one average performance on all domains.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Clearly motivated and well-structured: The authors clearly motivate their paper with a detailed discussion of the background literature and related works. The paper is structured sensibly in a way that is easy to follow. Figures are all clear and easy to understand. Commitment to reproducibility: the authors have included an anonymized link to their source code and extensive details regarding their implementation and experimental set up, as well as full details of their algorithm in pseudocode. Robust experimental validation: the authors evaluate their method across both single-domain and multi-source domain generalization tasks, following similar processes to other literature. They also include robust validations investigating sensitivity across various hyper parameters, generalization across architectures, and the importance of the various components of their proposed methodology. Such exhaustive experimentation is encouraging to see. Ablations provide clarity on the importance of the individual decisions made: Table 3 (b), in particular, investigates the contribution of each component of the proposed methodology, as well as a discussion as to why removing/changing each component leads to a drop in efficacy. This kind of interrogation of design choices in the method is really nice to see and provides a clear justification for all choices.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Incorrect “best model” highlighted in Tables: Tables 1 and 2 both highlight the best performing model in bold text. Across all test cases, PhaseAT is highlighted as being the best, even when it is not. This is likely just a LaTEX formatting mistake. For example, in Table 1 (a) under source domain C4, PhaseAT isn’t the best performing model in 2 of the 4 test cases (C1 and C3) nor on average, yet it is highlighted in bold. Missing statistical significance: Tables 1 and 2 report whether the best performing model shows a statistically significant performance improvement over other methods. Including statistical significance of the results would strengthen the claims around performance improvements as it would show that these are not simply due to noise in the results. No examples of adversarial images: The paper doesn’t show an example of an adversarial image generated by PhaseAT. I appreciate that page limits are tight, and the perturbations are learned during training, but the inclusion of an example would help to illustrate the image features that the Fourier phase perturbation changes in an image. Causes of differences in source domain performance are not discussed: Table 1, the chosen source domain has a significant impact on the model’s generalization (for example, with source domain C4 in the Camelyon1-WILDS dataset, the model struggles to generalize to all other domains). Do the authors have a theory for the reason behind this? Is this domain comprised of more challenging examples? Or does it represent a more extreme domain shift from the other sources?
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The overall narrative and logical flow of the paper are clear. 2.Research in medical domain generalization (DG) is of high practical importance.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The proposed phase perturbation as a data augmentation strategy contradicts prior insights and is internally inconsistent with the authors’ own claims. The paper states: “Since standard CNNs are biased toward texture cues [9], they frequently overfit to these unstable amplitude-driven correlations…”. If overfitting to amplitude-driven information is the issue, a more reasonable approach would be to introduce amplitude perturbations to improve robustness to cross-domain variations. Instead, the method perturbs the phase, which directly disrupts semantic structure. This may be unreliable, especially for medical tasks that heavily rely on structural information, such as segmentation and detection. 2.The novelty of the method is limited. Essentially, the approach applies Fourier-based data augmentation, which has already been widely explored in domain generalization literature. The only difference is that the perturbation is applied to the phase component rather than amplitude [1][2][3]. 3.The experimental scope is too limited. Medical image analysis typically involves more segmentation and detection tasks, and evaluating only classification datasets is insufficient to validate the effectiveness of the method. Broader experimental validation is needed. 4.Regarding the claim: “This not only improves computational efficiency but also produces more structured perturbations with fewer color artifacts,” the improvement in computational efficiency is unclear. What is the additional computational cost introduced by the learnable phase perturbation compared to the baseline? References: [1] Xu Q, Zhang R, Zhang Y, et al. A Fourier-based framework for domain generalization. CVPR 2021.[2] Xu Q, Zhang R, Fan Z, et al. Fourier-based augmentation with applications to domain generalization. Pattern Recognition, 2023.[3] Wang X, Zhao Q, Zhang C, et al. Enhanced dynamic feature representation learning framework by Fourier transform for domain generalization. Information Sciences, 2023.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer. The reviews confirm PhaseAT’s key advantages: a novel, well-motivated DG formulation that moves beyond style perturbations to adversarial Fourier-phase perturbations; strong and consistent gains, especially in single-source DG; and robust validation via multi-domain experiments, ablations, clear presentation, and reproducibility. We address all concerns below: Statistical Significance [R2, Meta] Tables 1–2 report mean ± std over 5 seeds, showing low variance and consistent performance across runs. The improvements over the strongest baselines are stable; e.g., in Table 1(a) (Source C0), Phase-AT achieves 71.30±1.3 vs. 69.06±1.9 for RAS⁴DG, and in Table 1(b) (Source Aptos), 44.99±1.9 vs. 41.50±2.3.We will report detailed paired t-test across the same 5 seeds and include 95% confidence intervals of the performance difference in the revision. Computational Cost [R4, Meta] PhaseAT, like other adversarial training methods, uses K inner maximization steps and is therefore more expensive than ERM; our efficiency claim is only relative to adversarial variants perturbing all RGB or all YCbCr channels. By restricting perturbations to luminance (Y), PhaseAT reduces the inner-maximization dimensionality by 3×. We acknowledge this does not directly translate to wall-clock savings and add training time and memory in the revision. Baselines (FedDG, DeepAug) [R1, Meta] Our evaluation covers three SOTA directions: style/intensity (AdverIN), disentanglement (ConDiSR), and Fourier-based methods (RAS⁴DG). FedDG and DeepAug are complementary but not directly aligned: FedDG focuses on cross-client amplitude mixing, while DeepAug uses pixel-space augmentations that emphasize texture cues. In contrast, PhaseAT operates in the Fourier domain with fixed amplitude and adversarial phase perturbations. Dense Prediction [R1, R4, Meta] We thank the reviewers for the suggestion. PhaseAT is currently scoped to medical classification DG. Due to space constraints, dense prediction tasks are left as future work. Source Domain Variability [R2] We agree that source-domain choice strongly affects SDG performance, as Camelyon17 centers differ in staining, scanners, and preparation, inducing different shortcut correlations. PhaseAT consistently improves over ERM across all sources, though gains vary (e.g., large for C2: 52.08→74.31, smaller for C4: 55.64→58.64), suggesting it is most effective when ERM relies more on domain-specific shortcuts. We will add this discussion and include a quantitative domain-distance analysis to better explain this variability. Bold Formatting [R2] The “Ours” row was bolded for formatting consistency rather than to indicate per-cell superiority. In the revision, we will highlight only the best value in each column. Adversarial Examples [R2] We appreciate the reviewers’ recognition of space constraints. We will make visualizations of adversarial examples available in the accompanying GitHub repository. Phase vs Amplitude Perturbation [R4] PhaseAT complements, rather than replaces, amplitude-based DG by enforcing robustness under fixed amplitude (appearance) via small, bounded phase perturbations. To preserve semantics, perturbations are constrained, saliency-masked, and applied only to luminance. Table 3(b) shows amplitude-only (77.89%) and phase+amplitude (78.50%) underperform PhaseAT (85.7%), indicating constrained, gradient-guided phase perturbation is more effective in our setting. Novelty [R4] PhaseAT’s novelty is not generic Fourier augmentation, but a constrained phase-adversarial objective: (i) inner maximization instead of stochastic mixing, (ii) phase-only perturbation with fixed amplitude, (iii) Wirtinger-style phase gradients, and (iv) saliency-masked, luminance-only perturbations for stability. Ablations show each is critical: random phase is weaker (81.90 vs. 85.7), removing the mask drops to 56.47, and RGB/YCbCr perturbations underperform.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Reviewers (scores 4, 4, 3) overall acknowledge that the paper has merit but have several concerns that the authors are encouraged to address in a rebuttal where possible. In particular: statistical testing details on computational complexity / runtime general clarifications and a discussion of differences in source domain performances (R2) Those seem addressable in a rebuttal. Concerns centered around the selection of baseline methods and performance on dense prediction tasks are further shared concerns among reviewers, that however, are likely challenging to address without additional experiments. | All three reviewers are positive post-rebuttal suggesting to Accept this paper. Reviewers appreciate the clarity and motivation of this work, as well as a comprehensive evaluation including ablation studies. Overall results and method are convincing. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): PhaseAT introduces a novel adversarial training approach in the Fourier phase domain, moving beyond conventional amplitude based or style based domain generalization methods. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes PhaseAT, a phase-aware adversarial training framework for medical domain generalization. title: Physics-Grounded Weakly Supervised Histopathological Tissue Segmentation via Frozen Tri-Domain Prototypes
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a real and important pathology-specific challenge: weak supervision is particularly fragile in histopathology due to strong morphological diversity and pseudo-label noise. 2.The overall framework is coherent, and the three components are reasonably well connected at the conceptual level. 3.The use of phase and amplitude information is intuitively meaningful in this domain, and the empirical results are competitive on the reported benchmarks.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The methodological novelty appears moderate rather than strong. While the exact combination is new, many core ingredients already have clear precedents in recent literature [7, 8, 12, 20, 21], including prototype-based guidance, prototype refinement/alignment for WSSS, and noise-aware pseudo-label handling. As a result, the paper reads more like a sophisticated recombination of existing ideas than a fundamentally new formulation. 2.A key methodological ambiguity is how the category-specific sets used for prototype construction are formed under weak supervision. Since only image-level labels are available and pathology patches may contain multiple tissue types, it is unclear how clean semantic, phase, and energy prototypes are obtained without substantial contamination from off-class regions. This point is central to the method, yet it is insufficiently specified. 3.The discrepancy supervisor is under-defined. The paper argues that cross-domain discrepancy can separate reliable pixels, true boundary ambiguity, and corrupted pseudo-labels, but the actual decision rule for assigning pixels to these regimes is not clearly described. Since pseudo-label noise handling is a major challenge in WSSS, the thresholding and regime-definition details are important for assessing soundness and reproducibility. 4.The paper makes strong mechanism-level claims that are not fully validated experimentally. For example, it repeatedly argues that frozen prototypes prevent semantic drift and that discrepancy disentangles boundary ambiguity from label noise, but these claims are supported mainly by overall performance gains and a limited ablation table, rather than direct evidence such as drift analysis or frozen-vs-learnable prototype comparisons. 5.The experimental section is somewhat thin for a method with several interacting components. Important ablations are missing, such as frozen vs. learnable prototypes, phase-only vs. energy-only variants, and analyses of the necessity of all three domains. 6.The fairness of comparison is not fully clear because the method uses MedCLIP-derived semantic prototypes, while it is unclear whether competing baselines are given access to comparably strong pretrained vision-language priors. Since MedCLIP is itself a strong medical vision-language pretraining model, this should be clarified and ideally isolated in ablation. 7.The “physics-grounded invariance” motivation is intuitively appealing, but it is not directly validated with robustness experiments. If the main argument is that phase and spectral-energy priors improve robustness to staining variation, appearance variation, or scanner/domain shifts, then targeted perturbation or cross-domain experiments would be important. In the current version, this claim remains more intuitive than empirically demonstrated.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Proposes a novel perspective by using frequency-domain representations as physically-grounded descriptors to stabilize weak supervision. Demonstrates superior performance over existing methods on two large-scale benchmarks, BCSS-WSSS and LUAD-HistoSeg, with clear gains in mDice and mIoU.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Although the authors claim the frequency-domain features are robust to staining fluctuations, the experiments are limited to two specific datasets; broader validation across more diverse scanning protocols and multi-center data would further strengthen the claims of physical invariance
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: It is an interesting idea to propose a physicssemantics synergistic framework which stabilizes weak supervision by anchoring representation learning to immutable physical priors. The results seem good as shown in Table 1 and Fig. 2.* Ablation analysis verified the efficiency of each component.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: It would be good to proof the efficiency of PhysPro mathematically, which would help readers to know its merits and how to use it in the future. It is suggested to show the evidence to show why the proposed mothod works for the given cases. I am also happy to know whether the proposed methed would work for the natural iamges besides medical images. It is better to apply this method for other cases.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: Response to Reviewer 1: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the thorough and constructive comments. Q1.Novelty. We understand the reviewer’s concern regarding novelty. PhysPro is not a simple recombination of prototypes, frequency-domain priors, and noise-aware supervision; it redefines the role of prototypes in WSSS. Instead of using prototypes only as semantic alignment targets, PhysPro builds frozen tri-domain references before training. The semantic, phase-morphological, and spectral-energy anchors encode class identity, structural consistency, and texture-frequency distribution, respectively. Their discrepancy is used as a diagnostic signal for supervision reliability, helping separate reliable interiors, boundary ambiguity, and corrupted pseudo-labels. This diagnostic use of frozen tri-domain prototypes differs from conventional prototype-based WSSS. Q2.Prototype Construction. S_c is built from training patches whose image-level label contains only a single tissue category; multi-category patches are excluded. No CAMs, pseudo-labels, or segmentation predictions are used, so construction is decoupled from training dynamics. We do not assume pixel-level purity; this subset provides a lower-contamination calibration pool, while Eq. (1) further suppresses residual off-class structures/outliers by density-weighted aggregation. Patch counts range from 679 to 4,738 per category on BCSS-WSSS. Q3.Decision Rules of PhyDS. For each pixel with pseudo-label c, PhyDS computes s_sem, s_phase, and s_energy; Delta = Var(s_sem, s_phase, s_energy). Confidence q combines mean tri-domain similarity with 3x3 local consistency using weights 0.7/0.3.Thresholds are batch-adaptive: 30th/70th percentiles for low/high Delta, and medians for high q and s_sem. Assignment: (1) low Delta, high q: reliable; (2) high Delta, high s_sem: boundary ambiguity; (3) high Delta, low s_sem: corrupted pseudo-label; (4) otherwise: attenuated supervision. Hyperparameters are beta=0.5, tau=0.1, T=0.5.We will add these details to Sec. 2.4.Q4/Q5/Q7.We thank the reviewer for the helpful suggestions. Table 2 provides component-level evidence: PhyTriSP yields the largest gain, and the full model further improves with PhyOrchMoE/PhyDS, supporting the contribution and complementarity of the modules. Finer single-domain variants can further disentangle the roles of semantic, phase, and energy priors; our tri-domain design is motivated by their complementarity rather than interchangeable comparison. Consistent gains on two public WSSS pathology benchmarks from different cancer types and data sources further support the effectiveness of this design. Q6.Fairness of MedCLIP. PBIP, the closest prototype baseline, also uses MedCLIP for prototype construction, so the comparison is not against a prototype method without comparable medical VLP priors. In PhysPro, MedCLIP only constructs the frozen offline P_sem; it is not the backbone and produces no dense predictions. Response to Reviewer 2: We sincerely thank the reviewer for recognizing the frequency-domain perspective and for the constructive suggestion. Broader multi-center and multi-protocol validation would further strengthen the physical-invariance analysis. In the current study, consistent improvements on two histopathology benchmarks provide empirical support for PhysPro across different dataset settings and support the effectiveness of its frequency-domain design. Response to Reviewer 3: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the encouraging assessment and thoughtful suggestions. Phase congruency is stable to monotonic intensity transformations, while log-polar angular integration reduces rotational dependence. These analytic properties support prototype stability. Together with semantic/phase/energy heterogeneity, they help Delta distinguish boundary ambiguity from label noise, as supported by Table 2 and Fig. 2.These general signal-processing principles also suggest potential applicability to natural-image WSSS.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a physics-grounded framework for weakly supervised histopathological segmentation. The reviewers’ scores are 3, 4, and 4, indicating mixed opinions. The reviewers agree that the problem is relevant and the proposed framework is interesting, with promising empirical results. However, concerns remain regarding the level of methodological novelty, insufficient clarification of key components, and limited experimental validation of the underlying claims. The AC therefore recommends inviting the paper for rebuttal. The authors are encouraged to clarify the construction and reliability of the proposed prototypes under weak supervision, provide stronger validation of the claimed mechanisms, and further justify the experimental design and comparisons. | The paper proposes PhysPro, a weakly supervised histopathology tissue segmentation framework that uses frozen prototypes from three domains: semantic, phase-morphological, and spectral-energy. These prototypes are used to guide a morphology/frequency mixture-of-experts module and a cross-domain discrepancy-based supervision strategy, with the goal of improving robustness to intra-class heterogeneity and noisy pseudo-labels in weakly supervised tissue segmentation. The initial reviews were mixed but overall slightly positive, with scores of 3 / 4 / 4.The reviewers appreciated the clinically relevant problem, the coherent design of the three-domain prototype framework, and the competitive results on BCSS-WSSS and LUAD-HistoSeg. However, several concerns were raised. Reviewer 1 questioned the degree of methodological novelty, arguing that the method appeared to recombine existing ideas such as prototype-guided learning, prototype refinement/alignment, and noise-aware pseudo-label handling. Additional concerns included insufficient clarity on how category-specific prototype sets are constructed under weak supervision, how the discrepancy supervisor assigns pixels to reliable/boundary/noisy regimes, limited mechanism-level evidence for the claimed role of frozen prototypes, and incomplete ablations and fairness analysis. The rebuttal addressed several of these points. The authors clarified that PhysPro is intended to redefine the role of prototypes in weakly supervised segmentation by constructing frozen tri-domain references before training, rather than using prototypes only as semantic alignment targets. They also explained how prototypes are constructed from single-label training patches, how the discrepancy decision rules are defined, and how the method differs from MedCLIP-based prototype baselines. They further clarified the role of the three components and the frequency-domain design, and argued that the frozen semantic, phase-morphological, and spectral-energy anchors provide complementary information. Some concerns remain. In particular, Reviewer 1 was only partially persuaded by the rebuttal and maintained that the novelty and mechanism-level evidence remain limited. The rebuttal improves the framing and clarifies several design choices, but it does not fully remove the concern that the method is a sophisticated combination of existing weakly supervised segmentation components. The final version should more clearly explain the prototype construction procedure, discrepancy-thresholding rules, and the specific evidence supporting the claimed role of frozen tri-domain prototypes. After rebuttal, the reviewer opinions are effectively R / A / A, treating the no-update weak accept reviewer as retaining the initial positive assessment. Reviewer 1 maintained reject because the novelty and mechanistic validation concerns were only partially addressed. Reviewer 2 recommended accept after the rebuttal, noting that the main questions were addressed. Reviewer 3 initially recommended weak accept and did not provide a post-rebuttal update, so I interpret that review as remaining positive. I recommend Accept. The paper remains somewhat borderline because the methodological novelty is not overwhelming and some mechanism-level evidence should be strengthened. However, the overall reviewer balance is positive, the rebuttal clarified several important design choices, and the paper addresses a relevant weakly supervised histopathology segmentation problem with a coherent framework and competitive empirical results. The remaining issues are important limitations, but I do not consider them fatal. The camera-ready version should clarify the novelty framing, prototype construction, discrepancy assignment rules, and remaining limitations. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers have quite different opinions for this paper. One reviewer is mainly concerned about novelty and validation of the method. While empirically the results are good on two commonly used dataset, the physics-aware aspects are more heuristic rather than formally formulated or validated. The overall method is also quite complex Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After rebuttal, this paper receives two accept recommendations and one rejection. The AC acknowledges that PhysPro addresses an important weakly supervised histopathology segmentation problem and proposes an interesting physics-semantics framework using frozen tri-domain prototypes across semantic, phase-morphological, and spectral-energy domains. The rebuttal clarifies several key methodological details, including prototype construction from lower-contamination single-category patches, batch-adaptive PhyDS decision rules, the role of MedCLIP, and the rationale for using cross-domain discrepancy to guide adaptive supervision. Although concerns remain regarding moderate novelty, limited mechanism-level validation, and the need for broader robustness studies under stain/scanner/domain shifts, the method is coherent, empirically competitive on two public benchmarks, and positively assessed by the majority of reviewers. Therefore, the AC recommends acceptance.

title: Positive Semi-definite Group-Aware Instance Disentangled Learning for WSI Representation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.This paper analyzes three existing challenges in WSI representation learning and designs targeted solutions, leading to improved classification performance. 2.The paper integrates positive semi-definite metric learning with KMeans, making the instance clustering better match the real distribution of WSI features. 3.The paper compares many MIL methods and conducts experiments on four datasets.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The authors submitted a supplementary material entitled Prototype Instance-semantic Disentanglement with Low-rank Regularized Subspace Clustering for WSIs Explainable Recognition, which appears unrelated to the main paper. Consequently, some critical information is missing, such as the description of the private dataset and the CID idea. 2.When instances from two different categories are mixed together due to K-means clustering error ,it is not clear how CID handles such clustering noise. 3.The method relies heavily on K-means clustering with a fixed K=3 (i. e. , Tumor, microenvironment, and background). This represents a oversimplification of the histological complexity in WSIs. Moreover, no sensitivity analysis is performed on the choice of K, which further limits this assumption. 4.Key ablation studies (Table2) are only conducted on a private dataset. Presenting ablation results on public datasets would greatly improve reproducibility.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper correctly identifies three types of entanglement (spatial, semantic, decision) in existing MIL frameworks, which is a valid and clinically relevant concern. Experiments show the superior performance on four datasets, with significant improvements over baselines.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: K-Means is Not Differentiable: The paper acknowledges this but proposes a “group-separation regularizer” d_reg as a workaround. However, this regularizer only encourages separation between tumor and non-tumor means. It does not actually optimize the clustering assignment. The gradients flow through a proxy loss that doesn’t directly correspond to the K-Means objective, creating a mismatch between training and inference. The CID module claims to use “counterfactual inference” but implements a simple ablation study. This is not genuine counterfactual inference in the causal inference sense. The work lacks comparison with attention-based MIL with k-means preprocessing and existing disentanglement methods adapted for MIL. Two of four datasets are private and cannot be verified. Results on these datasets show suspiciously large gaps, raising concerns about overfitting. The paper claims existing methods lack structural causal models to build disentangled relationships, yet recent work explicitly uses SCMs: Causal multiple instance learning, Interventional bag multi-instance learning.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This paper proposes a new WSI classification framework called PG-CIDL. The method is designed to reduce three types of entanglement in MIL based pathology models, spatial, semantic, and decision entanglement. It does this through three stages: latent factor grouping, cluster reasoning based disentangling, and instance effect re weighting. The overall contribution is a more interpretable and better performing WSI representation framework.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The causal interpretation is not fully convincing. Main concern is that the causal language feels stronger than the evidence provided. The leave one group out masking strategy is useful, but it does not fully establish causal validity in a real clinical sense. Also not fully convinced by the fixed assumption that each WSI can always be decomposed into exactly three groups: tumor, microenvironment, and background. That design choice may be too restrictive. In addition, some important details are pushed to the supplementary material, which makes it harder to fully judge the method from the main paper alone. Reproducibility is also somewhat limited since the code is not yet available.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: For Meta Reviewer: Please kindly refer to R1.2, 1.3, R2.1, 2.2 and R3.1 for your concerns. Reviewer #1: R1.1 The main paper and supplementary one are to comply with the MICCAI dual-submission policy for similar topics (see official guidelines). Critical information, datasets(section4) and CID idea(section3) are available via the abstract link. R1.2 Instances may be mixed in the original Euclidean space. Thus, we apply the positive semi-definite transformation via W=(A^T)A to project features into a new metric space ||A(xi-xj)||_2 for measurement. Besides the reported inter-group separation term d_reg​, we also use an intra-cluster compactness term d_compact, which minimizes the average distance between instances and their assigned cluster centroids. (See abstract link for details). R1.3 The choice K=3 is a coarse pathological prior rather than exactly three biological subtypes. In SCC setting, these three groups correspond to tumor, microenvironment or background such as blur, bubbles or staining artifacts. In other tasks, they can be coarsely divided into lesion, non-lesion and background. This partition is common across WSI analysis and generalizes across datasets. R1.4 Ablation experiments on CAMELYON16 shows that, compared with the baseline, PG-CIDL without PSD-LFG improves ACC/AUC by +2.86/+3.83, PG-CIDL without CID improves ACC/AUC by +5.71/+2.77, and the full PG-CIDL improves ACC/AUC by +8.57/+6.94.These results confirm that both PSD-LFG and CID also contribute on a public benchmark. Reviewer #2: R2.1 Besides d_reg, we omitted the intra-cluster term d_compact, which minimizes the average distance between instances and cluster centroids, completing the K-means objective (See abstract link: section2 for details). Also, background may has category-related meaning and thus contribute to prediction (e.g., vessel and lymphatic reaction). R2.2 We clarified our paradigm and codes of counterfactual inference: min{L_ce(f(Z_final), y’) + d(Z_final, Z)} in abstract link: section2.Here the minimal optimization generates the smallest perturbed counterfactual representations Z_final while successfully making a counterfactual prediction f(Z_final) to a counterfactual label transition y’. Specifically, y’ is for the pseudo labels from the second argmax of original logits f(Z). R2.3 PSD-constrained grouping and CID can be plug-and-play modules for commonly used MILs. On CAMELYON16, AUC improves by +3.68 for ABMIL and +6.37 for TransMIL. On AMU-LSCC, ABMIL improves by +3.62 ACC / +5.96 AUC. On AMU-CSCC, ABMIL gains +1.89 ACC, and TransMIL gains +0.48 AUC. These show our methods are not tied to one backbone. R2.4 Two private datasets had been released and will be verified when camera-ready. On public CAMELYON16, PG-CIDL achieves 0.8857 ACC / 0.9282 AUC, improving over the strongest baseline by +5.71 ACC / +10.29 AUC. Same for DHMC-LUNG. All methods use the same Swin-T features and evaluation protocol. Thus, the gains cannot be attributed only to private-data overfitting. R2.5 Existing works such as IBMIL and MFC-MIL do introduce SCMs ideas. Our aim is that PG-CIDL explicitly combines: (i) PSD latent factor grouping, (ii) group-level intervention-style effect estimation for semantic disentanglement, and (iii) effect-based decision re-weighting to address spatial, semantic, and decision entanglement within one WSI MIL framework. Reviewer #3: R3.1 PG-CIDL does not claim clinical causal validity but still has useful interpretability since it evaluates how much the prediction changes when each learned group is removed. Regarding K=3, we use it as a coarse pathological prior rather than a rigorous taxonomy. The model separates diagnostic tissue, microenvironment/non-lesion tissue, and background/artifacts. R3.2 We will move the CID idea, dataset statistics and training details to the main/camera-ready version where space permits. We have also separated the anonymous code material for PG-CIDL to improve reproducibility.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a three‑phase disentangled representation learning framework for WSI‑based MIL to reduce spatial, semantic, and decision entanglement. The reviewers agree that the three types of entanglement (spatial, semantic, decision) in existing MIL frameworks are valid and clinically meaningful challenges and recognize the strong empirical results. However, the reviewers also raised concerns about the oversimplified and rigid clustering assumption with a fixed number of clusters (K=3), the unconvincing causal / counterfactual claim, and the reproducibility and reliance on private datasets. Please respond to the main concerns of the reviewers, including the following ones: How does CID handle clustering errors, why is K=3 a sufficient or justified decomposition for all WSIs, how the proxy loss relates to the actual clustering objective and whether the gradient flow correctly optimizes the intended grouping, what is the genuine counterfactual/causal claim in CID, and how does it differ from a simple ablation. | The rebuttal has addressed most concerns of the reviewers and all three reviewers raised the score from weak accept to accept. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After considering the reviews and rebuttal, I recommend acceptance. The authors have adequately addressed the main concerns regarding the grouping strategy, intervention module, and methodological clarity. The rebuttal provides additional technical explanations, ablation studies, and cross-backbone evaluations showing that both proposed components contribute to performance gains. While some aspects, such as the justification of the group number and the discussion of related causal MIL methods, could be better explained in the final version, these are primarily issues of presentation rather than fundamental weaknesses. The method is technically sound, demonstrates consistent improvements on both public and private datasets, and offers a useful combination of semantic grouping and intervention-based interpretability for WSI analysis. Overall, the contribution is meaningful and sufficiently validated to merit acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a well-motivated framework to address multiple forms of entanglement in MIL-based WSI representation learning, including spatial, semantic, and decision entanglement. Reviewers appreciated the overall framework design, the integration of PSD-based metric learning and disentanglement strategies, and the strong experimental performance across multiple datasets. Overall, despite some remaining limitations regarding the causal framing and fixed clustering assumption, the paper presents a technically solid and practically meaningful contribution for interpretable WSI representation learning, supported by comprehensive experiments and improved performance. I support acceptance.

title: Prior-Anchored Debiasing for Long-Tailed Multi-Organ Pathology Report Generation
reviewer_1_strengths: The proposed method is supported by a rigorous evaluation across 11 different cancer types. The paper includes a thoroughly designed ablation study that clearly isolates and justifies the contribution of each individual component.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The necessity of the “meta-report” concept is questionable. Since pathology reports often follow standardized formats, it is unclear if this meta-report is a simple template or a structured representation of specific findings (e. g. , organ-specific mentions, staging). If it aims for the latter, an ontology-based graph approach might be more effective. While prototypes are efficient, they risk losing fine-grained details. Using only 4 prototypes seems insufficient for pathology, where micro-scale patterns (e. g. , Lymphovascular Invasion, LVI) are critical for diagnosis. Compared to methods like PANTHER (using 16 or 32 prototypes), the proposed approach may only capture macro-patterns, which is a significant concern for clinical utility. It is unclear whether the prototypes are organ-specific or universal. If the model relies on organ-specific learning, the claim of addressing “long-tail distributions” across a universal scale may be exaggerated. The authors should clarify the scope and implementation of these prototypes. The authors used a mix of UNI and PLIP. For better consistency and to isolate the contribution of the proposed method, using a single backbone (e. g. , PLIP) throughout the experiments would have been more appropriate.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The motivation is clear and clinically meaningful. Moving from single-organ to multi-organ pathology report generation is a realistic direction, and the observation that a long-tailed organ distribution induces both visual and textual biases is a reasonable framing that has not been explicitly studied before in this task. 2.The decomposition of the problem into two complementary bias sources is clean, and the proposed dual-prior design is conceptually aligned with these two sources. 3.The paper is clearly written and the figures communicate the proposed pipeline effectively.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Evaluation in the experiments relies only on BLEU-Mean, METEOR and ROUGE-L. However, these surface n-gram metrics have been shown to correlate poorly with clinical correctness in medical report generation. Since the central claim of the paper is improved diagnostic reliability on tail-class organs, the absence of any clinical or entity-level metric, and the absence of pathologist evaluation, makes it hard to verify that the method actually mitigates the “linguistically fluent but diagnostically erroneous” failure mode that it explicitly targets. 2.The reported improvements are small and their statistical reliability is not well established. Tail-class absolute gains are also modest and come from very small test sets. Results are reported from a single run without standard deviations, and the significance test uses n=11 organs as independent units rather than repeated runs, which provides limited statistical power. Under this protocol the improvements are not convincingly above noise. 3.No comparison against long-tail learning methods is included. 4.The capacity of VPAB appears insufficient and is not analyzed. Only K=4 prototypes are used to cover diagnostic patterns across 11 histologically heterogeneous organ types, and no sensitivity analysis on K is reported.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The proposed method is reasonable and well-validated. The PriOrGen addresses the distribution bias issue from both visual and text aspects. VPAB successfully compensates for scarce tail-class visual representations, while MRAB independently guards against textual overfitting during the decoding phase. 2.The ablation experiment is well organized and helpful. The paper not only evaluated the contribution of the VPAB and MRAB module, but also demonstrated the influence of hyperparameters like $\rho$ and $\mu$. 3.Code is provided with an anonymous link in the paper.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The proposed method is largely built on existing methods, such as LLMs like Gemini3-Pro and PLIP. While these methods are well-recognized in the field and are generally considered standard, it is still possible that these methods are not reliable in some aspects. A discussion about such influence should be included. 2.While the paper has evaluated the proposed method against multiple baselines, it would still be great if the proposed method were compared with a long-tail distribution-oriented method. Even simply comparing against a vanilla baseline trained with organ-wise balanced sampling can further highlight the contribution of the proposed method.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal

meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper targets multi-organ report generation, which is quite uniquely position compared to single-organ. Specifically, the authors try to solve report generation for multi-organ settings, where organ type follows a long-tailed distribution. The authors propose PriorGen - a dual-prior framework that addresses biases introduced by long tail (visual and textual biases). The authors have evaluated and benchmark on 11 TCGA cancer types. All the reviewers have agreed that this is an important problem setting that has been overlooked before and is well motivated clinically. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem of multi-organ pathology report generation under long-tail distributions. The proposed framework is technically sound and supported by comprehensive experiments. Several concerns were initially raised regarding the interpretation of the meta-report representation, the limited number of prototypes, the lack of clinical evaluation metrics, and missing comparisons with long-tail learning methods.
