title: SlideGuard: WSI Artifact Detection Benchmark
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper is very well written and easy to follow. Its organization is sound. The authors designed the first (soon to-be) publicly available dataset for artifact detection, filling an important gap in the highly unstandardized digital pathology ecosystem. Furthermore, the dataset covers multiple organs (and indications) and species, with data originating from three sources for human WSIs and one source for mouse WSIs. This enables the benchmarking of artifact detection methods in a non-trivial and realistic setting. In addition to slides containing artifacts, the authors also included near-perfect slides, as negative controls. The benchmark itself is convincing; the authors evaluate the main relevant methods, and account for the many discrepancies between existing methods (e. g. pixel-level segmentation of artifacts versus patch-level classification, or inconsistencies in artifact-type labels). The chosen metrics are relevant, and the results section includes comments on the limitations of these metrics in the context of the benchmark. The discussion section is thorough, suggests guidelines to drive the community forward and addresses the limitations of the work (e. g. partial annotation subjectivity).
reviewer_1_weaknesses: While the paper does not suffer from major weaknesses, we believe it could benefit from the following clarifications: The central claim that artifacts « impair the performance of automated algorithms » is currently backed by a single citation from 2021.Given the significant progress of computational pathology in the last 5 years (e. g. the paper cited by the authors does not use any pathology foundation models, which are now the backbone of most modern methods), it would be valuable to include more recent studies. Recent artifact detection methods, for instance, may provide more information on this topic. How the Dice score and other metrics are computed across settings is partially unclear. For instance, the authors state « Artifact detection performance was quantified using class-specific Dice scores, accuracy, precision, and recall. » but accuracy is not computed, and the following sentence can be found slightly below « Due to divergent artifact taxonomies among the benchmarked methods, class-specific precision and Dice score calculations were infeasible. ». This discrepancy likely stems from the fact that « class » equates to artifact type in the second statement, and « class » equates to artifact or not in the first, but this is initially confusing for the reader. Likewise, the subsequent sentence uses the term « label-agnostic recall » to indicate the recall for the artifact class. Standardizing the nomenclature would make the paper easier to read. The authors state « To compare methods producing artifact masks (pixel-level) and those calculating per-patch predictions, ground truth was discretized to each patch-level method’s native grid; a patch was labeled as an artifact if annotation coverage exceeded 25%. » Does this mean that segmentation methods are evaluated with a Dice score computed pixel-wise over the full WSI (or is there a per-patch computation averaged across the slide ?) and that the Dice is computed patch-wise across the full WSI for patch-level classification methods ? Likewise, how was the 25% cut-off chosen ? If possible, given the constrained MICCAI format and available information, it would be interesting to include the magnification used for all benchmarked methods and the sets of classes in the comparison table (Table 1). Additionally (again, if possible), it would be helpful to indicate explicitly the training sources of each of the methods (as opposed to only providing the number) as to enable the detection of a possible over-fitting to the training set artifacts. This would also better contextualize the discussion subsection around the fuzzy mapping between nominal magnification and resolution in MPP. The authors state « High recall for artifact categories not included in a model’s native label set indicates either cross-class false positives or a generalized sensitivity to morphological deviations from artifact-free tissue. ». Having the sets of classes for each method explicitly stated or via an asterisk added to the per-artifact recall table for instance (for the cases where the artifact type does not exist for a given method) would enable the reader to understand the situations in this actually happens compared to situations where the method is successfully able to point-out the specific artifact type.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Motivation: This paper addresses a major challenge in the field of digital pathology. Artifacts are often found in WSIs and there are several automated QC methods (histoQC, pathprofiler, DKL, TCNN, etc.), each with its own limitations. Such a curated dataset would aid in the development of robust artifact-detection and quantification algorithms. Rich dataset: Multi-source, multi-species dataset encompassing 11 artifact categories across 6 tissue types, 2 species, 6 organs, and 4 datasets. Rich pixel-level annotations: 2,116 detailed pixel level annotations for the eleven artifact classes Table 3 highlights variations in performance of different automated QC methods, warranting the need for such a dataset that might help build better QC methods
reviewer_2_weaknesses: o Fig 1 is unclear. The ground truth artifact mask shows the tissue as foreground and the rest as background. In this example, is the entire foreground an artifact? Or does the black region in the center of the mask represent the artifact? o The annotations were performed by a single reader. This may add subjectivity and bias to the dataset. o Although the dataset is valuable, the algorithms developed for evaluation i.e., to segment the tissue or to label the patches we not optimal. This may affect the results: o The tissue detection steps involve basic methods like “intensity thresholding at 200”, which is not a robust approach and the performance can vary with respect to staining variations. o “a patch was labeled as an artifact if annotation coverage exceeded 25%”. The algorithm outputs are at patch level although the annotations are at pixel level leading to loss of information.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1) First Independent third-party benchmark dataset for WSI artifact detection, from multiple sources (4 centers), species (human/mice), tissue types (6), and broad artifact taxonomy (11 artifacts). While annotated from a single expert, this is in line with practices of previous benchmarks for WSI QC quantification (GrandQC, Weng et al., Nature Communications 2024). 2) Breadth of method comparison, with evaluation spanning 7 methods from 2019 to 2024, 5 segmentation models and 2 patch classifiers (TCNN and PathProfiler), with these methods trained on varying data scales and domains. This is a valuable comparison for the community on existing tools, showcasing out-of-the box performance on a real world dataset. 3) Release of a practical standardized benchmarking tool for future QC method evaluation, promising to lower the barrier for future developers to situate their work within a common framework. 4) Importance of findings, that while methods reliably preserve artifact-free tissue, they do not perform consistently in artifact localization tasks across different sources and taxonomies.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1) “The first benchmark to test WSI QC methods” claim is overstated and misleading. GrandQC (Weng et al.) already provides a publicly released annotated test dataset of 318 WSIs across 4 organ types with pixel-level ground truth and a head-to-head comparison of multiple QC tools, making it a de facto benchmark for this task. SlideGuard’s genuine and significant novelty is that it is the first independent benchmark for this task, with a broader diversity of samples (multi-species, multi-center, 11 artifact classes). The authors need to reframe this contribution precisely along these lines, independence and diversity versus scale, and additionally verify and disclose whether any overlap exists between SlideGuard’s TCGA slides and GrandQC’s training set, as this would directly affect the validity of GrandQC’s evaluation within this benchmark. 2) Annotator subjectivity described in the ‘Detection Asymmetry’ paragraph and Conclusions section undermines the reliability of the dataset’s ground truth. This statement directly contradicts the single-annotator protocol: if boundary subjectivity is significant enough to alter or explain systematic performance gaps across all evaluated methods, then the absence of an extra annotator and inter-rater agreement analysis is a critical methodological gap, not a mere limitation. This is especially consequential for a benchmark paper, whose primary contribution is the ground truth itself. While GrandQC also relied on a primary single annotator for the test set, authors explicitly argue on the peer review process file, that inter-rater agreement is less critical for artifact detection due to its relatively objective nature. SlideGuard takes the opposite position by acknowledging annotation subjectivity as a key driver of performance variability, making the absence of inter-rater analysis a self-inflicted and particularly consequential contradiction that the authors must address. 3) At 53 WSIs, the dataset is substantially smaller than comparable benchmarks (GrandQC test set: 318 WSIs). No per-class annotation statistics are reported, making it impossible to assess class imbalance or evaluate whether rare artifact categories are sufficiently represented (should be reported in both table 2 and 3). Given this limited scale, the absence of uncertainty estimates, no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests, makes it difficult to quantify how different performance between methods is. 4) The inference resolution is never specified: the MPP or nominal magnification at which each method processes WSIs is not reported or standardized across the benchmark, despite the authors themselves identifying MPP inconsistency as a key practical limitation in the Discussion. This is a direct internal contradiction that must be resolved. The authors should explicitly state the extraction MPP for each method, clarify whether this is fixed or method-dependent, and discuss how resolution differences across methods may confound the reported performance comparisons. Furthermore, the recommendation to shift from nominal magnification to MPP in the Discussion is presented as a practical requirement but is entirely unsupported by the benchmark itself, no ablation or sensitivity analysis is performed comparing method performance across different MPP values (under the same nominal magnification), which would be the natural way to empirically ground this claim. 5) How sensitive is the performance of patch classifiers to the discretization threshold? An ablation on 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, 50% and 75% might explain how reliable are current results for TCNN and PathProfiler. The choice on 25% is not empirically validated. 6) Table 2 reports Dice scores for all methods without distinguishing between pixel-level spatial overlap Dice for segmentation methods and patch-level F1 score for TCNN and PathProfiler, which is what Dice mathematically reduces to when a single binary label is assigned per patch. These quantities should be clearly and distinctly presented. The authors must explicitly state what metric is being reported for each method type and clearly flag the weaknesses of cross-paradigm comparison.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive feedback. We are encouraged by the reviewers’ positive feedback on SlideGuard’s relevance and have carefully considered each suggestion to improve the manuscript. Below, we address the technical and editorial points raised. Regarding annotator subjectivity: We distinguish between semantic agreement and geometric precision. Artifact classification is an objective task for experienced histotechnicians. However, for artifacts like dust (soft edges) or ink (complex structures), manual polygons lack the pixel-level granularity of machine segmentation. This inherent spatial ambiguity, rather than annotator bias, may limit attainable Dice scores. Addressing magnification used by models: To ensure a fair comparison, models were evaluated using their native resolution requirements. Forcing an incorrect scale would inherently compromise the benchmark. Patch-level methods were provided with their exact requested MPP, whereas pixel-level methods processed the WSIs directly to manage resolution internally. Running tools ‘off-the-shelf’ this way exposes how they handle physical scale inconsistencies across centers, providing a realistic sensitivity analysis. In regard to the comparison modes: Pixel-level methods were evaluated pixel-wise and patch-level methods were evaluated patch-wise using their native output grids. The 25% discretization threshold was chosen empirically based on previous works, and we acknowledge the importance of a sensitivity study in future works. We also acknowledge that patch-level methods benefit from this task simplification, and we explicitly flag the weaknesses of this cross-paradigm comparison in the Results. To further address this, Tables 2 and 3 have been updated in the camera-ready version to group methods by output type to clearly distinguish these evaluation modes. As to the intensity masks: They were manually verified to ensure accurate ROIs. This step solely excludes background, focusing analysis on artifact localization rather than the models’ internal tissue detection. Large-scale datasets in the future will adopt more robust segmentation. We are thankful to the reviewer for pointing it out as a future direction. To address the “first benchmark” phrasing: We have reformulated the claim to more accurately reflect SlideGuard’s contribution as the first independent, cross-species benchmark. SlideGuard’s value lies in its high taxonomic granularity (11 artifact classes) and its inclusion of non-TCGA human and animal samples, providing a guarantee of unseen data samples. As to the expansion of tables: Thank you for the constructive suggestions to expand the comparison in Table 1 (including magnification and artifact types) and to provide a broader analysis of the annotation dataset. However, due to strict page constraints and the inability to include supplementary material, we are unable to accommodate these additions. Furthermore, presenting raw annotation metrics or dataset percentage alone, as a mere numerical addition to Table 3, would be misleading without a thorough contextual discussion of the variations in artifact sizes that we unfortunately cannot fit within the current space limits. Relevant information will, however, be included on the Grand Challenge page of the project. Regarding presentation and editorial clarity: We have expanded the literature review on the downstream impact of artifacts, unified our terminology (consistently using ‘class’, ‘label’, and ‘category’), and improved mask visibility in Figure 1.In Table 3, we also identified the bolding errors post-submission and have corrected the table along with the relevant commentary in the Results to accurately reflect the model rankings. These refinements, along with all other formatting suggestions, will be incorporated into the camera-ready version.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): SlideGuard proposes a heterogeneous multi-source artifact dataset and harmonized evaluation of segmentation- vs patch-QC detectors. The reviewers appreciated the clarity, community needs for standardized quality control benchmarking, and richness of taxonomy/sources. Conscientious limitation discussion on metrics, and partial subjectivity (R2–4). Raised issues include sharpening evidence that artifacts degrade modern pipelines versus a single dated citation plus clarifying Dice/accuracy nomenclature and patch-threshold derivation (R2), overstated “first benchmark” claim versus GrandQC and questions on overlap/train contamination (R4), interplay of annotation subjectivity with single-reader protocol lacking inter-rater study (R4), comparatively small corpus vs some benchmarks lacking uncertainty/per-class prevalence detail (R4), and presentation issues in comparative tables noted as minor polish (R4). The AC read the paper, reviewed it, and agrees that the paper has merit and that the benchmark with the dataset would be of interest to the community. The authors should address the raised concerns in their revised version.

title: Spectral-Semantic Consensus for Few-Shot Whole Slide Image Classification
reviewer_1_strengths: The introduction of a multi-view perspective for text-visual token alignment is a significant technical contribution. This approach helps the model induce more stable and robust representations, which is particularly beneficial in the data-constrained environment of few-shot learning.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The comparison seems potentially biased. Most baselines are standard MIL models that inherently struggle in few-shot scenarios. To claim superiority in few-shot learning, the authors should include more robust few-shot baselines or ensure the comparison is fair. The ablation study regarding uncertainty-guided fusion is insufficient. How does the model behave when the fusion weight is forcefully increased or decreased? A more thorough interpretation of this mechanism’s impact on performance is needed. The mention of SVTC lacks adequate explanation. It is unclear how it contributes to the final performance. An ablation study specifically testing the presence/absence of SVTC would be beneficial. The core strengths of the proposed model over baselines are not clearly articulated. It would be helpful to include a more detailed explanation of the baseline architectures to highlight the specific architectural improvements made in this work. There is a concern that the model relies too heavily on text features. It appears that the text information acts more as a feature engineering tool rather than boosting the weak association between images and labels. The authors should demonstrate that the image features are not merely auxiliary but are substantively integrated with the text.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Novel Problem Formulation: The authors mentioned “discriminative sparsity,” “semantic collapsing,” and “rigid semantic matching” found in existing text-guided WSI classification methods. The authors proposed a text-guided patch selection framework for few-shot WSI classification, which has clinical meaning. 2.Adaptive Dual-Route Patch Selection: The paper seamlessly integrates two complementary strategies. The DBPC module broadens evidence coverage and prevents overfitting by distributing the selection budget across multiple learnable prompts. Simultaneously, the SKP module filters background artifacts by scoring patches against a PCA-derived semantic subspace, acting as a robust structural prior. Crucially, these modules are dynamically balanced via an Uncertainty-guided Fusion mechanism. 3.Rigorous Experiments: The authors conducted experiments on three different datasets on different organs, and utilized a ten-fold cross-validation protocol to report mean and standard deviation, ensuring robust and trustworthy results.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Hyperparameter Sensitivity: The framework introduces specific hyperparameters, such as the number of learnable prompts ($K=5$) , the variance ratio ($\rho$) for SKP , and the divergence loss weight ($\lambda=0.2$). The paper does not provide sensitivity analysis on how varying these values affects cross-dataset generalization. 2.Limited Interpretability of the Spectral Subspace: While the SKP module improves robustness by projecting patches onto a principal semantic subspace, the specific “meaning” of these spectral components can be difficult for clinicians to interpret compared to direct keyword matching. 3.Computational Bottleneck of PCA and Eigendecomposition: The SKP module requires performing eigendecomposition and SVD on text tokens to build the knowledge subspace. This will add additional mathematical preprocessing. It is unknown how much additional computational efforts this method will introduce.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Significance of proposed SSC method is in addressing the fundamental weakness in few-shot MIL approach to WSI classification: a single retrieval query that can miss heterogenous diagnostic cues. The SSC method combines two approaches, DBPC and SKP, to select informative tokens (patches) which are fused and afterwards aggregated via prompt queries through cross-modal attention to produce the slide-level prediction. DBPC selects top-r patches per query. SKP selects top-L patches most aligned with principal subspace spanned by principal components of learnable tokens. Selected tokens (patches) are fused by newly proposed uncertainty-guided fusion method which is based on entropy of DBPC-selected patches. The idea is to fuse DBPC- and SKP-selected patches that are minimally redundant.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: To my understanding, the strength of proposed method described previously seems to be also its main weakness. To be specific, I mean on uncertainty-guided fusion method. It is, however, possible that presentation of this method was not clear enough. In equation (4) authors compute normalized entropy of DBPC scores over N patch embeddings. DBPC-module ratios are computed based on 1-entropy, and SKP-module ratios are computed based on entropy. However, entropy is only computed from DPLC-scores. It is based on idea that SKP module excludes prediction-task irrelevant regions (patches). Ablation study conducted in Figure 3 confirms performance improvement due to use of SKP module. I wonder whether authors considered to compute SKP-module ratios based on entropy computed from SKP scores and then using them for fusion model together with DBPC-module ratios? Corresponding ablation study should be carried out to confirm (reject) this assertion.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. Code will be released. 1.[R1-Q1] Comparison baselines: Great suggestion! We have compared to ViLa-MIL (CVPR 2024), a strong and widely used dedicated few-shot VLM for WSIs. Regarding the comparison to more recent few-shot baselines, we respectfully argue that our main consideration is to maintain the same annotation budget, feature extraction pipeline, data splits, and evaluation protocol. Some recent few-shot WSI methods introduce additional annotation assumptions, e.g., FAST (NeurIPS 2024), or unaligned version of released source codes, e.g., FOCUS (CVPR 2025, see the issue “confusion about text prompt #9” in its official implementation). Besides, since our SSC is a versatile framework rather than being exclusively tailored for few-shot scenarios, for a fair comparison, we evaluate our SSC against diverse WSI-MIL paradigms under the same strictly matched few-shot protocol. Therefore, in our defense, although the baselines are not exhaustive, the current comparison is fair and provides enough informative benchmark. 2.[R1-Q2] DBPC ablation: Excellent question! In our SSC, the fusion weight is a slide-adaptive budget allocation factor derived from DBPC retrieval uncertainty. If the fusion weight is forcefully increased, SSC becomes more prompt-similarity-dominant. This can help when text-image matching is confident. Under high uncertainty, it may over-select visually/textually similar yet incomplete or spurious regions, missing atypical diagnostic evidence. If the fusion weight is forcefully decreased, SSC relies more on the spectral semantic subspace, which can recover patches not captured by direct prompt matching. However, excessive SKP may introduce broadly relevant but less class-discriminative tissue regions. We will clarify this in the revision. 3.[R1-Q3] Contribution of SVTC: We adopt SVTC [21] for better redundant patch elimination. Yet, as claimed in the submission, SVTC [21] is not our proposed contribution. Therefore, we did not conduct ablation study on SVTC. As shown in Fig. 3, we have conducted ablation study on our proposed DBPC and SKP, where both the baseline and our method adopt the same SVTC [21]. 4.[R1-Q4] Core strengths compared to the baseline: Our DBPC module distributes budgets across multiple prompts to capture heterogeneous morphology, which can capture more heterogeneous diagnostic relevant patches, compared to the mean pooling strategy in baseline. Our SKP module injects a textual spectral subspace to structurally filter out noise. Visual information is continuous, which may not be captured by text prompt. Thus, SKP can further capture diversified patches by the alignment on subspace spanned by main semantic directions. 5.[R1-Q5] Text feature reliance: Our SSC does not introduce a text-only shortcut to classification. Text priors are only used to guide visual evidence selection, while the final prediction is made from selected WSI visual patch embeddings. 6.[R2-Q1] Hyperparameter sensitivity: Excellent suggestion! Our SSC achieves performance gains across highly heterogeneous cancer types using the same hyperparameter settings. Optimal hyperparameter tuning may yield better results. 7.[R2-Q2] Interpretability of spectral subspace: SKP is not intended to replace clinician-readable concepts. We will state this robustness–interpretability trade-off as a limitation. 8.[R2-Q3] Computational bottleneck: The cost of PCA in SKP—performed on the text-token matrix—depends on text token count and embedding dimension. Compared to thousands of WSI patches, the text token length is small. 9.[R3] DBPC VS SKP scores: SKP is used as a complementary fallback when DBPC becomes uncertain. 10.[R3] Patch selection: The selection budget of each prompt in DBPC is r, computed by max(1, floor(L/K)). Then, we union the selected K*r patches, making the number of selected patches in DBPC <=L. We will clarify this in the revision.

title: Synergistic Information Disentanglement for Omni-Modal Slide Representation Learning in Computational Pathology
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper tackles a genuinely important problem for multimodal pathology pretraining, and the deployment setup is practical since inference can still be unimodal. 2.The comparison study is reasonably solid, including both standard MIL baselines and several recent pathology foundation models. The gains are also fairly consistent across the few-shot settings. 3.The ablation studies are helpful and make it easier to see that both the architectural choices and the full loss design matter.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The pathology report pipeline deserves a more careful leakage analysis. Even if explicit diagnostic labels are removed, reports can still contain subtype-related wording, biomarker mentions, or other highly label-proximal cues. 2.The empirical comparison is slightly incomplete. In particular, MIRROR [23] is one of the most related papers and should be included in the comparison. 3.The interpretability analysis is interesting, but I do not think the t-SNE plots by themselves establish that the model is really capturing synergistic information.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: (1) The manuscript is clearly articulated and accessible. The figures and visualizations are both high-quality and illustrative. Furthermore, the study is underpinned by a thorough review of existing literature and a well-justified rationale for the proposed approach. (2) The authors perform extensive benchmark few-shot learning experiments on multiple cancer cohorts; the results validate its superiority for downstream analysis in comparison with an excellent choice of state-of-the-art supervised and self-supervised baselines. Detailed ablation studies are well-conducted for demonstrating the effect of each module and strategy design in the proposed method. (3) The design of maximizing the synergistic information of multimodal representation by mutual information is quite interesting, such a design is transferable to multiple scenarios in multimodal representation alignment and fusion. (4) The methodology is presented with clarity and appears reproducible. A significant strength of this work is the exclusive use of public datasets for experimental validation.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: I have identified no significant weaknesses in this work. However, I have provided several comments regarding the literature review, methodology details, and experimental settings in (12) to help improve the paper’s quality.
reviewer_2_rating: (6) Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Clear motivation: The paper rightly points out that standard contrastive learning forces different modalities together, which keeps redundant info but loses complementary signals. Using PID theory makes perfect clinical sense, since diagnosis relies on how modalities combine, not just what they share. 2.Most slide-level SSL papers only do two modalities. This paper jointly integrates WSI, RNA-seq, and pathology reports. 3.The experimental setup strictly follows the TANGLE (k-shot linear probing, 10 random seeds, macro-AUC). The evaluation spans 8 tasks across 5 external cohorts, and the performance is robust.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Mirror[1] also uses a similar idea to fix modality collapse. This paper needs to explain exactly why your PID approach is fundamentally better and add an experimental comparison with Mirror. [1] Wang, T., Fan, J., Zhang, D., Liu, D., Xia, Y., Huang, H., Cai, W.: Mirror: Multi-modal pathological self-supervised representation learning via modality alignment and retention. arXiv preprint arXiv:2503.00374 (2025) 2.Training on around 2,000 TCGA slides is small compared to recent foundation models. Also, testing TCGA-trained models on CPTAC often suffers from site-specific biases. 3.Lack of ablation, please add Image+Gene only and Image+Text only to isolate the contribution of text reports.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal

meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): he reviewers are overall positive about this submission, which proposes a synergistic information disentanglement framework for omni-modal slide representation learning using WSI, transcriptomics, and pathology reports during pretraining while requiring only WSI at inference. The work addresses an important problem in multimodal computational pathology, is clearly presented, and shows strong few-shot performance across multiple cancer cohorts with useful ablation studies and comparisons to several MIL and pathology foundation model baselines. The main remaining concerns are the need for a more careful leakage analysis of pathology reports, clearer positioning and ideally comparison against the closely related MIRROR method, additional modality-combination ablations such as Image+Gene and Image+Text, and more details on text cleaning and hyperparameter selection. Overall, despite these limitations, the methodological idea is interesting, the experimental evidence is reasonably strong, and the paper is likely to make a valuable contribution if the authors adequately address these issues in the final version.

title: TC-SSA: Token Compression via Semantic Slot Aggregation for Gigapixel Pathology Reasoning
reviewer_1_strengths: This manuscript is well organized and follows a clear logical flow. Overall, the contribution of this work is satisfying. The authors have provided an anonymous link to open-source code, demonstrating the reliability and reproducibility of the reported results in this work. The motivation of TC-SSA is quite meaningful to the facing the challenge of gigapixel WSIs when applying large-scale vision and language model in computational pathology.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The boundary of novelty could be clarified more clearly. In this work, several design choices, such as semantic slots and Top-2 routing, appear closely related to techniques commonly used in Mixture-of-Experts in the training of foundation model. It would be helpful for the authors to better clarify how the proposed design specifically adapts in token compression for WSIs. The conceptualization of the “semantic affinity clustering objective” is somewhat confusing. Based on the current formulation, it is difficult to see the relationship with a clustering process. It appears more like a loss design for improving slot balance and routing stability. A more precise conceptualization is needed for the demonstrations of method. Additionally, the loss in equation (2) and (3) are similar with the loss design in MoE, the difference should be emphasized. A more detailed analysis of this hyperparameter auxiliary loss weight λ would help readers better understand the stability and robustness of the proposed loss function (although the authors have provided the conclusion about what will happen when reducing λ). The visualization of Figure 3.It is currently difficult to understand what exactly is being visualized and how this figure supports the conclusion of meaningful semantic slots related to WSIs.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.This manuscript proposes TC-SSA, which leverages learnable semantic slots for efficient patch feature compression, effectively tackling the critical computational bottleneck in gigapixel WSI-level tasks. 2.This manuscript introduces a set of robust regularization terms to mitigate slot collapse and ensure routing stability. 3.This manuscript provides extensive experimental validation on downstream multiple-choice VQA and classification tasks, demonstrating that TC-SSA substantially reduces computational overhead while boosting performance.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The manuscript lacks individual ablation experiments for loss terms. 2.Building on the first weakness, the reviewer is particularly concerned about the validity of the load-balancing loss in this specific domain. In a single WSI, the number of background patches and diagnostically critical patches varies drastically (i.e., extreme inherent imbalance among patches with different semantics). Under such circumstances, is it biologically and methodologically sound to force a uniform distribution across slots? The reviewer strongly suggests an independent ablation study on the load-balancing loss to clarify its actual impact. 3.Figure 3 lacks sufficient explanation. The three different categories of patches do not appear to be well-separated in the visualization based on t-SNE. Furthermore, it is unclear whether the three displayed subplots represent the t-SNE results within three distinct semantic slots. 4.TC-SSA completely discards the learning of the local microenvironment and overall structures. Would this loss of spatial geometry lead to severe performance degradation in some downstream tasks, such as survival prediction? 5.In Section 3 (Ablation Studies), the authors explicitly claim to have conducted experiments replacing the CONCH encoder with the UNI encoder. However, the corresponding numerical results are entirely missing from the manuscript.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Novel formulation of token compression as semantic routing Rather than spatial sampling, patches are routed to learned semantic slots based on content affinity. This aggregates diagnostically relevant regions scattered across the slide; a meaningful departure from prior sampling or attention-pooling approaches. 2.Extreme compression with competitive performance Achieving 78.34% accuracy with only 32 tokens (58× compression) is strong. TC-SSA surpasses the uncompressed SlideChat on Diagnosis (77.14% vs 73.27%), suggesting compression can remove noise and improve signal for reasoning tasks. 3.Principled regularization for routing stability The auxiliary loss addressing slot collapse is well-motivated and empirically validated; performance degrades when removed, confirming it’s necessary rather than added complexity. 4.Consistent generalization Strong results across VQA benchmarks, MIL classification, different encoders (CONCH, UNI), and zero-shot transfer suggest the approach is robust rather than benchmark-specific. 5.Practical efficiency O(N·K) complexity with K=32 makes deployment tractable under real clinical memory and latency constraints
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Limited comparison with learnable compression methods Baselines are sampling-based (LLaVA-Med, Quilt-LLaVA) or uncompressed (SlideChat). Comparison with other learnable approaches; Perceiver-style cross-attention, Q-Former, or cited methods like LOC-PATH [7] and WSISum [20]; is missing. 2.Unexplained Microscopy performance gap TC-SSA underperforms SlideChat on Microscopy (81.94% vs 87.64%) but this isn’t analyzed. Why does semantic aggregation lose fine-grained morphological information? 3.Lack of qualitative analysis No visualization of patch-to-slot routing, failure cases, or slot specialization. The t-SNE (Figure 3) is too coarse to validate semantic grouping claims. 4.Arbitrary hyperparameter selection K=32 is chosen empirically with no guidance on scaling with slide complexity. The K=128 degradation (“over-fragmentation”) isn’t explained. 5.Incomplete efficiency evaluation Only FLOPs reported, no inference latency or memory usage despite clinical deployment claims.

author_feedback: We thank the ACs and reviewers for constructive feedback. We are deeply encouraged by your recognition, especially: 1) the novel semantic routing design for WSI token compression; 2) strong efficiency with high compression and competitive performance; 3) effective regularization for stable routing; and 4) extensive experiments and reproducible results. And, we have provided detailed clarifications and additional context to the primary concerns: 1.Figure 3 Explanation (R1W4, R2W3, R3W3). Each subplot corresponds to a different TCGA cohort. Each point is a patch embedding projected via t-SNE, with each color representing one semantic slot. The visualization shows patches routed to the same slot form coherent clusters across datasets, suggesting the gate consistently groups similar tissue patterns (tumor, stroma, necrosis). 2.Missing Results and Baselines (R2W5, R3W1). We clarify Table 2 uses UNI encoder as our ablation study. We now directly compare table 2 TCGA-BRCA with WSISum[20], which uses CONCH. We report comparisons using its cited baseline: ABMIL Full WSI scores 0.858 vs. WSISum 0.874; TransMIL Full WSI scores 0.843 vs. WSISum 0.818.Which confirm that our baselines are stronger representatives and that the cited methods do not outperform standard pooling on these benchmarks. Besides, we result LOC-PATH[7] achieving only 51.9% accuracy on SlideBench zero-shot, far below TC-SSA’s 78.34%. 3.Difference with MoE (R1W1). MoE routes tokens to expert networks, retaining the original sequence length with only Top-K experts active per token. TC-SSA routes patches to semantic slots for information compression (K«N) via weighted pooling(Eq. 1). Critically, all K slots are active outputs that participate in downstream reasoning, unlike MoE’s partial expert activation. TC-SSA borrows the routing intuition from MoE but repurposes it for semantic consolidation, not selective computation. 4.Semantic Affinity Clustering and Load-Balancing (R1W2, R2W1,2). We do not perform explicit clustering, patches with similar semantics naturally aggregate into the same slot as an emergent behavior of routing. L_switch is a soft regularizer that only penalizes the degenerate case where patches flood into one slot, it does not force equal distribution. The gate can still assign background patches to few slots while diagnostic regions occupy others. Without L_switch, the gate collapses: reducing λ causes the last 5 slots to receive nearly no patches. We will revise terminology to semantic slot regularization. 5.Loss Ablation and λ (R1W3, R2W4). Many thanks for this suggestion. We provide additional analysis: λ=0 yields 76.29% accuracy, while λ=0.5 yields 78.75%, confirming that increasing λ improves performance. We argue that when λ is too small, patches concentrate in only a few slots, under-utilizing the full semantic capacity. Entropy weight 0.5 and α=10^-4 follow standard sparse routing practice for numerical stability. 6.Spatial Geometry and Microscopy Gap (R2W4, R3W2). Spatial information is not entirely discarded. Each patch is extracted from a specific spatial location, so its embedding already captures local context. The impact of compression is task-dependent. Microscopy relies on fine-grained morphological detail, where compression incurs a 5.7% gap and outperforms all other compressed methods (vs. MedDr: 73.30%). Diagnosis relies on overall tissue composition, where TC-SSA (77.14%) surpasses the uncompressed SlideChat (73.27%). 7.K and Efficiency (R3W4,5). After extracting the local and global features of WSIs, the average response time was within 1 second, and GPU memory consumption was approximately 15GB(Slidechat 27GB). K=32 is validated by ablation (Figure 4): stable for K ∈ {16, 32, 64}, with degradation at K=128 due to over-fragmentation. TC-SSA’s O(NK) complexity guarantees tractable clinical inference. Thanks again for your effort! If you find our response satisfactory, could you please consider improving our score?

title: Think Global, Look Focal: Dual-Stream Retrieval-Augmented Pathology Report Generation for Whole Slide Images
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The architectural design is highly intuitive and aligns seamlessly with real-world clinical workflows. Decoupling the visual processing into a global stream (for tissue architecture) and a focal stream (for cellular details) is an elegant solution to the unique challenges posed by gigapixel WSIs. 2.The transition from unstructured raw corpora to a structured, CAP-protocol-guided atomic knowledge bank significantly reduces non-diagnostic redundancy. Coupled with the ACG module, which uses temperature-scaled softmax to calibrate confidence, the model effectively filters out irrelevant priors and curbs factual hallucinations. 3.The experimental results are convincing. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance not only on traditional NLP metrics (e. g. , a 10.4% relative improvement in BLEU-4) but also on clinical classification metrics (F1 score of 0.926 for subtype prediction) and factual correctness ($Fact_{ent}$). The ablation studies clearly isolate and validate the individual contributions of the dual-stream architecture, VPA, and ACG components.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The evaluation is exclusively conducted on the PathText (BRCA) benchmark, which focuses solely on breast cancer. Because morphological features and diagnostic complexities vary drastically across different organs and cancer types (e. g. , lung or prostate cancer), the lack of multi-center or multi-organ cross-validation makes it difficult to assess the true generalizability of the framework. 2.The retention ratio ($\kappa$) for the focal stream is fixed at 0.6.Given that the proportion of diagnostically relevant tissue—such as tumor bed size—fluctuates wildly from slide to slide, a fixed ratio might discard critical micro-morphological details in slides with extensive lesions, or conversely, introduce background noise in slides with extremely localized focal points. An adaptive retention mechanism would make the methodology more robust. 3.The reliance on the CAP protocol to construct the diagnostic memory bank is effective here, but it poses scalability challenges. The authors do not adequately discuss how this approach would translate to rare diseases or pathologies that lack standardized, well-documented reporting templates, which could result in high manual construction costs in broader clinical applications.

title: Through the Schrödinger Bridge: Benchmarking Antemortem Image Restoration from Postmortem Autolysis to Enhance Forensic Diagnostics
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Novel and clinically relevant problem formulation The paper addresses an important and underexplored challenge in forensic histopathology. The distinction between autolysis restoration and conventional image translation is clearly articulated and well-motivated. 2.Well-designed dataset with strong practical grounding The AutoPath dataset is a significant contribution. The use of spatially adjacent tissue blocks to construct homologous yet unpaired samples is a thoughtful and realistic solution to the lack of paired data. 3.Conceptually appropriate modeling choice The use of Schrödinger Bridge to model stochastic, irreversible degradation is well aligned with the problem characteristics. The decision to remove structural consistency constraints is also justified and differentiates this work from standard unpaired translation methods. 4.Clinically meaningful evaluation beyond FID The paper convincingly shows that lower FID does not correspond to better diagnostic quality. The proposed slide-level diagnostic distribution consistency is a strong contribution and more aligned with real-world forensic practice. 5.Comprehensive evaluation (quantitative + human + case-level) The combination of patch-level metrics, expert validation, and slide-level consistency provides a more holistic evaluation than typical generative modeling papers.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Limited methodological novelty beyond adaptation of SB framework While the formulation is well motivated, the model itself appears to be an adaptation of existing neural Schrödinger Bridge approaches with adversarial alignment. The primary novelty lies more in task formulation and evaluation rather than algorithmic innovation. 2.Insufficient implementation details and reproducibility concerns Key aspects of the method are under-specified, including model architecture, training schedule, SB loss implementation, and hyperparameters. This limits reproducibility. 3.Evaluation relies on a potentially weak intermediate classifier The slide-level evaluation depends on a classifier trained with ~300 annotated patches. The robustness and calibration of this classifier are not sufficiently validated, raising concerns about the reliability of WSDC/WKL metrics. 4.Limited statistical rigor in expert evaluation The expert validation results are promising but lack statistical analysis (e. g. , inter-rater agreement, confidence intervals, significance testing). The evaluation protocol may also introduce forced-choice bias. 5.Risk of hallucination and clinical misinterpretation not fully addressed Since the task does not enforce structural fidelity, the model may generate plausible but incorrect morphology. The paper does not sufficiently discuss the potential risks of such hallucinations in forensic diagnosis. 6.Limited dataset scope and generalization The dataset is restricted to liver tissue and a relatively small cohort (69 cases). It is unclear how well the method generalizes to other organs, magnifications, or varying degrees of autolysis. Baselines may not be sufficiently strong or recent 7.Comparisons are mainly against GAN-based unpaired methods. Stronger diffusion-based or medical-specific baselines would strengthen the claims.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.High Novelty and Forensic/Clinical Significance: Unlike previous “bypass” strategies that rely on specialized equipment (e.g., virtual staining via autofluorescence microscopy), this paper tackles the most challenging and common issue head-on: restoring routine H&E slides that have suffered from autolytic degradation. The introduction of this task fills a critical gap in the field and has immense practical application value. 2.Clever Dataset Design: The “homologous yet unpaired” data collection strategy elegantly addresses the impossibility of acquiring paired Ground Truth due to the destructive nature of tissue preparation. This provides an excellent and rigorous experimental paradigm for future research in this domain. 3.Reasonable Methodological Choice: Given that autolysis inherently destroys cellular structures, traditional unpaired translation methods relying on cycle consistency (e.g., CycleGAN) are fundamentally unsuitable. The authors’ choice to utilize the Schrödinger Bridge to model the stochastic dynamics between complex, structurally disparate distributions is logically sound and perfectly tailored to the task’s characteristics.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Insufficient Quantitative Metrics: The current evaluation lacks standard distribution-level metrics for generative models (e.g., FID, KID) to objectively measure image quality. Furthermore, a subjective evaluation by professional pathologists (e.g., Mean Opinion Score or a Turing Test) is missing, which is crucial for assessing morphological fidelity and the presence of generative artifacts. 2.Lack of Downstream Validation: The paper does not evaluate whether the restored images actually recover diagnostic value. Including a standard computational pathology task—such as nuclei instance segmentation or lesion classification—on the restored images is essential to prove the practical and clinical utility of the proposed method. 3.Limited Scope (Liver Tissue Only): The experiments are exclusively conducted on liver tissue. Since different organs (e.g., kidney, brain, heart) exhibit vastly different autolysis mechanisms and morphological changes, the generalizability of the proposed framework to other tissue types remains unverified.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Novel problem formulation: The paper defines an important and underexplored task in computational pathology—autolysis restoration for forensic diagnostics—which is both clinically relevant and technically challenging. Dataset contribution: The AutoPath dataset is a valuable contribution. The use of adjacent tissue blocks to approximate homologous but unpaired samples is a thoughtful and practical design that reflects real-world constraints. Principled modeling approach: Framing the problem as a Schrödinger Bridge is theoretically well-motivated for modeling stochastic, irreversible morphological degradation. This is a strong methodological choice for unpaired translation with large domain shifts. Clinically aligned evaluation: The paper correctly identifies limitations of FID and introduces a slide-level diagnostic distribution consistency framework, which is more meaningful for clinical applications. Inclusion of expert evaluation: The use of board-certified forensic pathologists for blinded evaluation adds credibility and relevance to the results. Comprehensive evaluation pipeline: The combination of patch-level metrics, expert validation, and slide-level consistency provides a multi-faceted evaluation strategy. Overall, the combination of a new task, dataset, and clinically motivated evaluation makes this a meaningful contribution to the field.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Limited dataset scale and diversity: The dataset consists of 69 cases from a single organ (liver), which may limit generalizability across tissues, disease types, and forensic scenarios. Weak supervision and label dependency in evaluation: The slide-level evaluation relies on a classifier trained on a relatively small number of annotated patches (~300), which may introduce bias and affect the reliability of the diagnostic distribution consistency metric. Lack of strong quantitative improvement: The method does not achieve the best FID score and the improvement in expert preference (23.81%) is relatively modest, raising questions about the magnitude of practical gains. Ambiguity in restoration validity: Since autolysis is irreversible, there is no ground truth for restored images. While the authors acknowledge this, the framework still assumes that generated images are diagnostically meaningful without rigorous validation beyond preference-based evaluation. Risk of hallucination in generative model: The Schrödinger Bridge model may introduce plausible but incorrect morphological structures, which could mislead downstream diagnosis. This risk is not deeply analyzed. Evaluation depends on downstream classifier: Slide-level consistency metrics rely on a trained classifier, making the evaluation indirect and dependent on classifier performance rather than purely on restoration quality. More importantly, the absence of ground truth for restoration combined with reliance on indirect evaluation metrics makes it difficult to assess whether the generated images are diagnostically correct or merely visually plausible.
